Computational: in-house retrobiosynthesis tool with 84 SMARTS reaction rules derived from KEGG third-level EC numbers (ChemAxon Reactor JChem 19.9.0 named as alternative); PubChemPy v1.0.4 MeSH Tree lookup; RDT v1.5.1; SWISS-MODEL homology modeling; AutoDock Vina v1.1.2 docking; BLASTP v2.10.1 against nr (250 homologous sequences).
analysis_methods.notes: No statistical significance testing reported; fold-changes and percent improvements are descriptive.

outcomes.value: In vitro: VlmD converted 12/13 precursors (glycine->methylamine failed); near or above 80% conversion for L-2-aminobutyrate, L-norvaline, L-valine, L-isovaline, L-isoleucine, 1-aminocyclohexanecarboxylic acid. In vivo feeding (PA01): 10/12 SCPAs produced (ethylamine 76.28, n-propylamine 873.31, iso-propylamine 337.57, n-butylamine 979.17, iso-butylamine 1289.18, (R)-sec-butylamine 936.70, iso-amylamine 1052.36, 2-methylbutylamine 1015.75, cyclopentylamine 264.03, cyclohexylamine 105.82 mg/L); n-amylamine and benzylamine not produced (precursors L-norleucine and L-2-phenylglycine poorly utilized). De novo from glucose: EA01 2.89 mg/L ethylamine with 22.78 mg/L L-alanine byproduct; iBA01 1155.74 mg/L iso-butylamine with no L-valine byproduct (vs 524.91 mg/L L-valine for NC02); iAA01 93.23 mg/L iso-amylamine with 991.23 mg/L L-leucine and 759.89 mg/L iso-butylamine byproducts. Fed-batch: iBA01 8.63 g/L iso-butylamine (productivity 0.21 g/L/h, yield 0.062 g/g); iBA02 10.67 g/L (0.36 g/L/h, yield 0.057 g/g, max OD600 60.5 vs 37.9 for iBA01) without amino-acid/vitamin supplementation. Enzyme engineering: V94I variant 5.69 mg/L ethylamine, 96.9% above EA01.
outcomes.notes: Author interpretations flagged as inference: 'VlmD has a strong driving force' (results_p034) and byproduct-attribution reasoning for iAA01 (results_p037, uses 'likely/might') are author_interpretation, not causally validated.

experiments.purpose: Design biosynthetic pathways for 15 SCPAs: retrobiosynthesis (84 reaction rules) followed by precursor selection (molecular type = amino acid; functional-group relative position matching VlmD's known substrates).
experiments.intervention: Computational pathway design; no wet-lab intervention.
experiments.conditions: In-house retrobiosynthesis tool; PubChemPy MeSH Tree; RDT v1.5.1; code at bitbucket.org/kaistsystemsbiology/retro-precursor-selection.
experiments.readout: 4-21 predicted precursors per SCPA; best amino-acid precursor identified for 13/15 SCPAs; tert-butylamine and aniline excluded (no suitable amino-acid precursor).
experiments.analysis: Retrosynthesis + structural filtering; all amino-acid precursors mapped to EC 4.1.1.- (reaction rule #51).
experiments.outcome: Pathway designs for 13 SCPAs; VlmD selected as proof-of-concept promiscuous decarboxylase.

ddr_annotation.decision_type_rationale: Q1 pass (active design choice defining all subsequent constructs), Q2 pass (this study updated reaction rules and ran the analysis), Q3 pass (determined which precursors/enzyme were tested downstream).
ddr_annotation.design_action_rationale: Pathway design/elucidation: retrobiosynthesis identified single-step decarboxylation routes and the precursor selection step fixed the amino-acid precursor per SCPA.
ddr_annotation.trigger_observation: Bio-based SCPA production absent despite industrial need; retrobiosynthesis predicted single enzymatic conversion from amino-acid precursors for all 15 SCPAs.
ddr_annotation.evidence_grading_rationale: Computational prediction (retrobiosynthesis tool + database filters); predictive, required experimental confirmation which was obtained downstream (EXP-01/02).
ddr_annotation.reason_nature_rationale: Paper explicitly states the rationale: amino-acid pathways are well characterized and carry high flux; decarboxylation irreversibility provides a driving force; functional-group position relative to the reaction center affects reaction feasibility and enzyme active-site binding.
ddr_annotation.generalizable_rule: When designing biosynthetic routes for a family of structurally related chemicals in E. coli, filter retrobiosynthesis-predicted precursors to amino acids whose amine/carboxyl groups sit at the same positions relative to the reaction-center carbon as the chosen promiscuous decarboxylase's known substrates, because amino-acid metabolism sustains high precursor flux and matched functional-group geometry preserves catalytic compatibility.
alternatives_considered: amino alcohols, other SCPAs and alkyl-CoA precursors - rejected: poorly characterized pathways
hydrocarbon precursors - rejected: short-chain hydrocarbon production considered harder than amino acids
tert-butylamine and aniline - dropped: no amino-acid precursor with matching functional-group positions

ddr_annotation.trigger_observation: PA01 feeding gave the highest in vivo titer for iso-butylamine (1289.18 mg/L), and an L-valine-overproducing chassis was already available.
ddr_annotation.evidence_grading_rationale: Measured titers in flask, later confirmed in fed-batch.
ddr_annotation.reason_nature_rationale: Paper explicitly states the Val (pKBRilvBNCED) strain and plasmid were previously developed/obtained from the earlier study (ref 21); the design step is reuse of an existing overproducer chassis.

experiments.purpose: De novo iso-amylamine production from glucose.
experiments.intervention: Additional overexpression of leuABCD (L-leucine biosynthesis) on pTac15-vlmDopt-pTac-leuABCD (strain iAA01).
experiments.conditions: NM2 without L-leucine; 30 C, 200 rpm, 48 h flask.
experiments.readout: Iso-amylamine, L-leucine, iso-butylamine titers (Fig. 6c, Supplementary Fig. 4).
experiments.analysis: Mean +/- s.d.
experiments.outcome: 93.23 mg/L iso-amylamine; byproducts 991.23 mg/L L-leucine and 759.89 mg/L iso-butylamine. Authors attribute L-leucine accumulation to suboptimal VlmD conversion and iso-butylamine to VlmD preference for L-valine generated from 2-ketoisovalerate (author_interpretation, 'likely/might' - not causally validated).

ddr_annotation.decision_type_rationale: Q1 pass (leuABCD overexpression), Q2 pass (constructed here), Q3 pass (revealed VlmD substrate-preference bottleneck informing future work).
ddr_annotation.design_action_rationale: Precursor supply enhancement: elevate intracellular L-leucine as the direct precursor of iso-amylamine.
ddr_annotation.trigger_observation: Iso-amylamine production requires L-leucine precursor; leuABCD genes are all involved in L-leucine biosynthesis.
ddr_annotation.evidence_grading_rationale: Measured product and byproduct titers.
ddr_annotation.reason_nature_rationale: Paper explicitly states leuABCD were overexpressed to increase the precursor L-leucine because they constitute the L-leucine biosynthesis pathway.
ddr_annotation.generalizable_rule: When producing an L-leucine-derived amine from glucose in E. coli, overexpress the leuABCD operon to raise L-leucine precursor supply, because these genes catalyze the committed steps of L-leucine biosynthesis; note that a promiscuous decarboxylase with higher activity toward L-valine will partially divert flux to the valine-derived amine.

experiments.purpose: Enhance iso-butylamine production by scale-up of iBA01 to fed-batch.
experiments.intervention: Fed-batch fermentation in 6.6 L bioreactor (2 L NM3), pH-stat 7.0 with ammonia, DO 40%, glucose feeding when residual glucose < 3 g/L.
experiments.conditions: 30 C; NM3 with L-Ile/L-Leu/D-pantothenate supplementation (auxotrophic host).
experiments.readout: OD600, glucose, iso-butylamine time profiles (Fig. 7a).
experiments.analysis: Titer/productivity/yield calculation.
experiments.outcome: 8.63 g/L iso-butylamine, productivity 0.21 g/L/h, yield 0.062 g/g (6.50-fold over flask).

ddr_annotation.decision_type_rationale: Q1 pass (fermentation-condition change), Q2 pass, Q3 pass (established the process baseline against which iBA02 was compared).
ddr_annotation.design_action_rationale: Fermentation/process step: fed-batch with DO and pH control to boost titer.
ddr_annotation.trigger_observation: iBA01 showed efficient iso-butylamine production without L-valine byproduct in flask cultivation.
ddr_annotation.evidence_grading_rationale: Measured fermentation profile.
ddr_annotation.reason_nature_rationale: No explicit rationale given for the specific NM3 formulation, DO setpoint (40%) or feeding trigger; presented as standard process optimization.

experiments.purpose: Remove iBA01 auxotrophies while retaining competing-pathway repression, then produce iso-butylamine without supplementation.
experiments.host: E. coli WLGBH (pKBRilvBNCED) - parental strain of Val with intact ilvA/leuA/panB
experiments.intervention: Synthetic sRNA knockdown of ilvA, leuA and panB via pTac15-vlmDopt-anti-ilvA-leuA-panB (strain iBA02), instead of the gene knockouts used in the Val strain.
experiments.conditions: Fed-batch as EXP-06 but NM3 without L-Ile/L-Leu/D-pantothenate (medium and feed).
experiments.readout: OD600, glucose, iso-butylamine profiles (Fig. 7b).
experiments.analysis: Titer/productivity/yield; max OD comparison.
experiments.outcome: 10.67 g/L iso-butylamine, productivity 0.36 g/L/h, yield 0.057 g/g (slightly lower than iBA01's 0.062), max OD600 60.5 (59.6% higher than iBA01's 37.9), no amino-acid/vitamin supplementation.

ddr_annotation.decision_type_rationale: Q1 pass (sRNA knockdown construct), Q2 pass (plasmid assembled in this study from ref-32 cassettes), Q3 pass (yielded the best-performing, prototrophic production strain).
ddr_annotation.design_action_rationale: Competing-pathway blocking: repress ilvA/leuA/panB to redirect flux toward L-valine/iso-butylamine.
ddr_annotation.trigger_observation: iBA01 (Val chassis) is auxotrophic for L-Ile, L-Leu and D-pantothenate because ilvA, leuA and panB were deleted to remove competing pathways - a critical industrial bioprocess problem.
ddr_annotation.evidence_grading_rationale: Measured fed-batch titer, productivity, yield and cell density improvements.
ddr_annotation.reason_nature_rationale: Stated logic: knockdown rather than knockout retains residual pathway activity, eliminating auxotrophy while still dampening competing fluxes; the sRNA delivery method itself is taken from ref 32.
ddr_annotation.generalizable_rule: When competing-pathway knockouts (ilvA, leuA, panB) cause auxotrophies in an L-valine-pathway-derived iso-butylamine production strain, replace them with synthetic sRNA-mediated knockdown of the same genes, because partial repression preserves prototrophic growth while still redirecting carbon flux toward the product.
alternatives_considered: gene knockouts as in Val (pKBRilvBNCED) - rejected because they cause the auxotrophies being solved

experiments.purpose: Improve VlmD activity toward L-alanine to enhance ethylamine production (proof-of-concept enzyme engineering).
experiments.host: E. coli WL3110 (12 strains, each overexpressing one vlmD variant + alaDopt)
experiments.intervention: Rational single-point mutagenesis of VlmD: homology model (SWISS-MODEL, template GAD67 PDB 2OKJ) + PLP-L-alanine docking (AutoDock Vina) identified 6 active-site residues; 12 candidate substitutions (V94I/L, V114I/L, T397A/V, W399L, S431T/V/L, D515K/N) selected from 250 BLASTP homologs; introduced by site-directed mutagenesis.
experiments.conditions: Flask culture as EA01 (MR + 20 g/L glucose, 37 C, 48 h).
experiments.readout: Ethylamine titer per variant (Fig. 8b).
experiments.analysis: Mean +/- s.d.; percent improvement vs EA01.
experiments.outcome: Best variant V94I: 5.69 mg/L ethylamine, +96.9% vs EA01 (2.89 mg/L); titer still low in absolute terms.

ddr_annotation.decision_type_rationale: Q1 pass (point mutations), Q2 pass, Q3 pass (demonstrated a transferable route to improve VlmD toward poor substrates).
ddr_annotation.design_action_rationale: Rate-limiting enzyme engineering: VlmD's low activity toward L-alanine was the identified bottleneck in EA01.
ddr_annotation.trigger_observation: EA01 secreted more L-alanine (22.78 mg/L) than ethylamine (2.89 mg/L); VlmD showed its lowest in vitro conversion on L-alanine among the 12 working substrates.
ddr_annotation.evidence_grading_rationale: Mutation selection rested on a homology model (19.76% sequence identity template) and docking predictions - predictive, required experimental confirmation; confirmation then obtained by flask titers (硬 outcome data), but the design-stage evidence is predictive.
ddr_annotation.reason_nature_rationale: Paper states an explicit structural mechanism: L-alanine is smaller than VlmD's preferred substrates, so introducing bulkier residues reduces active-site volume and increases interaction probability with PLP-L-alanine.
ddr_annotation.generalizable_rule: When a PLP-dependent decarboxylase shows poor activity toward a substrate smaller than its preferred substrates, mutate active-site residues contacting the ligand to bulkier amino acids drawn from homolog-sequence variation, because reducing active-site volume increases contacts with the smaller substrate (demonstrated for VlmD/ethylamine only).

unsupported_values: Design, construct and tune bifunctional (positive- and negative-response) glycolysis-flux biosensors based on the Cra-FBP pair that sense intracellular fructose-1,6-diphosphate (FBP) and dynamically regulate glycolysis flux, then apply them to balance biosynthesis of mevalonate (MVA) and N-acetylglucosamine (GlcNAc) in Escherichia coli.

Because intracellular FBP concentration is linearly related to glycolysis flux (via FBP feedforward activation of pyruvate kinase), a Cra/FBP-based transcriptional biosensor can report flux in vivo and drive autonomous, timely dynamic repression/activation of pathway genes, outperforming static knockout and IPTG-induced CRISPRi control.
E. coli BW25113 (control/parent for biosensor characterization and deficiency-strain comparison)
BW-pfkA, BW-ptsG, BW-pykF (single-gene deficiency strains used for biosensor validation)
BW-Pzwf::P23109 (zwf promoter replaced by P23109; non-regulated MVA control)
BW-PMT (pfkA promoter replaced by Ppam from pL19), BW-PR (pfkA promoter replaced by Ppar from pL25)
DN5 (modified DH5alpha, knockout of nag, ackA, poxB, ldhA, nan; constructed in previous studies)
DN5-IM, DN5-PM (pfkA promoter replaced by Ppam/Ppar), DN5-GM (pBacm), DN5-GAR (pBacar), DN5-IMM (DN5-IM + pBacm), DN5-IMAR (figure caption only)

Genomic promoter replacements: Pzwf -> P23109; PpfkA -> Ppam (pL19) or Ppar (pL25). Plasmid constructs: pL01-pL10/pL15-pL18 positive-response biosensors, pL19-pL30 negative-response biosensors, pL35 carrying Cra with amino acid mutations at positions 57, 58, 59, 60 under P23102; pBacm (glmS under PM23107 from pL09), pBacar (glmS under PR23107-cra from pL18 plus cra with P23102). DN5 knockout set: nag, ackA, poxB, ldhA, nan (prior work).

Genome promoter replacement (zwf, pfkA loci); construction of plasmid-based Cra/TFBS biosensor circuits; tuning via (1) core promoter strength, (2) TFBS position on promoter, (3) Cra-box sequence affinity, (4) Cra expression level (overexpression), (5) Cra ligand-binding affinity by site mutagenesis (aa 57-60); Hill-function-guided quantitative tuning; dynamic promoter swapping to create FBP-responsive repression of pfkA and activation of glmS.
Biosensor characterization: BW25113 harboring each biosensor plasmid (pL01-pL10, pL15-pL18, pL19-pL30, pL35), dose-response series with extracellular FBP
Deficiency-strain validation: BW-pfkA, BW-ptsG, BW-pykF vs BW25113, all harboring pL19
MVA: BW-Pzwf::P23109 (non-regulated), BW-PMT, BW-PR (shake flask; BW-PR also 1-L fermenter)
GlcNAc: DN5, DN5-PM, DN5-IM, DN5-GM, DN5-GAR, DN5-IMM, DN5-IMAR

BW25113 (fluorescence reference in Fig. 4); CK- (no pL18 plasmid), CK (0 g/L acetate, 0 mM FBP), and 0 mM FBP + 10 g/L acetate baseline in Fig. 2D; non-regulated strain BW-Pzwf::P23109 (MVA control); DN5 (GlcNAc control, 0.46 g/L); static-knockout BW-delta-pfkA EP-bifido strain and IPTG-CRISPRi EP-bifido strain (Li et al. 2021) as prior-art benchmarks.

Shake-flask fermentation for strain comparison; 1-L fermenter for BW-PR scale-up; glucose as sole carbon source in GlcNAc experiments; biosensor strains cultured 18 h before fluorescence detection; BW-PR reached stationary phase after 12 h; intracellular FBP in BW-PR dropped after 15 h.
Extracellular FBP added at 0.001-400 mM together with 10 g/L acetate for pL18 dose-response (Fig. 2D); no chemical inducer used for dynamic control (autonomous FBP sensing).
Fluorescence measured at 18 h of culture (Fig. 4); stationary phase after 12 h (BW-PR shake flask); intracellular FBP dropped suddenly after 15 h; fermenter cultivation 120 h.

Biosensor fluorescence output (dose-response curves); intracellular FBP concentration measurement; pfkA in vivo mRNA level; specific glucose consumption rate; specific growth rate; MVA and GlcNAc titers; acetate/byproduct profiling.

Hill function fitting of dose-response curves; derivation of dynamic range and threshold EC50; linear correlation analysis of intracellular FBP vs glucose consumption rate, growth rate and fluorescence; mRNA-level comparison between regulated and non-regulated strains.

Tuned negative-response biosensor pL19 detects intracellular FBP over ~0-50 mmol/g DCW, covering the reported physiological 0-31 mM/g DCW range; fluorescence of BW-pfkA, BW-ptsG, BW-pykF was 11.32, 7.13, 1.11x BW25113 at 18 h (order BW-pfkA > BW-ptsG > BW-pykF > BW25113). MVA: BW-PR produced 73.31 g/L MVA in shake flask (carbon yield 63.00 mol%, highest shake-flask MVA to date per authors) with <0.1 g/L acetate and no other byproducts; BW-PMT <2.47 g/L acetate; 111.3 g/L MVA after 120 h in 1-L fermenter with no by-products. GlcNAc: DN5-IM 8.65 g/L vs DN5 0.46 g/L; DN5-GM 6.33 and DN5-GAR 7.98 g/L; DN5-IMM 8.63 g/L; simultaneous pfkA repression + glmS activation gave no obvious titer increase over single regulation. Dynamic control outperformed IPTG-CRISPRi benchmark (8.53 g/L, Li et al. 2021; 0.12x of BW-PR).

unsupported_values: Design, construct and tune bifunctional (positive- and negative-response) glycolysis-flux biosensors based on the Cra-FBP pair that sense intracellular fructose-1,6-diphosphate (FBP) and dynamically regulate glycolysis flux, then apply them to balance biosynthesis of mevalonate (MVA) and N-acetylglucosamine (GlcNAc) in Escherichia coli.

Because intracellular FBP concentration is linearly related to glycolysis flux (via FBP feedforward activation of pyruvate kinase), a Cra/FBP-based transcriptional biosensor can report flux in vivo and drive autonomous, timely dynamic repression/activation of pathway genes, outperforming static knockout and IPTG-induced CRISPRi control.
E. coli BW25113 (control/parent for biosensor characterization and deficiency-strain comparison)
BW-pfkA, BW-ptsG, BW-pykF (single-gene deficiency strains used for biosensor validation)

DN5 (modified DH5alpha, knockout of nag, ackA, poxB, ldhA, nan; constructed in previous studies)
DN5-IM, DN5-PM (pfkA promoter replaced by Ppam/Ppar), DN5-GM (pBacm), DN5-GAR (pBacar), DN5-IMM (DN5-IM + pBacm), DN5-IMAR (figure caption only)

Genomic promoter replacements: Pzwf -> P23109; PpfkA -> Ppam (pL19) or Ppar (pL25). Plasmid constructs: pL01-pL10/pL15-pL18 positive-response biosensors, pL19-pL30 negative-response biosensors, pL35 carrying Cra with amino acid mutations at positions 57, 58, 59, 60 under P23102; pBacm (glmS under PM23107 from pL09), pBacar (glmS under PR23107-cra from pL18 plus cra with P23102). DN5 knockout set: nag, ackA, poxB, ldhA, nan (prior work).

Genome promoter replacement (zwf, pfkA loci); construction of plasmid-based Cra/TFBS biosensor circuits; tuning via (1) core promoter strength, (2) TFBS position on promoter, (3) Cra-box sequence affinity, (4) Cra expression level (overexpression), (5) Cra ligand-binding affinity by site mutagenesis (aa 57-60); Hill-function-guided quantitative tuning; dynamic promoter swapping to create FBP-responsive repression of pfkA and activation of glmS.
Biosensor characterization: BW25113 harboring each biosensor plasmid (pL01-pL10, pL15-pL18, pL19-pL30, pL35), dose-response series with extracellular FBP
Deficiency-strain validation: BW-pfkA, BW-ptsG, BW-pykF vs BW25113, all harboring pL19
MVA: BW-Pzwf::P23109 (non-regulated), BW-PMT, BW-PR (shake flask; BW-PR also 1-L fermenter)
GlcNAc: DN5, DN5-PM, DN5-IM, DN5-GM, DN5-GAR, DN5-IMM, DN5-IMAR

Shake-flask fermentation for strain comparison; 1-L fermenter for BW-PR scale-up; glucose as sole carbon source in GlcNAc experiments; biosensor strains cultured 18 h before fluorescence detection; BW-PR reached stationary phase after 12 h; intracellular FBP in BW-PR dropped after 15 h.
Extracellular FBP added at 0.001-400 mM together with 10 g/L acetate for pL18 dose-response (Fig. 2D); no chemical inducer used for dynamic control (autonomous FBP sensing).
Fluorescence measured at 18 h of culture (Fig. 4); stationary phase after 12 h (BW-PR shake flask); intracellular FBP dropped suddenly after 15 h; fermenter cultivation 120 h.

Biosensor fluorescence output (dose-response curves); intracellular FBP concentration measurement; pfkA in vivo mRNA level; specific glucose consumption rate; specific growth rate; MVA and GlcNAc titers; acetate/byproduct profiling.

Hill function fitting of dose-response curves; derivation of dynamic range and threshold EC50; linear correlation analysis of intracellular FBP vs glucose consumption rate, growth rate and fluorescence; mRNA-level comparison between regulated and non-regulated strains.

Tuned negative-response biosensor pL19 detects intracellular FBP over ~0-50 mmol/g DCW, covering the reported physiological 0-31 mM/g DCW range; fluorescence of BW-pfkA, BW-ptsG, BW-pykF was 11.32, 7.13, 1.11x BW25113 at 18 h (order BW-pfkA > BW-ptsG > BW-pykF > BW25113). MVA: BW-PR produced 73.31 g/L MVA in shake flask (carbon yield 63.00 mol%, highest shake-flask MVA to date per authors) with <0.1 g/L acetate and no other byproducts; BW-PMT <2.47 g/L acetate; 111.3 g/L MVA after 120 h in 1-L fermenter with no by-products. Dynamic control outperformed IPTG-CRISPRi benchmark (8.53 g/L, Li et al. 2021; 0.12x of BW-PR).

experiments.purpose: Create and tune positive-response FBP biosensors (pL01-pL10; refined pL15-pL18) with varied thresholds/dynamic ranges.

interventions.description: Promoter-architecture engineering of Cra-regulated promoters (core promoter strength, TFBS position, Cra-box sequence) to build pL01-pL10 and refined pL15-pL18.

ddr_annotation.decision_type_rationale: Q1 yes (de novo promoter circuit construction), Q2 yes (this study), Q3 yes (variants with distinct thresholds enabled later selection of Ppam/PM23107 for applications).
ddr_annotation.design_action_rationale: Construction of metabolite-responsive dynamic regulation components (sensor-regulator).
ddr_annotation.trigger_observation: Few biosensors exist for central glycolytic metabolites; glycolysis flux imbalance (overflow at high flux, poor growth at low flux) lacks autonomous regulation systems.
ddr_annotation.evidence_grading_rationale: Dose-response curves measured in vivo and Hill-fitted (Fig. 2A,C,E).
ddr_annotation.reason_nature_rationale: Design based on stated transcription-regulation equilibrium among FBP, Cra and operator DNA (4_discussion_p004), i.e., explicit mechanistic basis.
ddr_annotation.generalizable_rule: When building an FBP/Cra-based glycolysis-flux sensor in E. coli, tune core promoter strength, TFBS position and Cra-box affinity so the sensor threshold and dynamic range span the physiological intracellular FBP range, because sensor output is set by the FBP-Cra-DNA equilibrium. (Validated only for Cra/FBP biosensors in E. coli in this paper.)

interventions.description: Tuning by Cra overexpression and by mutating Cra ligand-binding affinity (positive-response branch, Fig. 2B).

ddr_annotation.decision_type_rationale: Deliberate modification of regulator level/affinity to shift sensor response; informs tunability claims.
ddr_annotation.design_action_rationale: Regulator-level tuning of the dynamic control circuit.
ddr_annotation.trigger_observation: Initial promoter variants did not cover desired thresholds/dynamic ranges (implied by need for further tuning axes).
ddr_annotation.evidence_grading_rationale: Resulting sensors characterized by measured dose-response (Fig. 2C,E).
ddr_annotation.reason_nature_rationale: Affinity/expression-level changes act on the Cra-FBP-DNA equilibrium, as explicitly reasoned in Discussion.
ddr_annotation.generalizable_rule: When a TF-based metabolite sensor's threshold is mismatched to the in vivo effector range in E. coli, adjust regulator expression level or ligand-binding affinity of the TF, because both shift the occupancy equilibrium of the operator. (Validated for Cra/FBP in E. coli only.)
alternatives_considered: Cra-overexpressing plasmid sensors were later excluded from application cases because of Cra's global regulatory impact (4_discussion_p004).

(Validated for Cra-based circuits in E. coli only.)

experiments.purpose: Replace static pfkA knockout in the EP-bifido pathway with FBP-responsive dynamic repression to resolve growth/production trade-off and maximize MVA.

interventions.description: Genomic replacement of the zwf promoter with the stronger P23109 promoter (strain BW-Pzwf::P23109).

ddr_annotation.decision_type_rationale: Q1 yes (promoter replacement this study), Q2 yes (performed here on the EP-bifido background), Q3 yes (creates the base strain onto which dynamic pfkA control is layered).
ddr_annotation.design_action_rationale: Enhancing PP pathway entry (G6P dehydrogenase, Zwf) to supply fructose-6-phosphate and NADPH for the EP-bifido route.
ddr_annotation.trigger_observation: Prior EP-bifido design (Wang et al. 2019) requires sufficient F6P and NADPH supply from the PP pathway; natural glycolysis was previously blocked by permanent pfkA deletion.
ddr_annotation.evidence_grading_rationale: Resulting strain phenotypes (growth, glucose uptake, MVA) measured in this study.
ddr_annotation.reason_nature_rationale: Rationale explicitly stated: stronger zwf promoter enhances PP pathway flux for F6P/NADPH supply (stoichiometric/pathway mechanism).
ddr_annotation.generalizable_rule: When an EP-bifido-type acetyl-CoA/F6P supply pathway in E. coli is limited by PP pathway throughput, up-regulate zwf via a stronger constitutive promoter, because Zwf controls carbon entry into the PP pathway that delivers F6P and NADPH. (Validated for MVA production in this E. coli EP-bifido system.)

interventions.description: Genomic replacement of the pfkA promoter with negative-response biosensor promoters Ppam (pL19) or Ppar (pL25), yielding BW-PMT and BW-PR (dynamic EP-bifido pathway).

ddr_annotation.decision_type_rationale: Q1 yes (genomic promoter replacement), Q2 yes (this study), Q3 yes (two thresholds compared; Ppar selected as superior, guiding the final strain).
ddr_annotation.design_action_rationale: Metabolite-responsive dynamic down-regulation of a competing glycolysis step.
ddr_annotation.trigger_observation: Permanent pfkA deletion severely suppressed growth and glucose uptake, capping MVA at 11.02 g/L despite 64.3 mol% yield - a measured growth/production trade-off demanding dynamic instead of static control.
ddr_annotation.evidence_grading_rationale: Measured titers, growth, mRNA and FBP time courses for BW-PMT/BW-PR vs non-regulated control.
ddr_annotation.reason_nature_rationale: Mechanistic logic explicit: sense FBP (flux proxy) to repress pfkA only after growth phase, switching flux into EP-bifido and uncoupling growth from production.
ddr_annotation.generalizable_rule: When static knockout of an essential glycolytic step (e.g., pfkA) in E. coli collapses growth and substrate uptake, replace the native promoter with a biosensor promoter negatively responsive to intracellular FBP, because FBP reports glycolytic flux and enables automatic growth-then-production switching. (Validated for MVA via EP-bifido in E. coli; extended to GlcNAc in EXP5.)
alternatives_considered: IPTG-induced CRISPRi repression of pfkA (Li et al. 2021) - external-inducer strategy; yielded only 8.53 g/L MVA (0.12x of BW-PR) and requires inducer timing; cited as inferior benchmark (background_citation).

interventions.description: Scale-up fermentation of BW-PR in a 1-L fermenter.

experiments.purpose: Balance glycolysis and GlcNAc biosynthesis at the F6P node by dynamically repressing pfkA and/or activating glmS.
experiments.host: E. coli DN5 (DH5alpha derivative, delta-nag delta-ackA delta-poxB delta-ldhA delta-nan; constructed in previous studies - background)

interventions.description: Genomic replacement of pfkA promoter in DN5 with Ppam (pL19) or Ppar (pL25), yielding DN5-IM and DN5-PM.

ddr_annotation.decision_type_rationale: Q1 yes, Q2 yes, Q3 yes (two promoter strengths compared for this second product context).
ddr_annotation.design_action_rationale: Same dynamic-control strategy transferred to a second pathway context.
ddr_annotation.trigger_observation: Lower glycolysis is a competitive pathway for GlcNAc synthesis from glucose; F6P is the shared precursor, so pfkA must be down-regulated.
ddr_annotation.evidence_grading_rationale: Measured GlcNAc titers, growth and glucose consumption for DN5-IM/DN5-PM vs DN5.
ddr_annotation.reason_nature_rationale: Explicit node-competition mechanism stated for F6P between glycolysis and GlcNAc pathway.
ddr_annotation.generalizable_rule: When a product draws fructose-6-phosphate as precursor in glucose-grown E. coli, dynamically repress pfkA with an FBP-negative-response promoter, because this diverts F6P from lower glycolysis to the product while preserving early growth. (Validated for GlcNAc in the DN5 background.)

interventions.description: Plasmid-based dynamic activation of glmS using positive-response promoters PM23107 (pBacm) and PR23107-cra plus cra/P23102 (pBacar), transformed into DN5 to give DN5-GM and DN5-GAR.

ddr_annotation.decision_type_rationale: Q1 yes, Q2 yes, Q3 yes (two activation architectures compared; FBP-responsiveness of glmS activation verified).
ddr_annotation.design_action_rationale: Metabolite-responsive up-regulation of the product-forming enzyme (F6P aminotransferase).
ddr_annotation.trigger_observation: glmS needs up-regulation for GlcNAc overproduction, but early-stage overexpression may cause bacterial lysis and growth inhibition (Deng et al. 2005), so constitutive strong expression is unsuitable.

ddr_annotation.reason_nature_rationale: Mechanistic need (F6P aminotransferase flux) combined with explicit literature-based toxicity concern (Deng et al. 2005) motivating timed activation.

objective.value: Design, construct and tune bifunctional (positive- and negative-response) glycolysis-flux biosensors based on the Cra-FBP pair that sense intracellular fructose-1,6-diphosphate (FBP) and dynamically regulate glycolysis flux, then apply them to balance biosynthesis of mevalonate (MVA) and N-acetylglucosamine (GlcNAc) in Escherichia coli.
objective.notes: Abstract explicitly states design/construction of bifunctional glycolysis flux biosensor and application to MVA and GlcNAc.

hypothesis.value: Because intracellular FBP concentration is linearly related to glycolysis flux (via FBP feedforward activation of pyruvate kinase), a Cra/FBP-based transcriptional biosensor can report flux in vivo and drive autonomous, timely dynamic repression/activation of pathway genes, outperforming static knockout and IPTG-induced CRISPRi control.

inference.rationale: Introduction (1_introduction_p003) presents the FBP-flux linear relationship (cited to Kochanowski et al. 2013, a background_citation) as the premise; Results compare dynamic control against permanent pfkA deletion and cite Li et al. 2021 CRISPRi as inferior, implying the tested hypothesis.

hypothesis.notes: The FBP-flux linearity premise itself is attributed to prior literature (background_citation), not newly demonstrated by this paper except via the deficiency-strain validation experiment.

experiments.purpose: Create and tune positive-response FBP biosensors (pL01-pL10; refined pL15-pL18) with varied thresholds/dynamic ranges.

interventions.description: Promoter-architecture engineering of Cra-regulated promoters (core promoter strength, TFBS position, Cra-box sequence) to build pL01-pL10 and refined pL15-pL18.

ddr_annotation.decision_type_rationale: Q1 yes (de novo promoter circuit construction), Q2 yes (this study), Q3 yes (variants with distinct thresholds enabled later selection of Ppam/PM23107 for applications).
ddr_annotation.design_action_rationale: Construction of metabolite-responsive dynamic regulation components (sensor-regulator).
ddr_annotation.trigger_observation: Few biosensors exist for central glycolytic metabolites; glycolysis flux imbalance (overflow at high flux, poor growth at low flux) lacks autonomous regulation systems.
ddr_annotation.evidence_grading_rationale: Dose-response curves measured in vivo and Hill-fitted (Fig. 2A,C,E).
ddr_annotation.reason_nature_rationale: Design based on stated transcription-regulation equilibrium among FBP, Cra and operator DNA (4_discussion_p004), i.e., explicit mechanistic basis.
ddr_annotation.generalizable_rule: When building an FBP/Cra-based glycolysis-flux sensor in E. coli, tune core promoter strength, TFBS position and Cra-box affinity so the sensor threshold and dynamic range span the physiological intracellular FBP range, because sensor output is set by the FBP-Cra-DNA equilibrium. (Validated only for Cra/FBP biosensors in E. coli in this paper.)

interventions.description: Tuning by Cra overexpression and by mutating Cra ligand-binding affinity (positive-response branch, Fig. 2B).

ddr_annotation.decision_type_rationale: Deliberate modification of regulator level/affinity to shift sensor response; informs tunability claims.
ddr_annotation.design_action_rationale: Regulator-level tuning of the dynamic control circuit.
ddr_annotation.trigger_observation: Initial promoter variants did not cover desired thresholds/dynamic ranges (implied by need for further tuning axes).
ddr_annotation.evidence_grading_rationale: Resulting sensors characterized by measured dose-response (Fig. 2C,E).
ddr_annotation.reason_nature_rationale: Affinity/expression-level changes act on the Cra-FBP-DNA equilibrium, as explicitly reasoned in Discussion.
ddr_annotation.generalizable_rule: When a TF-based metabolite sensor's threshold is mismatched to the in vivo effector range in E. coli, adjust regulator expression level or ligand-binding affinity of the TF, because both shift the occupancy equilibrium of the operator. (Validated for Cra/FBP in E. coli only.)
alternatives_considered: Cra-overexpressing plasmid sensors were later excluded from application cases because of Cra's global regulatory impact (4_discussion_p004).

ddr_annotation.decision_type_rationale: Q1 yes (genomic promoter replacement), Q2 yes (this study), Q3 yes (two thresholds compared; Ppar selected as superior, guiding the final strain).
ddr_annotation.design_action_rationale: Metabolite-responsive dynamic down-regulation of a competing glycolysis step.
ddr_annotation.trigger_observation: Permanent pfkA deletion severely suppressed growth and glucose uptake, capping MVA at 11.02 g/L despite 64.3 mol% yield - a measured growth/production trade-off demanding dynamic instead of static control.
ddr_annotation.evidence_grading_rationale: Measured titers, growth, mRNA and FBP time courses for BW-PMT/BW-PR vs non-regulated control.
ddr_annotation.reason_nature_rationale: Mechanistic logic explicit: sense FBP (flux proxy) to repress pfkA only after growth phase, switching flux into EP-bifido and uncoupling growth from production.
ddr_annotation.generalizable_rule: When static knockout of an essential glycolytic step (e.g., pfkA) in E. coli collapses growth and substrate uptake, replace the native promoter with a biosensor promoter negatively responsive to intracellular FBP, because FBP reports glycolytic flux and enables automatic growth-then-production switching. (Validated for MVA via EP-bifido in E. coli; extended to GlcNAc in EXP5.)
alternatives_considered: IPTG-induced CRISPRi repression of pfkA (Li et al. 2021) - external-inducer strategy; yielded only 8.53 g/L MVA (0.12x of BW-PR) and requires inducer timing; cited as inferior benchmark (background_citation).

interventions.description: Scale-up fermentation of BW-PR in a 1-L fermenter.

ddr_annotation.decision_type_rationale: Q3 not passed: fermentation of the already-selected BW-PR evaluates performance at scale without introducing a new design modification.

experiments.conditions: Shake flask; 1-L fermenter 120 h; feeding/medium unknown (Methods absent; Supplementary Figs. 6-7 not available).
experiments.controls: Non-regulated BW-Pzwf::P23109; prior static-knockout BW-delta-pfkA EP-bifido (background_citation benchmark, Wang et al. 2019); IPTG-CRISPRi strain (background_citation benchmark, Li et al. 2021).
experiments.readouts: MVA titer and carbon yield; growth; glucose uptake; acetate/byproducts; pfkA mRNA; intracellular FBP.
experiments.analysis: Time-course comparison of growth/production; mRNA and FBP trends as dynamic-control confirmation.
experiments.outcome: BW-PR: 73.31 g/L MVA, 63.00 mol% carbon yield, <0.1 g/L acetate, stationary phase after 12 h, FBP drop after 15 h; fermenter: 111.3 g/L at 120 h, no by-products. BW-PMT accumulated <2.47 g/L acetate.
experiments.scope_notes: Dynamic-regulation claims supported within tested conditions only; mRNA/FBP confirmation is correlative to promoter replacement (no inducer-timing sweep shown in main text).

experiments.purpose: Balance glycolysis and GlcNAc biosynthesis at the F6P node by dynamically repressing pfkA and/or activating glmS.
experiments.host: E. coli DN5 (DH5alpha derivative, delta-nag delta-ackA delta-poxB delta-ldhA delta-nan; constructed in previous studies - background)

interventions.description: Genomic replacement of pfkA promoter in DN5 with Ppam (pL19) or Ppar (pL25), yielding DN5-IM and DN5-PM.

ddr_annotation.decision_type_rationale: Q1 yes, Q2 yes, Q3 yes (two promoter strengths compared for this second product context).
ddr_annotation.design_action_rationale: Same dynamic-control strategy transferred to a second pathway context.
ddr_annotation.trigger_observation: Lower glycolysis is a competitive pathway for GlcNAc synthesis from glucose; F6P is the shared precursor, so pfkA must be down-regulated.
ddr_annotation.evidence_grading_rationale: Measured GlcNAc titers, growth and glucose consumption for DN5-IM/DN5-PM vs DN5.
ddr_annotation.reason_nature_rationale: Explicit node-competition mechanism stated for F6P between glycolysis and GlcNAc pathway.
ddr_annotation.generalizable_rule: When a product draws fructose-6-phosphate as precursor in glucose-grown E. coli, dynamically repress pfkA with an FBP-negative-response promoter, because this diverts F6P from lower glycolysis to the product while preserving early growth. (Validated for GlcNAc in the DN5 background.)

interventions.description: Plasmid-based dynamic activation of glmS using positive-response promoters PM23107 (pBacm) and PR23107-cra plus cra/P23102 (pBacar), transformed into DN5 to give DN5-GM and DN5-GAR.

ddr_annotation.decision_type_rationale: Q1 yes, Q2 yes, Q3 yes (two activation architectures compared; FBP-responsiveness of glmS activation verified).
ddr_annotation.design_action_rationale: Metabolite-responsive up-regulation of the product-forming enzyme (F6P aminotransferase).
ddr_annotation.trigger_observation: glmS needs up-regulation for GlcNAc overproduction, but early-stage overexpression may cause bacterial lysis and growth inhibition (Deng et al. 2005), so constitutive strong expression is unsuitable.
ddr_annotation.evidence_grading_rationale: Measured GlcNAc titers for DN5-GM (6.33 g/L) and DN5-GAR (7.98 g/L) vs DN5 (0.46 g/L).
ddr_annotation.reason_nature_rationale: Mechanistic need (F6P aminotransferase flux) combined with explicit literature-based toxicity concern (Deng et al. 2005) motivating timed activation.
ddr_annotation.generalizable_rule: When overexpression of a product-pathway enzyme is toxic in early growth (e.g., glmS in E. coli), drive it with a positive-response biosensor promoter activated as FBP accumulates, because induction is delayed until the production phase, avoiding lysis. (Validated for GlcNAc in DN5.)

interventions.description: Simultaneous dynamic repression of pfkA and activation of glmS (pBacm or pBacar into DN5-IM), yielding DN5-IMM and DN5-IMAR.

ddr_annotation.decision_type_rationale: Q1 yes, Q2 yes, Q3 yes (tests whether dual control exceeds single regulation - a design-relevant negative/comparative result).
ddr_annotation.design_action_rationale: Layered dual dynamic regulation at one metabolic node.
ddr_annotation.trigger_observation: Hypothesis that combining both arms of node control (repress competitor + activate product path) would further raise GlcNAc titer.
ddr_annotation.evidence_grading_rationale: Measured titer DN5-IMM 8.63 g/L vs single-regulation strains; FBP levels measured in DN5/DN5-IM/DN5-GAR/DN5-IMM.
ddr_annotation.reason_nature_rationale: Push-pull node engineering rationale explicitly described in Fig. 6A narrative.
ddr_annotation.generalizable_rule: When single dynamic repression of pfkA already restores most of the achievable F6P-to-GlcNAc flux in E. coli DN5, adding dynamic glmS activation on top gives no obvious further titer gain, because the node flux is already saturated by competitor repression. (Observed only in this DN5/GlcNAc context; do not generalize.)

experiments.conditions: Glucose as sole carbon source; shake-flask production implied; detailed conditions unknown (Methods absent; Supplementary Fig. 8 unavailable).
experiments.controls: DN5 (0.46 g/L GlcNAc).
experiments.readouts: GlcNAc titer; growth; glucose consumption; intracellular FBP.
experiments.analysis: Titer/growth comparison; FBP-level interpretation per strain.
experiments.outcome: DN5-IM 8.65 g/L; DN5-GM 6.33; DN5-GAR 7.98; DN5-IMM 8.63 g/L; dual regulation not obviously higher than single; FBP lower in DN5-IM/DN5-IMM, unchanged in DN5-GAR. DN5-IMAR titer not reported in available text.
experiments.scope_notes: Combination constructs (DN5-IMM, DN5-IMAR) are directly demonstrated in Fig. 6; DN5-IMAR outcome missing from parsed text (figure-dependent).

unsupported_values: Develop a GalP/Glk-dependent, PTS-defective Escherichia coli L-tryptophan producer with higher yield and specific productivity by combining rational engineering (ptsI knockout, galP/glk promoter engineering, integration of AroG^D6G-D7A and AnTrpC^R378F variants) with batch and continuous adaptive laboratory evolution using an automatic CRISPR/Cas9-facilitated growth-coupled sensor-guided screening system (auto-CGSS).

Replacing PTS glucose uptake with the PTS-independent GalP/Glk system increases phosphoenolpyruvate (PEP) availability and can theoretically raise the maximum Trp yield from 0.227 g/g (PTS) to 0.454 g/g; growth impairment of PTS-defective strains can be overcome by modulated galP/glk expression and evolution.

E. coli Trp producer S028 (parental, previously constructed by Chen and Zeng 2017) and derivatives constructed/used here: S028TS/pCas9 (Ptac-tnaC-eGFP biosensor integrated), G028 (ΔptsI), G028Δglk::CmR (G028Cm), G028Cm/pJC184/pCas9MT (G028JC), promoter-mutant pool G028a, reference G028GG (non-mutated ptac-galP-pJ23119-glk), batch-ALE strain K3, phase-1 continuous-evolution strain G028c, final evolved strain T5, and enzyme-variant integrants T5AA and S028AA; E. coli Top10 used as cloning host; E. coli W3110 used as WGS reference.

S028TS/pCas9: chromosomal Ptac-tnaC-eGFP Trp biosensor in S028/pCas9. G028: ΔptsI. G028Cm: glk promoter region (-50 to 0 bp) replaced by CmR. Promoter mutants: randomized -10/-35 regions of synthetic ptac-galP and pJ23119-glk cassettes chromosomally integrated. T5 (vs W3110 reference): 15 modified and 5 deleted genes incl. galP K137T/P195A/F204L, zwf Glu165Stop, mlc(dgsA) deletion, plus rationally designed aroG S180F, serA H344A/N364A, trpE S40F, rpsL K43R inherited from lineage. T5AA/S028AA: chromosomal integration of aroG^D6G-D7A and AntrpC^R378F.

CRISPR/Cas9 genome editing (ptsI knockout, biosensor integration, promoter cassette integration, plasmid curing); in vitro random mutagenesis of galP/glk promoter -10/-35 elements (PCR-based, DpnI, fusion, Top10 library pCmN20-GGMT); CGSS (growth-coupled + Trp biosensor-guided in vivo screening); batch-mode ALE of 12 mutants; continuous ALE in a 30 mL auxostat (auto-CGSS) combining pJC184 mutagenesis plasmid (arabinose-induced mutators), real-time OD and online flow-cytometric Trp-fluorescence monitoring; homology modeling (Modeller) and docking (AutoDock Vina) for GalP variant analysis.

Chloramphenicol 15 ug/mL and kanamycin 25 ug/mL in auxostat; L-arabinose 10% w/v in auxostat feed (2.3/4.3) but 0.1% w/v at induction time points per Fig. 4B caption; 10 mM L-arabinose in SOB for competent-cell prep; IPTG induction for pJC184 curing; initial glucose 25 g/L in fed-batch.

G028 M9 growth test ~60 h; deep-well fluorescence assay 10 h; shake-flask mutant characterization 20-24 h; continuous evolution phase 1: 0-380 h (fluorescence peak ~11,446 MFU at 126 h), phase 2: 381-550 h (peak ~13,541 MFU at ~390-438 h), colony sampling at 462 h etc.; fed-batch 65 h (yield compared at 50 h for K3); SynM agar 30 h colony growth.

Screening heat maps and shake-flask characterizations: 'two independent biological samples' (Fig. 1 and Fig. 5 captions); fed-batch fermentations: means+SD from 'two independent measurements'; fluorescence: MFI of 10,000 events per sample; 20 single colonies per evolution sample.

OD600 growth; Trp-biosensor eGFP fluorescence (MFU; ex 488 nm / em 509 nm; electronic gating vs PBS background); Trp quantification by sensitive spectrophotometric method (Nagaraja et al. 2003); glucose, shikimate (SA), 3-dehydroshikimate (DSA) by HPLC; pyruvate tracked in Fig. 2F (method not restated); WGS (BGISEQ) + PCR resequencing of key mutations.

Beckman Flow software with electronic gating (MFU); SOAPdenovo v1.05 assembly; SNP calling with MUMmer + BLAT; BLAST confirmation; InDel detection with LASTZ verified by BWA + samtools; homology modeling Modeller v9.24 (template STP10 PDB 6H7D); PyMoL structural alignment; AutoDock Vina docking in Chimera; stoichiometric theoretical-yield analysis (Fig. S1).

G028: severe growth defect (OD600 0.21±0.02 after 60 h from 0.10). Promoter screen: 12/84 mutants with growth >1.25 + high MFU; 4 (D10, E12, F8, G1) best in FM-III but below S028. unsupported_values: Develop a GalP/Glk-dependent, PTS-defective Escherichia coli L-tryptophan producer with higher yield and specific productivity by combining rational engineering (ptsI knockout, galP/glk promoter engineering, integration of AroG^D6G-D7A and AnTrpC^R378F variants) with batch and continuous adaptive laboratory evolution using an automatic CRISPR/Cas9-facilitated growth-coupled sensor-guided screening system (auto-CGSS).

Replacing PTS glucose uptake with the PTS-independent GalP/Glk system increases phosphoenolpyruvate (PEP) availability and can theoretically raise the maximum Trp yield from 0.227 g/g (PTS) to 0.454 g/g; growth impairment of PTS-defective strains can be overcome by modulated galP/glk expression and evolution.

E. coli Trp producer S028 (parental, previously constructed by Chen and Zeng 2017) and derivatives constructed/used here: S028TS/pCas9 (Ptac-tnaC-eGFP biosensor integrated), G028 (ΔptsI), G028Δglk::CmR (G028Cm), G028Cm/pJC184/pCas9MT (G028JC), promoter-mutant pool G028a, reference G028GG (non-mutated ptac-galP-pJ23119-glk), batch-ALE strain K3, phase-1 continuous-evolution strain G028c, final evolved strain T5, and enzyme-variant integrants T5AA and S028AA; E. coli Top10 used as cloning host; E. coli W3110 used as WGS reference.

S028TS/pCas9: chromosomal Ptac-tnaC-eGFP Trp biosensor in S028/pCas9. G028: ΔptsI. G028Cm: glk promoter region (-50 to 0 bp) replaced by CmR. Promoter mutants: randomized -10/-35 regions of synthetic ptac-galP and pJ23119-glk cassettes chromosomally integrated. T5 (vs W3110 reference): 15 modified and 5 deleted genes incl. galP K137T/P195A/F204L, zwf Glu165Stop, mlc(dgsA) deletion, plus rationally designed aroG S180F, serA H344A/N364A, trpE S40F, rpsL K43R inherited from lineage. ddr_annotation.decision_type_rationale: Q1 active ptsI knockout by authors; Q2 performed in this paper; Q3 created the chassis whose phenotype drove all subsequent promoter engineering and evolution.
ddr_annotation.design_action_rationale: PTS removal spares PEP (precursor/reducing-power supply for the Trp pathway) rather than modifying the product pathway itself.
ddr_annotation.trigger_observation: Stoichiometric analysis: PTS consumes 1 mol PEP per mol glucose, capping theoretical Trp yield at 0.227 g/g; >80% of PEP could be freed in a PTS-defective GalP/Glk strain (theoretical 0.454 g/g).
ddr_annotation.evidence_grading_rationale: Chemical-stoichiometry-based theoretical yield plus measured growth phenotype of the knockout.
ddr_annotation.reason_nature_rationale: Paper explicitly explains the PEP-consumption mechanism of PTS and its coupling to Trp precursor supply.
ddr_annotation.generalizable_rule: When producing PEP-dependent aromatics such as L-tryptophan in E. coli, apply PTS inactivation with a PTS-independent glucose uptake route (GalP/Glk), because PTS consumes one PEP per internalized glucose and its removal frees PEP for product biosynthesis.
alternatives_considered: Glf (Z. mobilis)/Glk and GalP/Glk activation cited as alternative glucose-uptake restorations (literature background, not tested here)

ddr_annotation.decision_type_rationale: Q1 deliberate genome edit; Q2 done in this work; Q3 enables the subsequent promoter-library integration/screening workflow.

ddr_annotation.trigger_observation: Need for an sgRNA target sequence at the glk locus to apply CRISPR/Cas9 promoter replacement.

ddr_annotation.reason_nature_rationale: Paper states the explicit functional logic (CmR provides sgRNA target + selection marker); a technical-mechanistic rationale rather than literature analogy.
ddr_annotation.generalizable_rule: When performing CRISPR/Cas9-mediated chromosomal promoter replacement in E. coli, first insert an antibiotic-resistance marker at the target locus, because it simultaneously provides selection and a unique sgRNA target for the subsequent library swap.

objective.value: Develop a GalP/Glk-dependent, PTS-defective Escherichia coli L-tryptophan producer with higher yield and specific productivity by combining rational engineering (ptsI knockout, galP/glk promoter engineering, integration of AroG^D6G-D7A and AnTrpC^R378F variants) with batch and continuous adaptive laboratory evolution using an automatic CRISPR/Cas9-facilitated growth-coupled sensor-guided screening system (auto-CGSS).
objective.notes: Primary research objective stated in abstract and final Introduction paragraph.

hypothesis.value: Replacing PTS glucose uptake with the PTS-independent GalP/Glk system increases phosphoenolpyruvate (PEP) availability and can theoretically raise the maximum Trp yield from 0.227 g/g (PTS) to 0.454 g/g; growth impairment of PTS-defective strains can be overcome by modulated galP/glk expression and evolution.
hypothesis.notes: Stoichiometric/theoretical-yield reasoning (Fig. S1) plus literature proposal that PEP availability limits Trp yield.

strain.value: E. coli Trp producer S028 (parental, previously constructed by Chen and Zeng 2017) and derivatives constructed/used here: S028TS/pCas9 (Ptac-tnaC-eGFP biosensor integrated), G028 (ΔptsI), G028Δglk::CmR (G028Cm), G028Cm/pJC184/pCas9MT (G028JC), promoter-mutant pool G028a, reference G028GG (non-mutated ptac-galP-pJ23119-glk), batch-ALE strain K3, phase-1 continuous-evolution strain G028c, final evolved strain T5, and enzyme-variant integrants T5AA and S028AA; E. coli Top10 used as cloning host; E. coli W3110 used as WGS reference.
strain.notes: Full strain/plasmid genotypes are in Supplementary Table S1 (not available): strain reconstruction blocked_pending_supplement. W3110 inferred as likely lineage background of S028 because it is the WGS reference and rational-design variants are annotated against it, but the paper does not explicitly state S028's parent in the main text.

genotype.value: S028TS/pCas9: chromosomal Ptac-tnaC-eGFP Trp biosensor in S028/pCas9. G028: ΔptsI. G028Cm: glk promoter region (-50 to 0 bp) replaced by CmR. Promoter mutants: randomized -10/-35 regions of synthetic ptac-galP and pJ23119-glk cassettes chromosomally integrated. T5 (vs W3110 reference): 15 modified and 5 deleted genes incl. galP K137T/P195A/F204L, zwf Glu165Stop, mlc(dgsA) deletion, plus rationally designed aroG S180F, serA H344A/N364A, trpE S40F, rpsL K43R inherited from lineage. T5AA/S028AA: chromosomal integration of aroG^D6G-D7A and AntrpC^R378F.
genotype.notes: Table 2 is OCR-garbled (row misalignment); mutation list should be verified against the published PDF/Supplement. Complete genotypes require Supplementary Table S1.

engineering_method.value: CRISPR/Cas9 genome editing (ptsI knockout, biosensor integration, promoter cassette integration, plasmid curing); in vitro random mutagenesis of galP/glk promoter -10/-35 elements (PCR-based, DpnI, fusion, Top10 library pCmN20-GGMT); CGSS (growth-coupled + Trp biosensor-guided in vivo screening); batch-mode ALE of 12 mutants; continuous ALE in a 30 mL auxostat (auto-CGSS) combining pJC184 mutagenesis plasmid (arabinose-induced mutators), real-time OD and online flow-cytometric Trp-fluorescence monitoring; homology modeling (Modeller) and docking (AutoDock Vina) for GalP variant analysis.
engineering_method.notes: CGSS approach itself was developed in a previous paper (Chen et al., 2019) - background method, adapted here.

outcomes.value: G028: severe growth defect (OD600 0.21±0.02 after 60 h from 0.10). Promoter screen: 12/84 mutants with growth >1.25 + high MFU; 4 (D10, E12, F8, G1) best in FM-III but below S028. Batch ALE strain K3: yield 0.137 g/g (< S028 0.150), restored late growth, glucose uptake 4.10 g/L/h (40-50 h), lower shikimate, ~5x higher pyruvate (2.95 g/L); no mutations in galP/glk/galR. Continuous auto-CGSS strain T5: yield 0.164 g/g (+9.33% vs S028, +19.71% vs K3), Trp 38.77 g/L, qTrp 25.28 mg/gDCW/h (+45% vs S028), biomass 32% lower. T5AA: yield 0.195 g/g, Trp 41.49 g/L, qTrp 28.83 mg/gDCW/h; S028AA: 0.185 g/g, 48.27 g/L, qTrp 23.74, Vp 0.77 > T5AA 0.67. T5 genomics: 15 modified + 5 deleted genes incl. mlc deletion, zwf E165Stop, galP K137T/P195A/F204L. Yields remain below theoretical maxima (0.227/0.454 g/g); SA/DSA still accumulate.
outcomes.notes: Mechanistic links (mlc derepression -> PEP, GalP mutations -> transport, zwf stop -> growth/NADPH effects) are author hypotheses requiring confirmation - inference, not validated causality.

ddr_annotation.design_action_rationale: PTS removal spares PEP (precursor/reducing-power supply for the Trp pathway) rather than modifying the product pathway itself.
ddr_annotation.trigger_observation: Stoichiometric analysis: PTS consumes 1 mol PEP per mol glucose, capping theoretical Trp yield at 0.227 g/g; >80% of PEP could be freed in a PTS-defective GalP/Glk strain (theoretical 0.454 g/g).
ddr_annotation.evidence_grading_rationale: Chemical-stoichiometry-based theoretical yield plus measured growth phenotype of the knockout.
ddr_annotation.reason_nature_rationale: Paper explicitly explains the PEP-consumption mechanism of PTS and its coupling to Trp precursor supply.
ddr_annotation.generalizable_rule: When producing PEP-dependent aromatics such as L-tryptophan in E. coli, apply PTS inactivation with a PTS-independent glucose uptake route (GalP/Glk), because PTS consumes one PEP per internalized glucose and its removal frees PEP for product biosynthesis.
alternatives_considered: Glf (Z. mobilis)/Glk and GalP/Glk activation cited as alternative glucose-uptake restorations (literature background, not tested here)

unsupported_values: Develop a general strategy combining retrobiosynthesis and a precursor selection step to design biosynthetic pathways for 15 short-chain primary amines (SCPAs), and construct platform E. coli strains producing SCPAs first from fed amino-acid precursors and then de novo from glucose, including enhanced iso-butylamine and ethylamine production.

Amino acids are ideal precursors for SCPAs because their pathways are well characterized and carry high flux; a sufficiently promiscuous PLP-dependent decarboxylase (S. viridifaciens VlmD, EC 4.1.1.-) can convert selected amino-acid precursors to the corresponding SCPAs, and irreversible decarboxylation provides a strong flux-driving force.

Production host: E. coli WL3110 (lacI knockout mutant of W3110). Enzyme overexpression host: E. coli BL21(DE3). Cloning host: E. coli NEB 10-beta. Precursor-overproducing chassis: E. coli Val (pKBRilvBNCED) (L-valine overproducer, constructed previously, ref 21) and its parent WLGBH (intact ilvA/leuA/panB). Engineered strains: PA01, EA01, iBA01, iAA01, iBA02, and 12 EA01-derived VlmD-variant strains. Controls: NC01, NC02, NC03.

PA01 = WL3110 / pTac15-vlmDopt (codon-optimized S. viridifaciens vlmD in pTac15K, EcoRI/KpnI). EA01 = WL3110 / pTac15-vlmDopt-alaDopt (codon-optimized G. stearothermophilus alaD, KpnI/PstI). iBA01 = Val (pKBRilvBNCED) / pTac15-vlmDopt; Val background carries deletions ilvA, leuA, panB (auxotrophic for L-Ile, L-Leu, D-pantothenate). iAA01 = iBA01 + pTac-driven leuABCD overexpression. iBA02 = WLGBH (pKBRilvBNCED) / pTac15-vlmDopt-anti-ilvA-leuA-panB (sRNA knockdown cassettes). VlmD variants: V94I, V94L, V114I, V114L, T397A, T397V, W399L, S431T, S431V, S431L, D515K, D515N on pTac15-vlmDopt-alaDopt. NC02 = Val (pKBRilvBNCED) with empty plasmid (no vlmD). NC03 = L-leucine-producing strain without vlmD.

Computational retrobiosynthesis (in-house tool, 84 SMARTS reaction rules) + precursor selection (PubChem MeSH Tree via PubChemPy; RDT v1.5.1 functional-group position analysis); heterologous expression of codon-optimized vlmD and alaD on pTac15K plasmids; overexpression of leuABCD; synthetic sRNA knockdown of ilvA/leuA/panB (Gibson-assembled cassettes, method per ref 32); rational protein engineering via SWISS-MODEL homology modeling (template GAD67, PDB 2OKJ) + AutoDock Vina docking + BLASTP homolog-scanning to nominate 12 single mutations introduced by site-directed mutagenesis; fed-batch fermentation optimization.

(1) In vitro: purified His-VlmD + each of 13 amino-acid precursors (incl. glycine). (2) In vivo feeding: PA01 fed 2 g/L of each of 12 precursors individually. (3) De novo flask: NC01 vs EA01 (ethylamine); NC02 vs iBA01 (iso-butylamine); NC03 vs iAA01 (iso-amylamine). (4) Fed-batch: iBA01 in NM3 with Ile/Leu/pantothenate; iBA02 in NM3 without supplementation. (5) Enzyme engineering: EA01 plus 12 single-mutation VlmD-variant strains, flask ethylamine production.

In vitro: reactions without VlmD (no-enzyme controls, black chromatograms in Fig. 3). De novo flask: NC01 (control for EA01, exact genotype requires Supplementary Table 2), NC02 = Val (pKBRilvBNCED) harboring empty plasmid without vlmD (control for iBA01), NC03 = L-leucine-producing strain without vlmD (control for iAA01). Fed-batch comparison: iBA01 with supplementation serves as reference for iBA02. Enzyme engineering: EA01 with native VlmD as baseline for the 12 variants.

Flask: seed in 10 mL LB at 37 C for 8 h; 1.5 mL seed into 50 mL medium in 300 mL baffled flask; PA01 at 37 C, 200 rpm, 36 h; EA01 at 37 C, 200 rpm, 48 h; iBA01/iAA01 at 30 C, 200 rpm, 48 h. Enzyme overexpression: BL21(DE3)/pET-his-vlmDopt in 200 mL LB at 37 C, 1 mM IPTG induction after 3 h, harvest after further 5 h. Fed-batch: 6.6 L Bioflo 3000 with 2 L NM3, 30 C, pH 7.0 (28% ammonia), air 2 L/min, DO 40% via agitation 200-1000 rpm + pure O2, 100 mL feeding solution added when residual glucose < 3 g/L.

MR medium (pH 7.0; per L: 6.67 g KH2PO4, 4 g (NH4)2HPO4, 0.8 g MgSO4.7H2O, 0.8 g citric acid, 5 mL trace metal solution) + 10 g/L glucose + 2 g/L amino-acid precursor for PA01; MR + 20 g/L glucose for EA01. NM2 medium (per ref 21; 50 g/L glucose, 30 g/L CaCO3, 12.5 g/L (NH4)2SO4, 4.0 g/L KH2PO4, 2.0 g/L MgSO4.7H2O, yeast extract, 0.262 g/L L-Ile, 0.262 g/L L-Leu, 0.425 mg/L sodium D-pantothenate, 5 mL trace metal) for iBA01; NM2 without L-leucine for iAA01. NM3 for fed-batch (20 g/L glucose, 20 g/L (NH4)2SO4, 2 g/L KH2PO4, 0.4 g/L MgSO4.7H2O, 1.6 g/L NaCl, 5 g/L yeast extract, 0.262 g/L L-Ile, 0.262 g/L L-Leu, 0.362 mg/L sodium D-pantothenate, 5 mL trace metal). Feeding solution: 400 g/L glucose, 20 g/L KH2PO4, 2.1 g/L L-Ile, 2.1 g/L L-Leu, 3.62 mg/L sodium D-pantothenate. LB for cloning/seed.

Precursor feeding 2 g/L (each of 12 precursors, individually). In vitro assay: 1 mM amino-acid precursor, 0.1 mM PLP, 150 ug/mL purified His-VlmD in 50 mM potassium phosphate pH 7.5. IPTG 1 mM. unsupported_values: Develop a general strategy combining retrobiosynthesis and a precursor selection step to design biosynthetic pathways for 15 short-chain primary amines (SCPAs), and construct platform E. coli strains producing SCPAs first from fed amino-acid precursors and then de novo from glucose, including enhanced iso-butylamine and ethylamine production.

Amino acids are ideal precursors for SCPAs because their pathways are well characterized and carry high flux; a sufficiently promiscuous PLP-dependent decarboxylase (S. viridifaciens VlmD, EC 4.1.1.-) can convert selected amino-acid precursors to the corresponding SCPAs, and irreversible decarboxylation provides a strong flux-driving force.

Production host: E. coli WL3110 (lacI knockout mutant of W3110). Enzyme overexpression host: E. coli BL21(DE3). Cloning host: E. coli NEB 10-beta. Precursor-overproducing chassis: E. coli Val (pKBRilvBNCED) (L-valine overproducer, constructed previously, ref 21) and its parent WLGBH (intact ilvA/leuA/panB). Engineered strains: PA01, EA01, iBA01, iAA01, iBA02, and 12 EA01-derived VlmD-variant strains. Controls: NC01, NC02, NC03.

PA01 = WL3110 / pTac15-vlmDopt (codon-optimized S. viridifaciens vlmD in pTac15K, EcoRI/KpnI). EA01 = WL3110 / pTac15-vlmDopt-alaDopt (codon-optimized G. stearothermophilus alaD, KpnI/PstI). iBA01 = Val (pKBRilvBNCED) / pTac15-vlmDopt; Val background carries deletions ilvA, leuA, panB (auxotrophic for L-Ile, L-Leu, D-pantothenate). iAA01 = iBA01 + pTac-driven leuABCD overexpression. iBA02 = WLGBH (pKBRilvBNCED) / pTac15-vlmDopt-anti-ilvA-leuA-panB (sRNA knockdown cassettes). VlmD variants: V94I, V94L, V114I, V114L, T397A, T397V, W399L, S431T, S431V, S431L, D515K, D515N on pTac15-vlmDopt-alaDopt. NC02 = Val (pKBRilvBNCED) with empty plasmid (no vlmD). NC03 = L-leucine-producing strain without vlmD.

Computational retrobiosynthesis (in-house tool, 84 SMARTS reaction rules) + precursor selection (PubChem MeSH Tree via PubChemPy; RDT v1.5.1 functional-group position analysis); heterologous expression of codon-optimized vlmD and alaD on pTac15K plasmids; overexpression of leuABCD; synthetic sRNA knockdown of ilvA/leuA/panB (Gibson-assembled cassettes, method per ref 32); rational protein engineering via SWISS-MODEL homology modeling (template GAD67, PDB 2OKJ) + AutoDock Vina docking + BLASTP homolog-scanning to nominate 12 single mutations introduced by site-directed mutagenesis; fed-batch fermentation optimization.

(1) In vitro: purified His-VlmD + each of 13 amino-acid precursors (incl. glycine). (2) In vivo feeding: PA01 fed 2 g/L of each of 12 precursors individually. (3) De novo flask: NC01 vs EA01 (ethylamine); NC02 vs iBA01 (iso-butylamine); NC03 vs iAA01 (iso-amylamine). (4) Fed-batch: iBA01 in NM3 with Ile/Leu/pantothenate; iBA02 in NM3 without supplementation. (5) Enzyme engineering: EA01 plus 12 single-mutation VlmD-variant strains, flask ethylamine production.

In vitro: reactions without VlmD (no-enzyme controls, black chromatograms in Fig. 3). De novo flask: NC01 (control for EA01, exact genotype requires Supplementary Table 2), NC02 = Val (pKBRilvBNCED) harboring empty plasmid without vlmD (control for iBA01), NC03 = L-leucine-producing strain without vlmD (control for iAA01). Flask: seed in 10 mL LB at 37 C for 8 h; 1.5 mL seed into 50 mL medium in 300 mL baffled flask; PA01 at 37 C, 200 rpm, 36 h; EA01 at 37 C, 200 rpm, 48 h; iBA01/iAA01 at 30 C, 200 rpm, 48 h. Fed-batch: 6.6 L Bioflo 3000 with 2 L NM3, 30 C, pH 7.0 (28% ammonia), air 2 L/min, DO 40% via agitation 200-1000 rpm + pure O2, 100 mL feeding solution added when residual glucose < 3 g/L.
