experimental_design_object.title: Systematic strategies for developing phage resistant Escherichia coli strains

experiments.purpose: Validate that plasmid-borne SspBCDE from E. coli 3234/A confers DNA PT modification and broad phage protection in laboratory/industrial E. coli hosts without growth cost
experiments.host: E. coli K-12 MG1655 (primary); extended to MG1655(DE3), W3110, BW25113, JM109, E. coli B OP50, wild-type E. coli W
experiments.intervention: Transformation with pWHU3640 (pBluescript II SK(+) carrying ~8 kb sspBCDE cassette cloned from E. coli 3234/A genomic DNA via PCR + Gibson assembly)
experiments.conditions: LB, 37 C, 100 ug/mL ampicillin; phage challenge at MOI 0.05/0.5/5 at OD600 0.6 (growth curves, 12 h) or t=0 per Fig. 1c caption; plaque spot assay 12 h; EOP overnight
experiments.control: Same hosts with empty vector pBluescript II SK(+); LB blank reference
experiments.replicates: three independent experiments (mean +/- SD); plaque morphology assay repeated at least three times
experiments.readout: OD600 growth curves, plaque size/morphology, EOP fold protection
experiments.analysis: EOP ratio pWHU3640-host / empty-vector-host; descriptive comparison of growth curves
experiments.outcome: Up to 10^6-fold protection against most tested coliphages; no protection against T5; no growth impairment; protection observed across all 7 host backgrounds

ddr_annotation.decision_type_rationale: Q1 pass: authors actively cloned the sspBCDE cassette and constructed pWHU3640 transformants. Q2 pass: cloning and host introduction performed in this study (system identified in their earlier work, but this construct and these host introductions are new). Q3 pass: results (broad protection except T5, plus plasmid-system limitations) directly motivated the subsequent genome-integration and host-factor-mutation decisions.
ddr_annotation.design_action_rationale: Introducing a heterologous defense system relieves the host's intrinsic susceptibility to phage DNA replication; closest controlled category is 'derepression of a limiting/relief mechanism' (M3 解除调控) in the sense of adding a defensive barrier, though the vocabulary does not map perfectly to antiphage defense.
ddr_annotation.trigger_observation: The SspABCD-SspE system was recently identified by the group as a PT-modulated defense system with broad antiphage activity and no toxicity to hosts lacking sspABCD, making it a candidate module for host protection (p005); plasmid delivery chosen as the quick evaluation route before genome integration.
ddr_annotation.evidence_grading_rationale: Outcome measured directly by EOP, plaque assays and growth curves.
ddr_annotation.reason_nature_rationale: Choice of module rests on the group's prior published characterization of SspABCD-SspE (ref 30) and its established non-toxicity relative to R-M systems; no new mechanistic derivation in this paper drove the choice.
ddr_annotation.generalizable_rule: When engineering phage resistance into phage-sensitive E. coli production hosts, first evaluate the candidate defense module on a plasmid across multiple host backgrounds and a phage panel spanning all three Caudovirales morphological families, because module efficacy is host- and phage-dependent and plasmid delivery allows rapid screening before committing to genome integration.
alternatives_considered: Plasmid-encoded natural antiphage systems previously used in dairy starter strains (CRISPR-Cas, Abi, antisense mRNA, R-M) noted as background approaches with narrow range or postsegregational killing risk
R-M systems rejected implicitly because REase loss causes host cell death; SspE chosen because it is non-toxic without sspABCD

experiments.purpose: Generate stable phage-resistant strain avoiding plasmid incompatibility, instability, copy-number variation and metabolic burden
experiments.intervention: Integration of 5.4 kb sspBCD at safe site SS9 (int(aslA-glmZ)) via pKOV-Kan two-step double crossover (pWHU6401); subsequent lambda-red recombineering integration of 2.6 kb sspE with FRT-Kan marker (pKD46 induced with 0.2% arabinose; pKD13 template), marker excision with pCP20, plasmid curing at 42 C, verification by colony PCR and genome sequencing -> E. coli-PT strains
experiments.conditions: LB, 37 C; kanamycin 50 ug/mL selection; overnight 42 C curing
experiments.control: MG1655 parent and MG1655(pWHU3640) for growth and expression comparison
experiments.replicates: unknown for construction; phenotypic EOP comparisons at least three independent experiments (Fig. 2d)
experiments.readout: Colony PCR, genome sequencing, growth profile, RT-qPCR sspE:sspBCD ratio, EOP
experiments.analysis: Comparison of expression ratio and fold protection vs plasmid-borne module
experiments.outcome: MG1655-PT grows like MG1655(pWHU3640); sspE:sspBCD ratio slightly higher; at least 10-fold increased protection against T1, T4, EEP, lambda vs plasmid system

ddr_annotation.decision_type_rationale: Q1 pass: deliberate chromosomal integration of sspBCDE. Q2 pass: performed in this study. Q3 pass: established the -PT platform from which fhuA/trxA mutations and the three EPR strains were derived, and demonstrated improved protection vs plasmid, confirming genome integration as the strategy backbone.
ddr_annotation.design_action_rationale: Stable genomic installation of the defense barrier to permanently relieve phage susceptibility (defense-module installation; nearest category M3).
ddr_annotation.trigger_observation: Plasmid-encoded defense is limited by plasmid incompatibility, instability, copy-number variability and metabolic burden of plasmid maintenance (results_p002, citing refs 36, 37).
ddr_annotation.evidence_grading_rationale: Integration verified by colony PCR and genome sequencing; protection gain measured by EOP.
ddr_annotation.reason_nature_rationale: SS9 chosen because published work (ref 40, Bassalo et al.) identified it as an intergenic safe site with high integration efficiency and expression without viability cost; rationale adopted from literature rather than newly derived mechanistically in this paper.
ddr_annotation.generalizable_rule: When converting a plasmid-borne defense or pathway module into a stable industrial E. coli host, integrate the module at a characterized intergenic safe site (e.g., SS9) using markerless two-step double-crossover plus lambda-red recombineering, because chromosomal integration removes plasmid-instability and antibiotic-selection burdens while preserving host viability.
alternatives_considered: Continued use of plasmid-borne sspBCDE (rejected due to plasmid incompatibility/instability/copy-number/metabolic burden)

experiments.purpose: Achieve tolerance to phages T5 and T7, which evaded or were insufficiently restricted by SspBCDE alone
experiments.intervention: Deletion of FhuA extracellular loop 8 (fhuA Delta552-558 with NESG peptide insertion to preserve beta-barrel formation) via pWHU6402 two-step double crossover, followed by trxA deletion via pWHU6403 -> E. coli-EPR strains
experiments.conditions: LB, 37 C; sequential construction; verification by genome sequencing
experiments.control: WT, plasmid-bearing and -PT counterparts in each background
experiments.replicates: plaque assays representative of three independent experiments; EOP data at least three times
experiments.readout: Plaque assay, EOP, growth curves at MOI up to 10, phage cocktail challenge
experiments.analysis: Qualitative plaque formation and quantitative EOP/growth-curve comparison across the four genotypes per background
experiments.outcome: Plaques barely formed on EPR lawns even at highest phage titer; no lysis by T1/T5/EEP/JMPW2 at MOI 10; significant resistance to T4/T7 at MOI 0.1 and lambda at MOI 0.5; identical growth to parents; resistant to 7-phage cocktail

ddr_annotation.decision_type_rationale: Q1 pass: targeted genomic deletions of fhuA loop 8 and trxA. Q2 pass: constructed in this study. Q3 pass: produced the final EPR chassis used for all production demonstrations and defined the paper's 3-step strategy.
ddr_annotation.design_action_rationale: Blocking phage infection routes by removing the host receptor determinant (FhuA loop 8 for T1/T5/phi80) and an essential host factor (TrxA processivity factor for T7 DNA polymerase) - functional analogue of removing competing/enabling pathway elements (M5 竞争/旁路通量阻断).
ddr_annotation.trigger_observation: EOP data showed phage T5 was insensitive to SspBCDE defense (results_p001) and T7 remained a threat; known biology: T1/T5/phi80 use FhuA as receptor (ref 41) and T7 uses host TrxA as processivity factor (ref 42).
ddr_annotation.evidence_grading_rationale: Insensitivity of T5 measured by EOP (hard data); receptor/factor roles grounded in cited experimental literature; outcome verified by plaque/EOP/growth assays.
ddr_annotation.reason_nature_rationale: Choice of fhuA loop 8 and trxA is directly based on published identification of FhuA as the T1/T5/phi80 receptor and TrxA as the T7 polymerase processivity factor; the paper cites these studies rather than deriving the targets de novo. Mechanistic logic (receptor removal blocks adsorption/injection) underlies it, so both tags apply.
ddr_annotation.generalizable_rule: When a DNA-level defense system leaves specific phages unrestricted in an E. coli production host, layer receptor/essential-host-factor mutations targeting those phages' infection cycle (e.g., delete FhuA loop 8 for FhuA-dependent phages, delete trxA for T7-family polymerase dependence) on top of the defense module, because phages unable to inject or replicate DNA cannot escape through restriction-insensitivity mechanisms.

experiments.purpose: Test whether EPR strains maintain recombinant protein production under high-titer phage cocktail challenge
experiments.host: MG1655-EPR and W3110-EPR carrying pGEMKT-DAAO; MG1655(DE3)-EPR carrying pWHU6404
experiments.intervention: Transformation of production plasmids (constitutive dao from Trigonopsis variabilis; IPTG-inducible T7-driven nsp8) into EPR strains; phage cocktail added at start of cultivation
experiments.conditions: 2 L baffled flasks, 1 L LB, 37 C; DAAO 12 h; nsp8 induced 0.1 mM IPTG at OD600 0.6 then 28 C for 18 h; cocktail: 4.0x10^9 PFU/L T4+T7, 2.0x10^10 PFU/L lambda, 4.0x10^11 PFU/L T1/JMPW2/T5/EEP
experiments.control: SM-buffer blank (no phage) for each strain/plasmid; WT parents with plasmid +/- cocktail
experiments.readout: OD600, DAAO activity (U/mL), soluble nsp8 concentration (SDS-PAGE + Bradford)
experiments.analysis: One-way ANOVA followed by Tukey's test
experiments.outcome: EPR strains grew robustly and produced DAAO (2.03 +/- 0.07 and 1.88 +/- 0.10 U/mL) and nsp8 (~64 mg/L) under cocktail challenge, comparable to unchallenged parents; WT controls died under cocktail

ddr_annotation.decision_type_rationale: Q1 fails for the production test itself: no new engineering action is introduced here - already-constructed EPR strains are transformed with standard expression plasmids and benchmarked; it validates the prior engineering decisions without generating a new design choice.

experiments.purpose: Assess EPR strain robustness during fed-batch fermentation, the industrial mode most vulnerable to phage attack
experiments.host: MG1655-EPR(pGEMKT-DAAO), W3110-EPR(pGEMKT-DAAO), MG1655(DE3)-EPR(pWHU6404) with WT counterparts
experiments.intervention: Fed-batch cultivation in 5 L bioreactor with high-concentration phage cocktail added at start; IPTG (1 mM) induction at OD600 20 with 28 C shift for nsp8
experiments.conditions: 1.9 L initial medium (20 g/L tryptone, 14 g/L yeast extract, 10 g/L NaCl, 20 g/L glycerol); pH 7.5 (5 M NaOH); 4 L/min air; 400-600 rpm; feed 200 g/L glycerol + 40 g/L tryptone + 20 g/L yeast extract; 48 h; cocktail 5.0x10^9 PFU/L T4+T7, 2.5x10^10 PFU/L lambda, 5.0x10^11 PFU/L T1/JMPW2/T5/EEP
experiments.control: SM-buffer/no-phage fermentation of each strain; WT + cocktail groups
experiments.readout: OD600, DO profiles, DAAO activity, nsp8 titer
experiments.analysis: Profile comparison; mean of duplicates
experiments.outcome: EPR strains matched unchallenged growth/DO profiles; DAAO 28.53 +/- 2.79 U/mL (MG1655-EPR + cocktail) vs ~0 for challenged WT; nsp8 1.46 +/- 0.09 g/L with cocktail vs 1.52 +/- 0.16 for WT without; no phage escape observed over 48 h

ddr_annotation.decision_type_rationale: Q1 fails: no new genetic or process engineering decision - the fixed EPR chassis and standard fed-batch operation are benchmarked against phage challenge; results confirm the strategy rather than drive a new modification.

experiments.purpose: Determine inheritance of phage resistance and fermentation stability of EPR strains over long-term propagation
experiments.intervention: Serial transfer every 12 h at 1:1000 dilution for 47 transfers (~400 generations) at 37 C; periodic phenotyping
experiments.conditions: LB, 37 C; sampling every 20 generations (shake-flask fermentation) and every 40 generations (plaque assay)
experiments.control: none beyond initial-generation baseline (no separate control strain described)
experiments.readout: Plaque assay (resistance), shake-flask fermentation performance; LM-PCR for genomic integrity
experiments.analysis: Qualitative comparison across generations
experiments.outcome: Resistance and production maintained through ~400 generations; no genomic changes detected by LM-PCR even after phage-cocktail exposure

ddr_annotation.decision_type_rationale: Q1 fails: serial passaging here is a stability measurement campaign, not a deliberate engineering modification or selection campaign intended to create a new trait; it characterizes the already-built strains.

experimental_design_object.causal_chain: Plasmid validation (EXP1) identified SspBCDE breadth and the T5 gap -> genome integration (EXP2) removed plasmid liabilities and improved protection -> host-factor mutation (EXP3) closed T5/T7 gaps yielding EPR chassis -> flask (EXP4), fed-batch (EXP5) and 400-generation stability (EXP6) validated industrial applicability.

objective.value: Develop phage-resistant Escherichia coli host strains for laboratory and industrial bioprocesses by simultaneous genomic integration of the DNA phosphorothioation-based SspBCDE defense module and mutation of host components essential for phage infection cycles, while preserving growth and recombinant protein production capability.
objective.notes: Stated in abstract and Introduction ('In this work, we choose the E. coli MG1655, MG1655 (DE3), and W3110 strains... with the objective of constructing E. coli host strains with broad antiphage activities').

hypothesis.value: Combining a sequence-independent PT-modification-based restriction barrier (SspBCDE, which is non-toxic to hosts lacking sspABCD) with removal/mutation of phage-essential host factors (FhuA receptor loop 8 for T1/T5/phi80; TrxA processivity factor for T7) will confer broader and stronger phage resistance than either mechanism alone, without impairing cell growth or recombinant protein production.

inference.method: synthesis of explicit design rationale statements across Introduction and Results
inference.rationale: Paper states SspBCDE alone did not protect against T5 (results_p001, EOP data) and that 'To achieve a sufficient level of tolerance to phages T5 and T7, the elements in the MG1655-PT strain that are essential to the infection cycle of these phages were modified' (results_p004/p006); Introduction states SspE is non-toxic unlike R-M systems (p005). The combined-strategy hypothesis is implied by the 3-step design and Fig. 5 schematic but is not stated verbatim as a formal hypothesis.

hypothesis.notes: No explicit 'we hypothesize' statement; hypothesis reconstructed from design logic.

engineering_method.value: Three-step genome engineering strategy: (1) chromosomal integration of the sspBCD cluster at safe site SS9 (aslA-glmZ intergenic region) using pKOV-Kan two-step double-crossover gene replacement; (2) lambda Red-mediated recombineering to integrate sspE adjacent to sspBCD, FRT/Kan marker removal with pCP20 FLP recombinase, plasmid curing at 42 C, verification by colony PCR and genome sequencing; (3) sequential two-step double-crossover mutations deleting FhuA extracellular loop 8 (fhuA Delta552-558 with NESG peptide insertion) and deleting trxA. Prior plasmid-based validation used pWHU3640 (Gibson assembly into pBluescript II SK(+)).
engineering_method.notes: Discussion describes this as a '3-step feasible strategy'. Intermediate strain naming: E. coli int(aslA-glmZ)::sspBCD then E. coli-PT then E. coli-EPR.

experimental_design_object.title: Systematic strategies for developing phage resistant Escherichia coli strains

experiments.purpose: Validate that plasmid-borne SspBCDE from E. coli 3234/A confers DNA PT modification and broad phage protection in laboratory/industrial E. coli hosts without growth cost
experiments.host: E. coli K-12 MG1655 (primary); extended to MG1655(DE3), W3110, BW25113, JM109, E. coli B OP50, wild-type E. coli W
experiments.intervention: Transformation with pWHU3640 (pBluescript II SK(+) carrying ~8 kb sspBCDE cassette cloned from E. coli 3234/A genomic DNA via PCR + Gibson assembly)
experiments.conditions: LB, 37 C, 100 ug/mL ampicillin; phage challenge at MOI 0.05/0.5/5 at OD600 0.6 (growth curves, 12 h) or t=0 per Fig. 1c caption; plaque spot assay 12 h; EOP overnight
experiments.control: Same hosts with empty vector pBluescript II SK(+); LB blank reference
experiments.replicates: three independent experiments (mean +/- SD); plaque morphology assay repeated at least three times
experiments.readout: OD600 growth curves, plaque size/morphology, EOP fold protection
experiments.analysis: EOP ratio pWHU3640-host / empty-vector-host; descriptive comparison of growth curves
experiments.outcome: Up to 10^6-fold protection against most tested coliphages; no protection against T5; no growth impairment; protection observed across all 7 host backgrounds

ddr_annotation.decision_type_rationale: Q1 pass: authors actively cloned the sspBCDE cassette and constructed pWHU3640 transformants. Q2 pass: cloning and host introduction performed in this study (system identified in their earlier work, but this construct and these host introductions are new). Q3 pass: results (broad protection except T5, plus plasmid-system limitations) directly motivated the subsequent genome-integration and host-factor-mutation decisions.
ddr_annotation.design_action_rationale: Introducing a heterologous defense system relieves the host's intrinsic susceptibility to phage DNA replication; closest controlled category is 'derepression of a limiting/relief mechanism' (M3 解除调控) in the sense of adding a defensive barrier, though the vocabulary does not map perfectly to antiphage defense.
ddr_annotation.trigger_observation: The SspABCD-SspE system was recently identified by the group as a PT-modulated defense system with broad antiphage activity and no toxicity to hosts lacking sspABCD, making it a candidate module for host protection (p005); plasmid delivery chosen as the quick evaluation route before genome integration.
ddr_annotation.evidence_grading_rationale: Outcome measured directly by EOP, plaque assays and growth curves.
ddr_annotation.reason_nature_rationale: Choice of module rests on the group's prior published characterization of SspABCD-SspE (ref 30) and its established non-toxicity relative to R-M systems; no new mechanistic derivation in this paper drove the choice.
ddr_annotation.generalizable_rule: When engineering phage resistance into phage-sensitive E. coli production hosts, first evaluate the candidate defense module on a plasmid across multiple host backgrounds and a phage panel spanning all three Caudovirales morphological families, because module efficacy is host- and phage-dependent and plasmid delivery allows rapid screening before committing to genome integration.
alternatives_considered: Plasmid-encoded natural antiphage systems previously used in dairy starter strains (CRISPR-Cas, Abi, antisense mRNA, R-M) noted as background approaches with narrow range or postsegregational killing risk
R-M systems rejected implicitly because REase loss causes host cell death; SspE chosen because it is non-toxic without sspABCD

experiments.purpose: Generate stable phage-resistant strain avoiding plasmid incompatibility, instability, copy-number variation and metabolic burden
experiments.intervention: Integration of 5.4 kb sspBCD at safe site SS9 (int(aslA-glmZ)) via pKOV-Kan two-step double crossover (pWHU6401); subsequent lambda-red recombineering integration of 2.6 kb sspE with FRT-Kan marker (pKD46 induced with 0.2% arabinose; pKD13 template), marker excision with pCP20, plasmid curing at 42 C, verification by colony PCR and genome sequencing -> E. coli-PT strains
experiments.conditions: LB, 37 C; kanamycin 50 ug/mL selection; overnight 42 C curing
experiments.control: MG1655 parent and MG1655(pWHU3640) for growth and expression comparison
experiments.replicates: unknown for construction; phenotypic EOP comparisons at least three independent experiments (Fig. 2d)
experiments.readout: Colony PCR, genome sequencing, growth profile, RT-qPCR sspE:sspBCD ratio, EOP
experiments.analysis: Comparison of expression ratio and fold protection vs plasmid-borne module
experiments.outcome: MG1655-PT grows like MG1655(pWHU3640); sspE:sspBCD ratio slightly higher; at least 10-fold increased protection against T1, T4, EEP, lambda vs plasmid system

ddr_annotation.decision_type_rationale: Q1 pass: deliberate chromosomal integration of sspBCDE. Q2 pass: performed in this study. Q3 pass: established the -PT platform from which fhuA/trxA mutations and the three EPR strains were derived, and demonstrated improved protection vs plasmid, confirming genome integration as the strategy backbone.
ddr_annotation.design_action_rationale: Stable genomic installation of the defense barrier to permanently relieve phage susceptibility (defense-module installation; nearest category M3).
ddr_annotation.trigger_observation: Plasmid-encoded defense is limited by plasmid incompatibility, instability, copy-number variability and metabolic burden of plasmid maintenance (results_p002, citing refs 36, 37).
ddr_annotation.evidence_grading_rationale: Integration verified by colony PCR and genome sequencing; protection gain measured by EOP.
ddr_annotation.reason_nature_rationale: SS9 chosen because published work (ref 40, Bassalo et al.) identified it as an intergenic safe site with high integration efficiency and expression without viability cost; rationale adopted from literature rather than newly derived mechanistically in this paper.
ddr_annotation.generalizable_rule: When converting a plasmid-borne defense or pathway module into a stable industrial E. coli host, integrate the module at a characterized intergenic safe site (e.g., SS9) using markerless two-step double-crossover plus lambda-red recombineering, because chromosomal integration removes plasmid-instability and antibiotic-selection burdens while preserving host viability.
alternatives_considered: Continued use of plasmid-borne sspBCDE (rejected due to plasmid incompatibility/instability/copy-number/metabolic burden)

experiments.purpose: Achieve tolerance to phages T5 and T7, which evaded or were insufficiently restricted by SspBCDE alone
experiments.intervention: Deletion of FhuA extracellular loop 8 (fhuA Delta552-558 with NESG peptide insertion to preserve beta-barrel formation) via pWHU6402 two-step double crossover, followed by trxA deletion via pWHU6403 -> E. coli-EPR strains
experiments.conditions: LB, 37 C; sequential construction; verification by genome sequencing
experiments.control: WT, plasmid-bearing and -PT counterparts in each background
experiments.replicates: plaque assays representative of three independent experiments; EOP data at least three times
experiments.readout: Plaque assay, EOP, growth curves at MOI up to 10, phage cocktail challenge
experiments.analysis: Qualitative plaque formation and quantitative EOP/growth-curve comparison across the four genotypes per background
experiments.outcome: Plaques barely formed on EPR lawns even at highest phage titer; no lysis by T1/T5/EEP/JMPW2 at MOI 10; significant resistance to T4/T7 at MOI 0.1 and lambda at MOI 0.5; identical growth to parents; resistant to 7-phage cocktail

ddr_annotation.decision_type_rationale: Q1 pass: targeted genomic deletions of fhuA loop 8 and trxA. Q2 pass: constructed in this study. Q3 pass: produced the final EPR chassis used for all production demonstrations and defined the paper's 3-step strategy.
ddr_annotation.design_action_rationale: Blocking phage infection routes by removing the host receptor determinant (FhuA loop 8 for T1/T5/phi80) and an essential host factor (TrxA processivity factor for T7 DNA polymerase) - functional analogue of removing competing/enabling pathway elements (M5 竞争/旁路通量阻断).
ddr_annotation.trigger_observation: EOP data showed phage T5 was insensitive to SspBCDE defense (results_p001) and T7 remained a threat; known biology: T1/T5/phi80 use FhuA as receptor (ref 41) and T7 uses host TrxA as processivity factor (ref 42).
ddr_annotation.evidence_grading_rationale: Insensitivity of T5 measured by EOP (hard data); receptor/factor roles grounded in cited experimental literature; outcome verified by plaque/EOP/growth assays.
ddr_annotation.reason_nature_rationale: Choice of fhuA loop 8 and trxA is directly based on published identification of FhuA as the T1/T5/phi80 receptor and TrxA as the T7 polymerase processivity factor; the paper cites these studies rather than deriving the targets de novo. Mechanistic logic (receptor removal blocks adsorption/injection) underlies it, so both tags apply.
ddr_annotation.generalizable_rule: When a DNA-level defense system leaves specific phages unrestricted in an E. coli production host, layer receptor/essential-host-factor mutations targeting those phages' infection cycle (e.g., delete FhuA loop 8 for FhuA-dependent phages, delete trxA for T7-family polymerase dependence) on top of the defense module, because phages unable to inject or replicate DNA cannot escape through restriction-insensitivity mechanisms.

experiments.purpose: Test whether EPR strains maintain recombinant protein production under high-titer phage cocktail challenge
experiments.host: MG1655-EPR and W3110-EPR carrying pGEMKT-DAAO; MG1655(DE3)-EPR carrying pWHU6404
experiments.intervention: Transformation of production plasmids (constitutive dao from Trigonopsis variabilis; IPTG-inducible T7-driven nsp8) into EPR strains; phage cocktail added at start of cultivation
experiments.conditions: 2 L baffled flasks, 1 L LB, 37 C; DAAO 12 h; nsp8 induced 0.1 mM IPTG at OD600 0.6 then 28 C for 18 h; cocktail: 4.0x10^9 PFU/L T4+T7, 2.0x10^10 PFU/L lambda, 4.0x10^11 PFU/L T1/JMPW2/T5/EEP
experiments.control: SM-buffer blank (no phage) for each strain/plasmid; WT parents with plasmid +/- cocktail
experiments.readout: OD600, DAAO activity (U/mL), soluble nsp8 concentration (SDS-PAGE + Bradford)
experiments.analysis: One-way ANOVA followed by Tukey's test
experiments.outcome: EPR strains grew robustly and produced DAAO (2.03 +/- 0.07 and 1.88 +/- 0.10 U/mL) and nsp8 (~64 mg/L) under cocktail challenge, comparable to unchallenged parents; WT controls died under cocktail

ddr_annotation.decision_type_rationale: Q1 fails for the production test itself: no new engineering action is introduced here - already-constructed EPR strains are transformed with standard expression plasmids and benchmarked; it validates the prior engineering decisions without generating a new design choice.

experiments.purpose: Assess EPR strain robustness during fed-batch fermentation, the industrial mode most vulnerable to phage attack
experiments.host: MG1655-EPR(pGEMKT-DAAO), W3110-EPR(pGEMKT-DAAO), MG1655(DE3)-EPR(pWHU6404) with WT counterparts
experiments.intervention: Fed-batch cultivation in 5 L bioreactor with high-concentration phage cocktail added at start; IPTG (1 mM) induction at OD600 20 with 28 C shift for nsp8
experiments.conditions: 1.9 L initial medium (20 g/L tryptone, 14 g/L yeast extract, 10 g/L NaCl, 20 g/L glycerol); pH 7.5 (5 M NaOH); 4 L/min air; 400-600 rpm; feed 200 g/L glycerol + 40 g/L tryptone + 20 g/L yeast extract; 48 h; cocktail 5.0x10^9 PFU/L T4+T7, 2.5x10^10 PFU/L lambda, 5.0x10^11 PFU/L T1/JMPW2/T5/EEP
experiments.control: SM-buffer/no-phage fermentation of each strain; WT + cocktail groups
experiments.readout: OD600, DO profiles, DAAO activity, nsp8 titer
experiments.analysis: Profile comparison; mean of duplicates
experiments.outcome: EPR strains matched unchallenged growth/DO profiles; DAAO 28.53 +/- 2.79 U/mL (MG1655-EPR + cocktail) vs ~0 for challenged WT; nsp8 1.46 +/- 0.09 g/L with cocktail vs 1.52 +/- 0.16 for WT without; no phage escape observed over 48 h

ddr_annotation.decision_type_rationale: Q1 fails: no new genetic or process engineering decision - the fixed EPR chassis and standard fed-batch operation are benchmarked against phage challenge; results confirm the strategy rather than drive a new modification.

experiments.purpose: Determine inheritance of phage resistance and fermentation stability of EPR strains over long-term propagation
experiments.intervention: Serial transfer every 12 h at 1:1000 dilution for 47 transfers (~400 generations) at 37 C; periodic phenotyping
experiments.conditions: LB, 37 C; sampling every 20 generations (shake-flask fermentation) and every 40 generations (plaque assay)
experiments.control: none beyond initial-generation baseline (no separate control strain described)
experiments.readout: Plaque assay (resistance), shake-flask fermentation performance; LM-PCR for genomic integrity
experiments.analysis: Qualitative comparison across generations
experiments.outcome: Resistance and production maintained through ~400 generations; no genomic changes detected by LM-PCR even after phage-cocktail exposure

ddr_annotation.decision_type_rationale: Q1 fails: serial passaging here is a stability measurement campaign, not a deliberate engineering modification or selection campaign intended to create a new trait; it characterizes the already-built strains.

unsupported_values: Fine-tune the EMP:PPP glycolytic flux ratio in the previously constructed EP-bifido pathway of E. coli to improve mevalonate (MVA) production, by (1) enhancing PPP flux for NADPH supply via genomic replacement of the zwf promoter with Anderson-library promoters of different strengths, and (2) time-controlled down-regulation of pfkA using an IPTG-inducible CRISPRi system to mitigate the growth defect caused by pfkA knockout.

The previously detected EMP:PPP carbon split (0.43:0.57) in the EP-bifido pathway deviates from the theoretical optimum (1:6, giving 86% mol/mol maximum MVA conversion), leaving PPP flux and NADPH supply insufficient; increasing zwf expression and dynamically (rather than permanently) suppressing pfkA should redirect carbon flux toward the PPP, balance reducing power, relieve the growth defect of the pfkA knockout, and increase MVA yield.

unsupported_values: Fine-tune the EMP:PPP glycolytic flux ratio in the previously constructed EP-bifido pathway of E. coli to improve mevalonate (MVA) production, by (1) enhancing PPP flux for NADPH supply via genomic replacement of the zwf promoter with Anderson-library promoters of different strengths, and (2) time-controlled down-regulation of pfkA using an IPTG-inducible CRISPRi system to mitigate the growth defect caused by pfkA knockout.

The previously detected EMP:PPP carbon split (0.43:0.57) in the EP-bifido pathway deviates from the theoretical optimum (1:6, giving 86% mol/mol maximum MVA conversion), leaving PPP flux and NADPH supply insufficient; increasing zwf expression and dynamically (rather than permanently) suppressing pfkA should redirect carbon flux toward the PPP, balance reducing power, relieve the growth defect of the pfkA knockout, and increase MVA yield.

ddr_annotation.design_action_rationale: Graded tuning of zwf expression level using a promoter-strength series is expression balancing of a pathway enzyme to redirect flux, rather than enzyme engineering or dynamic control.
ddr_annotation.trigger_observation: Prior 13C-MFA of the EP-bifido MVA strain showed insufficient NADPH supply from oxidative PPP and a measured EMP:PPP split (0.43:0.57) far from the theoretical 1:6 optimum, indicating PPP flux as the limiting factor.
ddr_annotation.evidence_grading_rationale: Trigger is based on experimentally measured 13C-MFA flux data from the prior study and confirmed here by fermentation titers and new 13C-MFA; not a purely predictive tool output.
ddr_annotation.reason_nature_rationale: Paper explicitly states the mechanistic chain: zwf encodes the first key PPP enzyme; enhancing its expression increases PPP dehydrogenase flux, raising NADPH supply for the NADPH-dependent MVA pathway; NADPH level shown to correlate positively with promoter strength.
ddr_annotation.generalizable_rule: When an acetyl-CoA-derived, NADPH-dependent product (e.g., mevalonate in E. coli EP-bifido system) is limited by reducing-power supply from the oxidative PPP, apply graded genomic promoter tuning of the PPP entry enzyme (zwf) to rebalance the EMP:PPP split, because increased glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase flux directly raises NADPH generation and shifts the main NADPH source from TCA isocitrate dehydrogenase to the PPP.

ddr_annotation.design_action_rationale: Inducible, time-controlled CRISPRi repression of a competing-pathway enzyme is dynamic regulation: repression is switched on at 12 h by IPTG rather than being constitutive.
ddr_annotation.trigger_observation: The permanent ΔpfkA in the EP-bifido strain caused severe growth defects limiting application, and static metabolic engineering cannot dedicate carbon to biomass in early growth; a tunable repression system was needed to time the EMP-flux reduction.
ddr_annotation.evidence_grading_rationale: Trigger (pfkA-knockout growth defect) was experimentally observed in the prior study and reproduced knowledge in literature [19]; the intervention outcome is measured fermentation data.
ddr_annotation.reason_nature_rationale: The paper motivates CRISPRi by citing its wide use and good inhibition effect in metabolic engineering [26, 27] and target-site-dependent repression [28], and dynamic regulation precedents [23-25]; it does not provide a new mechanistic derivation of why CRISPRi on pfkA is optimal beyond these analogies, though the growth-defect problem itself is mechanistically understood. The dominant stated basis for choosing this tool is literature analogy.
ddr_annotation.generalizable_rule: When a competing-pathway knockout (e.g., ΔpfkA blocking EMP flux in E. coli EP-bifido MVA production) causes unacceptable growth defects, apply inducible CRISPRi repression of the same node with a weak dCas9 promoter and sgRNAs targeting the promoter-proximal region, because time-delayed, titratable transcriptional repression preserves early-growth carbon assimilation while still redirecting flux toward the production pathway.
alternatives_considered: promoter replacement of the target gene (noted as requiring genome editing, which CRISPRi avoids)
post-transcriptional/post-translational tools such as anti-sense RNA and RNAi (mentioned as alternatives, not tested here)

objective.value: Fine-tune the EMP:PPP glycolytic flux ratio in the previously constructed EP-bifido pathway of E. coli to improve mevalonate (MVA) production, by (1) enhancing PPP flux for NADPH supply via genomic replacement of the zwf promoter with Anderson-library promoters of different strengths, and (2) time-controlled down-regulation of pfkA using an IPTG-inducible CRISPRi system to mitigate the growth defect caused by pfkA knockout.
objective.notes: Objective stated in Abstract, Background and Results; no user target system was provided, so this reflects only the paper's own aim.

hypothesis.value: The previously detected EMP:PPP carbon split (0.43:0.57) in the EP-bifido pathway deviates from the theoretical optimum (1:6, giving 86% mol/mol maximum MVA conversion), leaving PPP flux and NADPH supply insufficient; increasing zwf expression and dynamically (rather than permanently) suppressing pfkA should redirect carbon flux toward the PPP, balance reducing power, relieve the growth defect of the pfkA knockout, and increase MVA yield.
hypothesis.notes: The mechanistic rationale (insufficient NADPH from oxidative PPP revealed by prior 13C-MFA; growth defect of pfkA disruption) is stated in Background; the causal link to higher MVA yield is validated experimentally in this study.

experimental_design_object.title: Fine tuning the glycolytic flux ratio of EP-bifido pathway for mevalonate production by enhancing glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (Zwf) and CRISPRi suppressing 6-phosphofructose kinase (PfkA) in Escherichia coli

experiments.purpose: Enhance PPP flux and NADPH supply by graded overexpression of zwf via genomic promoter replacement

ddr_annotation.decision_type_rationale: Q1 yes (active genomic promoter replacement of zwf), Q2 yes (constructed in this study, Table 1 'This study'), Q3 yes (results guided which promoter strength benefits MVA production and informed subsequent 13C-MFA and strain selection).
ddr_annotation.design_action_rationale: Graded tuning of zwf expression level using a promoter-strength series is expression balancing of a pathway enzyme to redirect flux, rather than enzyme engineering or dynamic control.
ddr_annotation.trigger_observation: Prior 13C-MFA of the EP-bifido MVA strain showed insufficient NADPH supply from oxidative PPP and a measured EMP:PPP split (0.43:0.57) far from the theoretical 1:6 optimum, indicating PPP flux as the limiting factor.
ddr_annotation.evidence_grading_rationale: Trigger is based on experimentally measured 13C-MFA flux data from the prior study and confirmed here by fermentation titers and new 13C-MFA; not a purely predictive tool output.
ddr_annotation.reason_nature_rationale: Paper explicitly states the mechanistic chain: zwf encodes the first key PPP enzyme; enhancing its expression increases PPP dehydrogenase flux, raising NADPH supply for the NADPH-dependent MVA pathway; NADPH level shown to correlate positively with promoter strength.
ddr_annotation.generalizable_rule: When an acetyl-CoA-derived, NADPH-dependent product (e.g., mevalonate in E. coli EP-bifido system) is limited by reducing-power supply from the oxidative PPP, apply graded genomic promoter tuning of the PPP entry enzyme (zwf) to rebalance the EMP:PPP split, because increased glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase flux directly raises NADPH generation and shifts the main NADPH source from TCA isocitrate dehydrogenase to the PPP.

ddr_annotation.decision_type_rationale: Q1 yes (built and applied an inducible CRISPRi repression system against pfkA), Q2 yes (strains constructed in this study), Q3 yes (comparing three sgRNA target sites changed future design choice — sgRNA1-type promoter targeting identified as most suitable for this system).
ddr_annotation.design_action_rationale: Inducible, time-controlled CRISPRi repression of a competing-pathway enzyme is dynamic regulation: repression is switched on at 12 h by IPTG rather than being constitutive.
ddr_annotation.trigger_observation: The permanent ΔpfkA in the EP-bifido strain caused severe growth defects limiting application, and static metabolic engineering cannot dedicate carbon to biomass in early growth; a tunable repression system was needed to time the EMP-flux reduction.
ddr_annotation.evidence_grading_rationale: Trigger (pfkA-knockout growth defect) was experimentally observed in the prior study and reproduced knowledge in literature [19]; the intervention outcome is measured fermentation data.
ddr_annotation.reason_nature_rationale: The paper motivates CRISPRi by citing its wide use and good inhibition effect in metabolic engineering [26, 27] and target-site-dependent repression [28], and dynamic regulation precedents [23-25]; it does not provide a new mechanistic derivation of why CRISPRi on pfkA is optimal beyond these analogies, though the growth-defect problem itself is mechanistically understood. The dominant stated basis for choosing this tool is literature analogy.
ddr_annotation.generalizable_rule: When a competing-pathway knockout (e.g., ΔpfkA blocking EMP flux in E. coli EP-bifido MVA production) causes unacceptable growth defects, apply inducible CRISPRi repression of the same node with a weak dCas9 promoter and sgRNAs targeting the promoter-proximal region, because time-delayed, titratable transcriptional repression preserves early-growth carbon assimilation while still redirecting flux toward the production pathway.
alternatives_considered: promoter replacement of the target gene (noted as requiring genome editing, which CRISPRi avoids)
post-transcriptional/post-translational tools such as anti-sense RNA and RNAi (mentioned as alternatives, not tested here)

ddr_annotation.trigger_observation: Known/anticipated growth inhibition caused by dCas9 expression in the CRISPRi system.
ddr_annotation.evidence_grading_rationale: The anticipation of dCas9 toxicity was predictive/literature-based at design time (refs [31, 32] cited later in Discussion); toxicity in this system was confirmed only after implementation. Predictive rationale, requires measurement to confirm.
ddr_annotation.reason_nature_rationale: Weak-promoter choice rests on reported dCas9 toxicity in certain hosts and general Anderson-library promoter tuning practice rather than a measured mechanism in this strain.
ddr_annotation.generalizable_rule: When deploying plasmid-based CRISPRi in E. coli production strains that already bear growth burdens, drive dcas9 from a weak constitutive promoter (e.g., BBa-J23134) to reduce dCas9 toxicity, because high dCas9 expression inhibits growth of pathway-expressing cells.

unsupported_values: Fine-tune the glycolytic flux ratio between the EMP pathway and the pentose phosphate pathway (PPP) in the previously constructed EP-bifido pathway in Escherichia coli to improve NADPH supply, carbon conversion rate and mevalonate (MVA) production, by (1) enhancing zwf expression via genomic promoter replacement and (2) dynamically down-regulating pfkA using a CRISPRi system.

The detected EMP:PPP carbon split (0.43:0.57) deviates from the theoretical optimum (1:6), yielding insufficient NADPH; enhancing PPP flux by up-regulating zwf, and time-controlled repression of pfkA (whose knockout causes severe growth defects) via CRISPRi, will redirect flux, balance reducing power and improve MVA yield.

Escherichia coli BW25113 (wild type; F- Δ(araD-araB)567, ΔlacZ4787(::rrnB-3), λ-, rph-1, Δ(rhaD-rhaB)568, hsdR514; lab stock) as background; BW-P (BW25113 derivative, ΔpfkA::FRT, from [13]) as starting strain for zwf promoter replacement; engineered strains BW-P 23100/23104/23105/23108/23114-zwf, production strains BW-P10 BF, BW-P04 BF, BW-P05 BF, BW-P08 BF, BW-P14 BF, BPB-series, BW25113 23100-zwf, and CRISPRi strains BiBF1-3, BiB1F, BiB2F, BiB3F plus control strains BB1F, BBFd, BiBd1F, BBF.

BW-P: BW25113 ΔpfkA::FRT. zwf-enhanced strains: BW-P with native zwf promoter replaced by Anderson promoters BBa-J23100/23104/23105/23108/23114 (CmR marker). BW25113 23100-zwf: BW25113 with zwf promoter::BBa-J23100 (no ΔpfkA). CRISPRi strains additionally carry dcas9 and one of three anti-pfkA sgRNAs on plasmids. Production strains carry pBSA (pTrc99a with atoB from E. coli, mvaS and mvaA from L. casei, tac promoter, AmpR) and pFF (pCDFduet with fxpk from B. adolescentis and fbp from E. coli).

(1) Red-mediated homologous recombination (pTKRED helper, pKD3/pKD4 template CmR/kan cassettes, 300-500 bp homology arms, electroporation of ssDNA/PCR fragments) to replace the genomic zwf promoter with Anderson library promoters of graded strengths. (2) Plasmid reconstruction replacing the tac promoter of pBSA with five Anderson promoters. (3) CRISPRi: dcas9 under weak promoter BBa-J23134 and three sgRNAs targeting pfkA (promoter region; +100 bp and +200 bp downstream of start codon), assembled into pFF and pBSA under IPTG-inducible promoter; induction with 200 µM IPTG at 12 h of fermentation. (4) GFP reporter assay to characterize promoter strength.

EXP2: BW-P BF (EP-bifido strain with native zwf promoter) as baseline control. EXP3: BW-P BF control plus wild-type BW25113 as reference for cofactor derivation analysis. EXP4/EXP5: BBF (BW25113 23100-zwf + pFF + pBSA, no CRISPRi), BB1F (sgRNA1 only), BBFd (dCas9 only), BiBd1F (sgRNA1-dCas9 single-plasmid) to isolate effects of dCas9 toxicity and leaky expression.

Plasmid preparation: LB, 37 °C, 220 rpm, test tubes, 5 mL. MVA production: 50-mL shake flasks, M9 minimal medium + 0.2% yeast extract + 20 g/L glucose, 2% inoculation from 5-mL LB overnight culture, 37 °C, 120 rpm, 48 h (Methods states 48 h; Results/abstract report MVA titer at 72 h - see conflicts). Promoter replacement: SOB medium; cells grown at 30 °C, 220 rpm. Antibiotics: Amp 100 µg/mL, Spc 50 µg/mL, Cm 25 µg/mL.

LB (g/L): tryptone 10, yeast extract 5, NaCl 10. M9 (g/L): Na2HPO4·12H2O 15.138, KH2PO4 3, NaCl 0.5, NH4Cl 1, supplemented with 0.2% yeast extract and 20 g/L glucose for fermentation. SOB (g/L): tryptone 20, yeast extract 5, NaCl 5 (for integration procedure). 13C-MFA: 100% [1-13C]glucose at 10 g/L in chemical defined medium.

Glucose 20 g/L in fermentation medium (10 g/L [1-13C]glucose for MFA); yeast extract 0.2%; inoculation 2% (v/v) for flasks, 1% for SOB cultures; IPTG 200 µM at 12 h for CRISPRi induction; IPTG 0.5 mM for λ-Red induction; antibiotics Amp 100 µg/mL, Spc 50 µg/mL, Cm 25 µg/mL; selection plates 25 µg/mL kan or 18 µg/mL spc; ssDNA mixture 1 µM for electroporation.

Fermentation: Results report MVA titers after 72 h (Fig. 1 b-d cover 72 h); Methods state 48-h cultivation. CRISPRi induction at 12 h post-inoculation. GFP promoter characterization fluorescence read at 16 h. Pre-cultures: overnight (12 h for BW-P at 30 °C in Red protocol). DpnI digest 1 h at 37 °C; recovery 1 h after electroporation. 13C-MFA: cells harvested at exponential phase; hydrolysis 24 h at 120 °C; derivatization 1 h at 105 °C.

OD600 spectrophotometry for growth; HPLC (ion-exchange HPX-87H, RID-10A refractive index detector, 5 mM H2SO4 mobile phase at 0.5 mL/min, 65 °C) for glucose, MVA, acetate, pyruvate; GFP fluorescence normalized to OD600 at 16 h for promoter strength; 13C-MFA via GC-MS (Agilent 7890A/5975C, DB-1 column) of derivatized proteinogenic amino acids with flux estimation in 13C-Flux software; colony PCR verification of constructs.

Spectrophotometer (OD600, model unspecified); HPLC with Shimadzu RID-10A differential refractive index detector and Bio-Rad HPX-87H ion-exchange column; GC-MS Agilent 7890A GC + 5975C Mass Selective Detector with DB-1 column; electroporator (2.5 kV setting); rotary shakers (220 rpm / 120 rpm).

13C metabolic flux analysis: isotope correction for natural abundance of C/H/O/N/Si, flux estimation by minimizing residual sum of squares between measured and model-predicted 13C enrichment using 13C-Flux software (Wiechert lab; ref [33] = 13CFLUX2); MFA simulation results in Additional file 2. MVA molar conversion rate (mol/mol from glucose) computed as primary performance metric. No formal statistical tests reported.

Promoter ladder: BBa-J23100 strongest, native zwf promoter weak (between J23108 and J23114). zwf enhancement: BW-P10 BF produced 11.2 g/L MVA at 72 h with 62.2% molar conversion (abstract; Discussion states 62.2% abstract vs '64.3% and 62.3% for BBa-J23100 and BBa-J23108' in Results EXP2 paragraph - reported as strain-yield attribution nuance); BW-P08 BF 9.12 g/L. NADPH level positively correlated with zwf promoter strength; main NADPH source shifted from TCA isocitrate dehydrogenase to PPP glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase; NADH total decreased; ATP total decreased but yield increased. CRISPRi: sgRNA1 (targeting pfkA promoter) best; strain BiB1F reached 8.53 g/L MVA and 68.7% conversion rate - claimed highest MVA conversion in shake-flask fermentation; CRISPRi strains showed inhibited growth/glucose consumption and almost no acetate/ethanol byproducts.

objective.value: Fine-tune the glycolytic flux ratio between the EMP pathway and the pentose phosphate pathway (PPP) in the previously constructed EP-bifido pathway in Escherichia coli to improve NADPH supply, carbon conversion rate and mevalonate (MVA) production, by (1) enhancing zwf expression via genomic promoter replacement and (2) dynamically down-regulating pfkA using a CRISPRi system.

hypothesis.notes: Hypothesis grounded in prior 13C-MFA observation of suboptimal PPP split ratio and known growth defect of pfkA deletion.

ddr_annotation.decision_type_rationale: Q1 passes (active promoter replacement on genome), Q2 passes (strains constructed in this study, Table 1 'This study'), Q3 passes (results demonstrate non-monotonic promoter-strength/yield relation, informing future fine-tuning choices).
ddr_annotation.design_action_rationale: Enhancing zwf (glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase) expression increases oxidative PPP flux specifically to boost NADPH supply - a reducing-power supply intervention (M2 前体与还原力供给).
ddr_annotation.trigger_observation: Prior 13C-MFA of the EP-bifido MVA strain showed PPP split ratio too low (0.43:0.57 EMP:PPP vs theoretical optimum 1:6) with insufficient NADPH from oxidative PPP.
ddr_annotation.evidence_grading_rationale: Trigger and outcome are measured: prior 13C-MFA split ratio, fermentation titers, and this study's 13C-MFA showing increased oxidative PPP flux and promoter-strength-correlated NADPH.
ddr_annotation.reason_nature_rationale: Paper explicitly states the mechanism: zwf is the first key PPP gene, its enhancement raises dehydrogenase flux and NADPH generation, and measured NADPH correlated with promoter strength; mechanistic link (stoichiometric NADPH generation by G6PDH) underlies the design.
ddr_annotation.generalizable_rule: When an acetyl-CoA-derived, NADPH-dependent product (e.g., mevalonate in an E. coli EP-bifido system) is limited by an EMP/PPP split skewed toward EMP, apply graded-strength promoter replacement at the zwf locus, because increasing G6PDH flux stoichiometrically raises NADPH supply - while noting yield does not scale monotonically with promoter strength, so a promoter ladder rather than the single strongest promoter should be screened.

ddr_annotation.decision_type_rationale: Q1 passes (designed and built a tunable CRISPRi repression system targeting pfkA), Q2 passes (all CRISPRi strains constructed in this study), Q3 passes (comparison of three target sites yielded actionable finding that promoter-targeting sgRNA1 is optimal, informing future dynamic-regulation designs).
ddr_annotation.design_action_rationale: Time-controlled, inducible down-regulation of a competing-pathway node (pfkA) is dynamic regulation (M7 动态调控), replacing a permanent knockout.
ddr_annotation.trigger_observation: The static pfkA knockout in the EP-bifido strain caused severe growth defects, limiting applicability; early-growth carbon should ideally go to biomass, so flexible/timed repression was needed.
ddr_annotation.evidence_grading_rationale: Fermentation outcomes (growth, glucose, MVA titer/yield, byproducts) were measured for all six CRISPRi strains and four component controls.
ddr_annotation.reason_nature_rationale: Paper gives mechanistic reasoning: promoter-targeting sgRNA1 blocks RNA-polymerase binding via dCas9 steric hindrance while coding-region sgRNAs block elongation, yielding different repression ranges; growth-defect mechanism of pfkA loss is the stated trigger. Choice of weak promoter BBa-J23134 for dcas9 explicitly motivated by avoiding dCas9 toxicity.
ddr_annotation.generalizable_rule: When a competing-glycolytic-pathway knockout (e.g., pfkA) improves product yield but causes severe growth defects in an E. coli acetyl-CoA-derived production system, apply inducible CRISPRi repression targeting the gene's promoter region with a weakly expressed dCas9, because tunable, time-delayed transcriptional repression preserves early-growth EMP flux while still redirecting carbon toward the product pathway after induction.
alternatives_considered: Promoter-replacement methods for down-regulation (rejected: CRISPRi does not require genome editing of the target gene)
Post-transcriptional/post-translational tools such as anti-sense RNA and RNAi (mentioned as alternatives, not tested)

objective.value: Fine-tune the glycolytic flux ratio between the EMP pathway and the pentose phosphate pathway (PPP) in the previously constructed EP-bifido pathway in Escherichia coli to improve NADPH supply, carbon conversion rate and mevalonate (MVA) production, by (1) enhancing zwf expression via genomic promoter replacement and (2) dynamically down-regulating pfkA using a CRISPRi system.
objective.notes: The EP-bifido pathway itself (fxpk + fbp introduction, edd and pfkA knockout) was constructed in a previous study [13]; this paper optimizes it.

hypothesis.value: The detected EMP:PPP carbon split (0.43:0.57) deviates from the theoretical optimum (1:6), yielding insufficient NADPH; enhancing PPP flux by up-regulating zwf, and time-controlled repression of pfkA (whose knockout causes severe growth defects) via CRISPRi, will redirect flux, balance reducing power and improve MVA yield.
hypothesis.notes: Hypothesis grounded in prior 13C-MFA observation of suboptimal PPP split ratio and known growth defect of pfkA deletion.

Production strains carry pBSA (pTrc99a with atoB from E. coli, mvaS and mvaA from L. casei, tac promoter, AmpR) and pFF (pCDFduet with fxpk from B. adolescentis and fbp from E. coli).

engineering_method.value: (1) Red-mediated homologous recombination (pTKRED helper, pKD3/pKD4 template CmR/kan cassettes, 300-500 bp homology arms, electroporation of ssDNA/PCR fragments) to replace the genomic zwf promoter with Anderson library promoters of graded strengths. (2) Plasmid reconstruction replacing the tac promoter of pBSA with five Anderson promoters. (3) CRISPRi: dcas9 under weak promoter BBa-J23134 and three sgRNAs targeting pfkA (promoter region; +100 bp and +200 bp downstream of start codon), assembled into pFF and pBSA under IPTG-inducible promoter; induction with 200 µM IPTG at 12 h of fermentation. (4) GFP reporter assay to characterize promoter strength.

ddr_annotation.decision_type_rationale: Q1 passes (active promoter replacement on genome), Q2 passes (strains constructed in this study, Table 1 'This study'), Q3 passes (results demonstrate non-monotonic promoter-strength/yield relation, informing future fine-tuning choices).
ddr_annotation.design_action_rationale: Enhancing zwf (glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase) expression increases oxidative PPP flux specifically to boost NADPH supply - a reducing-power supply intervention (M2 前体与还原力供给).
ddr_annotation.trigger_observation: Prior 13C-MFA of the EP-bifido MVA strain showed PPP split ratio too low (0.43:0.57 EMP:PPP vs theoretical optimum 1:6) with insufficient NADPH from oxidative PPP.
ddr_annotation.evidence_grading_rationale: Trigger and outcome are measured: prior 13C-MFA split ratio, fermentation titers, and this study's 13C-MFA showing increased oxidative PPP flux and promoter-strength-correlated NADPH.
ddr_annotation.reason_nature_rationale: Paper explicitly states the mechanism: zwf is the first key PPP gene, its enhancement raises dehydrogenase flux and NADPH generation, and measured NADPH correlated with promoter strength; mechanistic link (stoichiometric NADPH generation by G6PDH) underlies the design.
ddr_annotation.generalizable_rule: When an acetyl-CoA-derived, NADPH-dependent product (e.g., mevalonate in an E. coli EP-bifido system) is limited by an EMP/PPP split skewed toward EMP, apply graded-strength promoter replacement at the zwf locus, because increasing G6PDH flux stoichiometrically raises NADPH supply - while noting yield does not scale monotonically with promoter strength, so a promoter ladder rather than the single strongest promoter should be screened.

experiments.purpose: Confirm that zwf enhancement redistributed flux from EMP to PPP and quantify cofactor (NADPH/NADH/ATP) generation changes

experiments.analysis: 13C-Flux software minimizing residual sum of squares; isotope natural-abundance correction
experiments.outcome: Oxidative PPP flux increased, TCA flux decreased in zwf-enhanced strains; NADPH main source shifted from ICDH (TCA) to G6PDH (PPP); NADH decreased; ATP yield per glucose increased but total ATP decreased; TCA flux difference between BW-P10 BF and BW-P08 BF may explain growth differences

experiments.purpose: Replace the static, growth-damaging pfkA knockout with time-controlled, tunable CRISPRi repression to dynamically balance EMP/PPP flux and improve MVA conversion
experiments.host: BW25113 23100-zwf (pfkA intact, zwf promoter replaced with BBa-J23100) carrying CRISPRi plasmid combinations: pBSA-dCas9+pFF-sgRNA1/2/3 (BiBF1-3) or pBSA-sgRNA1/2/3+pFF-dCas9 (BiB1F/BiB2F/BiB3F)
experiments.intervention: CRISPRi system: dcas9 under weak promoter BBa-J23134; three sgRNAs targeting pfkA promoter region (sgRNA1), +100 bp (sgRNA2) and +200 bp (sgRNA3) downstream of start codon; IPTG-inducible expression, induced with 200 µM IPTG at 12 h

experiments.control: BBF (BW25113 23100-zwf + pFF + pBSA, no CRISPRi); additional component controls BB1F, BBFd, BiBd1F (EXP5, Figure S1)

experiments.analysis: comparison across three sgRNA target sites and vs controls
experiments.outcome: sgRNA1 (promoter-targeting) gave best repression balance; BiB1F reached 8.53 g/L MVA and 68.7% molar conversion - highest reported shake-flask MVA conversion; CRISPRi introduction reduced growth and glucose consumption (attributed to dCas9 toxicity/leaky expression); acetate/ethanol byproducts hardly detected

ddr_annotation.decision_type_rationale: Q1 passes (designed and built a tunable CRISPRi repression system targeting pfkA), Q2 passes (all CRISPRi strains constructed in this study), Q3 passes (comparison of three target sites yielded actionable finding that promoter-targeting sgRNA1 is optimal, informing future dynamic-regulation designs).
ddr_annotation.design_action_rationale: Time-controlled, inducible down-regulation of a competing-pathway node (pfkA) is dynamic regulation (M7 动态调控), replacing a permanent knockout.
ddr_annotation.trigger_observation: The static pfkA knockout in the EP-bifido strain caused severe growth defects, limiting applicability; early-growth carbon should ideally go to biomass, so flexible/timed repression was needed.
ddr_annotation.evidence_grading_rationale: Fermentation outcomes (growth, glucose, MVA titer/yield, byproducts) were measured for all six CRISPRi strains and four component controls.
ddr_annotation.reason_nature_rationale: Paper gives mechanistic reasoning: promoter-targeting sgRNA1 blocks RNA-polymerase binding via dCas9 steric hindrance while coding-region sgRNAs block elongation, yielding different repression ranges; growth-defect mechanism of pfkA loss is the stated trigger. Choice of weak promoter BBa-J23134 for dcas9 explicitly motivated by avoiding dCas9 toxicity.
ddr_annotation.generalizable_rule: When a competing-glycolytic-pathway knockout (e.g., pfkA) improves product yield but causes severe growth defects in an E. coli acetyl-CoA-derived production system, apply inducible CRISPRi repression targeting the gene's promoter region with a weakly expressed dCas9, because tunable, time-delayed transcriptional repression preserves early-growth EMP flux while still redirecting carbon toward the product pathway after induction.
alternatives_considered: Promoter-replacement methods for down-regulation (rejected: CRISPRi does not require genome editing of the target gene)
Post-transcriptional/post-translational tools such as anti-sense RNA and RNAi (mentioned as alternatives, not tested)

unsupported_values: Design, construct and tune bifunctional (positive- and negative-response) glycolysis-flux biosensors based on the Cra-FBP pair that sense intracellular fructose-1,6-diphosphate (FBP) and dynamically regulate glycolysis flux, then apply them to balance biosynthesis of mevalonate (MVA) and N-acetylglucosamine (GlcNAc) in Escherichia coli.

Because intracellular FBP concentration is linearly related to glycolysis flux (via FBP feedforward activation of pyruvate kinase), a Cra/FBP-based transcriptional biosensor can report flux in vivo and drive autonomous, timely dynamic repression/activation of pathway genes, outperforming static knockout and IPTG-induced CRISPRi control.
E. coli BW25113 (control/parent for biosensor characterization and deficiency-strain comparison)
BW-pfkA, BW-ptsG, BW-pykF (single-gene deficiency strains used for biosensor validation)
BW-Pzwf::P23109 (zwf promoter replaced by P23109; non-regulated MVA control)
BW-PMT (pfkA promoter replaced by Ppam from pL19), BW-PR (pfkA promoter replaced by Ppar from pL25)
DN5 (modified DH5alpha, knockout of nag, ackA, poxB, ldhA, nan; constructed in previous studies)
DN5-IM, DN5-PM (pfkA promoter replaced by Ppam/Ppar), DN5-GM (pBacm), DN5-GAR (pBacar), DN5-IMM (DN5-IM + pBacm), DN5-IMAR (figure caption only)

Genomic promoter replacements: Pzwf -> P23109; PpfkA -> Ppam (pL19) or Ppar (pL25). Plasmid constructs: pL01-pL10/pL15-pL18 positive-response biosensors, pL19-pL30 negative-response biosensors, pL35 carrying Cra with amino acid mutations at positions 57, 58, 59, 60 under P23102; pBacm (glmS under PM23107 from pL09), pBacar (glmS under PR23107-cra from pL18 plus cra with P23102). DN5 knockout set: nag, ackA, poxB, ldhA, nan (prior work).

Genome promoter replacement (zwf, pfkA loci); construction of plasmid-based Cra/TFBS biosensor circuits; tuning via (1) core promoter strength, (2) TFBS position on promoter, (3) Cra-box sequence affinity, (4) Cra expression level (overexpression), (5) Cra ligand-binding affinity by site mutagenesis (aa 57-60); Hill-function-guided quantitative tuning; dynamic promoter swapping to create FBP-responsive repression of pfkA and activation of glmS.
Biosensor characterization: BW25113 harboring each biosensor plasmid (pL01-pL10, pL15-pL18, pL19-pL30, pL35), dose-response series with extracellular FBP
Deficiency-strain validation: BW-pfkA, BW-ptsG, BW-pykF vs BW25113, all harboring pL19
MVA: BW-Pzwf::P23109 (non-regulated), BW-PMT, BW-PR (shake flask; BW-PR also 1-L fermenter)
GlcNAc: DN5, DN5-PM, DN5-IM, DN5-GM, DN5-GAR, DN5-IMM, DN5-IMAR

BW25113 (fluorescence reference in Fig. 4); CK- (no pL18 plasmid), CK (0 g/L acetate, 0 mM FBP), and 0 mM FBP + 10 g/L acetate baseline in Fig. 2D; non-regulated strain BW-Pzwf::P23109 (MVA control); DN5 (GlcNAc control, 0.46 g/L); static-knockout BW-delta-pfkA EP-bifido strain and IPTG-CRISPRi EP-bifido strain (Li et al. 2021) as prior-art benchmarks.

Shake-flask fermentation for strain comparison; 1-L fermenter for BW-PR scale-up; glucose as sole carbon source in GlcNAc experiments; biosensor strains cultured 18 h before fluorescence detection; BW-PR reached stationary phase after 12 h; intracellular FBP in BW-PR dropped after 15 h.
Extracellular FBP added at 0.001-400 mM together with 10 g/L acetate for pL18 dose-response (Fig. 2D); no chemical inducer used for dynamic control (autonomous FBP sensing).
Fluorescence measured at 18 h of culture (Fig. 4); stationary phase after 12 h (BW-PR shake flask); intracellular FBP dropped suddenly after 15 h; fermenter cultivation 120 h.

Biosensor fluorescence output (dose-response curves); intracellular FBP concentration measurement; pfkA in vivo mRNA level; specific glucose consumption rate; specific growth rate; MVA and GlcNAc titers; acetate/byproduct profiling.

Hill function fitting of dose-response curves; derivation of dynamic range and threshold EC50; linear correlation analysis of intracellular FBP vs glucose consumption rate, growth rate and fluorescence; mRNA-level comparison between regulated and non-regulated strains.

Tuned negative-response biosensor pL19 detects intracellular FBP over ~0-50 mmol/g DCW, covering the reported physiological 0-31 mM/g DCW range; fluorescence of BW-pfkA, BW-ptsG, BW-pykF was 11.32, 7.13, 1.11x BW25113 at 18 h (order BW-pfkA > BW-ptsG > BW-pykF > BW25113). MVA: BW-PR produced 73.31 g/L MVA in shake flask (carbon yield 63.00 mol%, highest shake-flask MVA to date per authors) with <0.1 g/L acetate and no other byproducts; BW-PMT <2.47 g/L acetate; 111.3 g/L MVA after 120 h in 1-L fermenter with no by-products. GlcNAc: DN5-IM 8.65 g/L vs DN5 0.46 g/L; DN5-GM 6.33 and DN5-GAR 7.98 g/L; DN5-IMM 8.63 g/L; simultaneous pfkA repression + glmS activation gave no obvious titer increase over single regulation. Dynamic control outperformed IPTG-CRISPRi benchmark (8.53 g/L, Li et al. 2021; 0.12x of BW-PR).

inference.rationale: Introduction (1_introduction_p003) presents the FBP-flux linear relationship (cited to Kochanowski et al. 2013, a background_citation) as the premise; Results compare dynamic control against permanent pfkA deletion and cite Li et al. 2021 CRISPRi as inferior, implying the tested hypothesis.

hypothesis.notes: The FBP-flux linearity premise itself is attributed to prior literature (background_citation), not newly demonstrated by this paper except via the deficiency-strain validation experiment.

outcomes.value: Tuned negative-response biosensor pL19 detects intracellular FBP over ~0-50 mmol/g DCW, covering the reported physiological 0-31 mM/g DCW range; fluorescence of BW-pfkA, BW-ptsG, BW-pykF was 11.32, 7.13, 1.11x BW25113 at 18 h (order BW-pfkA > BW-ptsG > BW-pykF > BW25113). MVA: BW-PR produced 73.31 g/L MVA in shake flask (carbon yield 63.00 mol%, highest shake-flask MVA to date per authors) with <0.1 g/L acetate and no other byproducts; BW-PMT <2.47 g/L acetate; 111.3 g/L MVA after 120 h in 1-L fermenter with no by-products. GlcNAc: DN5-IM 8.65 g/L vs DN5 0.46 g/L; DN5-GM 6.33 and DN5-GAR 7.98 g/L; DN5-IMM 8.63 g/L; simultaneous pfkA repression + glmS activation gave no obvious titer increase over single regulation. Dynamic control outperformed IPTG-CRISPRi benchmark (8.53 g/L, Li et al. 2021; 0.12x of BW-PR).
outcomes.notes: Author claims ('highest to date', 'timely and gradually blocked') are author_interpretation; titer numbers are direct_observations bound to stated strains/conditions.

experiments.purpose: Create and tune positive-response FBP biosensors (pL01-pL10; refined pL15-pL18) with varied thresholds/dynamic ranges.

interventions.description: Promoter-architecture engineering of Cra-regulated promoters (core promoter strength, TFBS position, Cra-box sequence) to build pL01-pL10 and refined pL15-pL18.

ddr_annotation.decision_type_rationale: Q1 yes (de novo promoter circuit construction), Q2 yes (this study), Q3 yes (variants with distinct thresholds enabled later selection of Ppam/PM23107 for applications).
ddr_annotation.design_action_rationale: Construction of metabolite-responsive dynamic regulation components (sensor-regulator).
ddr_annotation.trigger_observation: Few biosensors exist for central glycolytic metabolites; glycolysis flux imbalance (overflow at high flux, poor growth at low flux) lacks autonomous regulation systems.
ddr_annotation.evidence_grading_rationale: Dose-response curves measured in vivo and Hill-fitted (Fig. 2A,C,E).
ddr_annotation.reason_nature_rationale: Design based on stated transcription-regulation equilibrium among FBP, Cra and operator DNA (4_discussion_p004), i.e., explicit mechanistic basis.
ddr_annotation.generalizable_rule: When building an FBP/Cra-based glycolysis-flux sensor in E. coli, tune core promoter strength, TFBS position and Cra-box affinity so the sensor threshold and dynamic range span the physiological intracellular FBP range, because sensor output is set by the FBP-Cra-DNA equilibrium. (Validated only for Cra/FBP biosensors in E. coli in this paper.)

interventions.description: Tuning by Cra overexpression and by mutating Cra ligand-binding affinity (positive-response branch, Fig. 2B).

ddr_annotation.decision_type_rationale: Deliberate modification of regulator level/affinity to shift sensor response; informs tunability claims.
ddr_annotation.design_action_rationale: Regulator-level tuning of the dynamic control circuit.
ddr_annotation.trigger_observation: Initial promoter variants did not cover desired thresholds/dynamic ranges (implied by need for further tuning axes).
ddr_annotation.evidence_grading_rationale: Resulting sensors characterized by measured dose-response (Fig. 2C,E).
ddr_annotation.reason_nature_rationale: Affinity/expression-level changes act on the Cra-FBP-DNA equilibrium, as explicitly reasoned in Discussion.
ddr_annotation.generalizable_rule: When a TF-based metabolite sensor's threshold is mismatched to the in vivo effector range in E. coli, adjust regulator expression level or ligand-binding affinity of the TF, because both shift the occupancy equilibrium of the operator. (Validated for Cra/FBP in E. coli only.)
alternatives_considered: Cra-overexpressing plasmid sensors were later excluded from application cases because of Cra's global regulatory impact (4_discussion_p004).

experiments.purpose: Create and tune negative-response FBP biosensors (pL19-pL30; pL35 with Cra aa57-60 mutations).

interventions.description: Promoter engineering to convert Cra regulation into negative-response output (pL19-pL30); site mutagenesis of Cra at amino acids 57-60 under P23102 (pL35).

ddr_annotation.decision_type_rationale: New circuit construction plus rationally placed TF mutations; pL19/pL25 later selected for pfkA control.
ddr_annotation.design_action_rationale: Negative-response sensor-regulator for dynamic down-regulation.
ddr_annotation.trigger_observation: Need to down-regulate glycolysis (pfkA) autonomously when FBP (flux proxy) is high; positive-response sensors alone cannot repress.
ddr_annotation.evidence_grading_rationale: Measured dose-response curves and Hill fits (Fig. 3A,C); pL35 characterized by dose-response (Fig. 3B).
ddr_annotation.reason_nature_rationale: TFBS position and TF structural changes alter regulation mode (4_discussion_p006) - mechanistic reasoning given by authors.
ddr_annotation.generalizable_rule: When a pathway gene must be repressed at high glycolysis flux in E. coli, place Cra TFBS so that FBP-bound Cra relieves/reorganizes repression to yield negative FBP-response, and tune via Cra ligand-affinity mutations, because regulation sign and dose-response are set by TFBS position and TF-ligand affinity. (Validated for Cra-based circuits in E. coli only.)

experiments.purpose: Replace static pfkA knockout in the EP-bifido pathway with FBP-responsive dynamic repression to resolve growth/production trade-off and maximize MVA.

interventions.description: Genomic replacement of the zwf promoter with the stronger P23109 promoter (strain BW-Pzwf::P23109).

ddr_annotation.decision_type_rationale: Q1 yes (promoter replacement this study), Q2 yes (performed here on the EP-bifido background), Q3 yes (creates the base strain onto which dynamic pfkA control is layered).
ddr_annotation.design_action_rationale: Enhancing PP pathway entry (G6P dehydrogenase, Zwf) to supply fructose-6-phosphate and NADPH for the EP-bifido route.
ddr_annotation.trigger_observation: Prior EP-bifido design (Wang et al. 2019) requires sufficient F6P and NADPH supply from the PP pathway; natural glycolysis was previously blocked by permanent pfkA deletion.
ddr_annotation.evidence_grading_rationale: Resulting strain phenotypes (growth, glucose uptake, MVA) measured in this study.
ddr_annotation.reason_nature_rationale: Rationale explicitly stated: stronger zwf promoter enhances PP pathway flux for F6P/NADPH supply (stoichiometric/pathway mechanism).
ddr_annotation.generalizable_rule: When an EP-bifido-type acetyl-CoA/F6P supply pathway in E. coli is limited by PP pathway throughput, up-regulate zwf via a stronger constitutive promoter, because Zwf controls carbon entry into the PP pathway that delivers F6P and NADPH. (Validated for MVA production in this E. coli EP-bifido system.)

interventions.description: Genomic replacement of the pfkA promoter with negative-response biosensor promoters Ppam (pL19) or Ppar (pL25), yielding BW-PMT and BW-PR (dynamic EP-bifido pathway).

ddr_annotation.decision_type_rationale: Q1 yes (genomic promoter replacement), Q2 yes (this study), Q3 yes (two thresholds compared; Ppar selected as superior, guiding the final strain).
ddr_annotation.design_action_rationale: Metabolite-responsive dynamic down-regulation of a competing glycolysis step.
ddr_annotation.trigger_observation: Permanent pfkA deletion severely suppressed growth and glucose uptake, capping MVA at 11.02 g/L despite 64.3 mol% yield - a measured growth/production trade-off demanding dynamic instead of static control.
ddr_annotation.evidence_grading_rationale: Measured titers, growth, mRNA and FBP time courses for BW-PMT/BW-PR vs non-regulated control.
ddr_annotation.reason_nature_rationale: Mechanistic logic explicit: sense FBP (flux proxy) to repress pfkA only after growth phase, switching flux into EP-bifido and uncoupling growth from production.
ddr_annotation.generalizable_rule: When static knockout of an essential glycolytic step (e.g., pfkA) in E. coli collapses growth and substrate uptake, replace the native promoter with a biosensor promoter negatively responsive to intracellular FBP, because FBP reports glycolytic flux and enables automatic growth-then-production switching. (Validated for MVA via EP-bifido in E. coli; extended to GlcNAc in EXP5.)
alternatives_considered: IPTG-induced CRISPRi repression of pfkA (Li et al. 2021) - external-inducer strategy; yielded only 8.53 g/L MVA (0.12x of BW-PR) and requires inducer timing; cited as inferior benchmark (background_citation).

interventions.description: Scale-up fermentation of BW-PR in a 1-L fermenter.

ddr_annotation.decision_type_rationale: Q3 not passed: fermentation of the already-selected BW-PR evaluates performance at scale without introducing a new design modification.

experiments.conditions: Shake flask; 1-L fermenter 120 h; feeding/medium unknown (Methods absent; Supplementary Figs. 6-7 not available).
experiments.controls: Non-regulated BW-Pzwf::P23109; prior static-knockout BW-delta-pfkA EP-bifido (background_citation benchmark, Wang et al. 2019); IPTG-CRISPRi strain (background_citation benchmark, Li et al. 2021).
experiments.readouts: MVA titer and carbon yield; growth; glucose uptake; acetate/byproducts; pfkA mRNA; intracellular FBP.
experiments.analysis: Time-course comparison of growth/production; mRNA and FBP trends as dynamic-control confirmation.
experiments.outcome: BW-PR: 73.31 g/L MVA, 63.00 mol% carbon yield, <0.1 g/L acetate, stationary phase after 12 h, FBP drop after 15 h; fermenter: 111.3 g/L at 120 h, no by-products. BW-PMT accumulated <2.47 g/L acetate.
experiments.scope_notes: Dynamic-regulation claims supported within tested conditions only; mRNA/FBP confirmation is correlative to promoter replacement (no inducer-timing sweep shown in main text).

experiments.purpose: Balance glycolysis and GlcNAc biosynthesis at the F6P node by dynamically repressing pfkA and/or activating glmS.
experiments.host: E. coli DN5 (DH5alpha derivative, delta-nag delta-ackA delta-poxB delta-ldhA delta-nan; constructed in previous studies - background)

interventions.description: Genomic replacement of pfkA promoter in DN5 with Ppam (pL19) or Ppar (pL25), yielding DN5-IM and DN5-PM.

ddr_annotation.decision_type_rationale: Q1 yes, Q2 yes, Q3 yes (two promoter strengths compared for this second product context).
ddr_annotation.design_action_rationale: Same dynamic-control strategy transferred to a second pathway context.
ddr_annotation.trigger_observation: Lower glycolysis is a competitive pathway for GlcNAc synthesis from glucose; F6P is the shared precursor, so pfkA must be down-regulated.
ddr_annotation.evidence_grading_rationale: Measured GlcNAc titers, growth and glucose consumption for DN5-IM/DN5-PM vs DN5.
ddr_annotation.reason_nature_rationale: Explicit node-competition mechanism stated for F6P between glycolysis and GlcNAc pathway.
ddr_annotation.generalizable_rule: When a product draws fructose-6-phosphate as precursor in glucose-grown E. coli, dynamically repress pfkA with an FBP-negative-response promoter, because this diverts F6P from lower glycolysis to the product while preserving early growth. (Validated for GlcNAc in the DN5 background.)

interventions.description: Plasmid-based dynamic activation of glmS using positive-response promoters PM23107 (pBacm) and PR23107-cra plus cra/P23102 (pBacar), transformed into DN5 to give DN5-GM and DN5-GAR.

ddr_annotation.decision_type_rationale: Q1 yes, Q2 yes, Q3 yes (two activation architectures compared; FBP-responsiveness of glmS activation verified).
ddr_annotation.design_action_rationale: Metabolite-responsive up-regulation of the product-forming enzyme (F6P aminotransferase).
ddr_annotation.trigger_observation: glmS needs up-regulation for GlcNAc overproduction, but early-stage overexpression may cause bacterial lysis and growth inhibition (Deng et al. 2005), so constitutive strong expression is unsuitable.
ddr_annotation.evidence_grading_rationale: Measured GlcNAc titers for DN5-GM (6.33 g/L) and DN5-GAR (7.98 g/L) vs DN5 (0.46 g/L).
ddr_annotation.reason_nature_rationale: Mechanistic need (F6P aminotransferase flux) combined with explicit literature-based toxicity concern (Deng et al. 2005) motivating timed activation.
ddr_annotation.generalizable_rule: When overexpression of a product-pathway enzyme is toxic in early growth (e.g., glmS in E. coli), drive it with a positive-response biosensor promoter activated as FBP accumulates, because induction is delayed until the production phase, avoiding lysis. (Validated for GlcNAc in DN5.)

interventions.description: Simultaneous dynamic repression of pfkA and activation of glmS (pBacm or pBacar into DN5-IM), yielding DN5-IMM and DN5-IMAR.

ddr_annotation.decision_type_rationale: Q1 yes, Q2 yes, Q3 yes (tests whether dual control exceeds single regulation - a design-relevant negative/comparative result).
ddr_annotation.design_action_rationale: Layered dual dynamic regulation at one metabolic node.
ddr_annotation.trigger_observation: Hypothesis that combining both arms of node control (repress competitor + activate product path) would further raise GlcNAc titer.
ddr_annotation.evidence_grading_rationale: Measured titer DN5-IMM 8.63 g/L vs single-regulation strains; FBP levels measured in DN5/DN5-IM/DN5-GAR/DN5-IMM.
ddr_annotation.reason_nature_rationale: Push-pull node engineering rationale explicitly described in Fig. 6A narrative.
ddr_annotation.generalizable_rule: When single dynamic repression of pfkA already restores most of the achievable F6P-to-GlcNAc flux in E. coli DN5, adding dynamic glmS activation on top gives no obvious further titer gain, because the node flux is already saturated by competitor repression. (Observed only in this DN5/GlcNAc context; do not generalize.)

experiments.conditions: Glucose as sole carbon source; shake-flask production implied; detailed conditions unknown (Methods absent; Supplementary Fig. 8 unavailable).
experiments.controls: DN5 (0.46 g/L GlcNAc).
experiments.readouts: GlcNAc titer; growth; glucose consumption; intracellular FBP.
experiments.analysis: Titer/growth comparison; FBP-level interpretation per strain.
experiments.outcome: DN5-IM 8.65 g/L; DN5-GM 6.33; DN5-GAR 7.98; DN5-IMM 8.63 g/L; dual regulation not obviously higher than single; FBP lower in DN5-IM/DN5-IMM, unchanged in DN5-GAR. DN5-IMAR titer not reported in available text.
