objective.value: Design, construct and tune bifunctional (positive- and negative-response) glycolysis-flux biosensors based on the Cra-FBP pair that sense intracellular fructose-1,6-diphosphate (FBP) and dynamically regulate glycolysis flux, then apply them to balance biosynthesis of mevalonate (MVA) and N-acetylglucosamine (GlcNAc) in Escherichia coli.
objective.notes: Abstract explicitly states design/construction of bifunctional glycolysis flux biosensor and application to MVA and GlcNAc.

hypothesis.value: Because intracellular FBP concentration is linearly related to glycolysis flux (via FBP feedforward activation of pyruvate kinase), a Cra/FBP-based transcriptional biosensor can report flux in vivo and drive autonomous, timely dynamic repression/activation of pathway genes, outperforming static knockout and IPTG-induced CRISPRi control.

inference.rationale: Introduction (1_introduction_p003) presents the FBP-flux linear relationship (cited to Kochanowski et al. 2013, a background_citation) as the premise; Results compare dynamic control against permanent pfkA deletion and cite Li et al. 2021 CRISPRi as inferior, implying the tested hypothesis.

hypothesis.notes: The FBP-flux linearity premise itself is attributed to prior literature (background_citation), not newly demonstrated by this paper except via the deficiency-strain validation experiment.

outcomes.value: Tuned negative-response biosensor pL19 detects intracellular FBP over ~0-50 mmol/g DCW, covering the reported physiological 0-31 mM/g DCW range; fluorescence of BW-pfkA, BW-ptsG, BW-pykF was 11.32, 7.13, 1.11x BW25113 at 18 h (order BW-pfkA > BW-ptsG > BW-pykF > BW25113). MVA: BW-PR produced 73.31 g/L MVA in shake flask (carbon yield 63.00 mol%, highest shake-flask MVA to date per authors) with <0.1 g/L acetate and no other byproducts; BW-PMT <2.47 g/L acetate; 111.3 g/L MVA after 120 h in 1-L fermenter with no by-products. Dynamic control outperformed IPTG-CRISPRi benchmark (8.53 g/L, Li et al. 2021; 0.12x of BW-PR).

experiments.purpose: Create and tune positive-response FBP biosensors (pL01-pL10; refined pL15-pL18) with varied thresholds/dynamic ranges.

interventions.description: Promoter-architecture engineering of Cra-regulated promoters (core promoter strength, TFBS position, Cra-box sequence) to build pL01-pL10 and refined pL15-pL18.

ddr_annotation.decision_type_rationale: Q1 yes (de novo promoter circuit construction), Q2 yes (this study), Q3 yes (variants with distinct thresholds enabled later selection of Ppam/PM23107 for applications).
ddr_annotation.design_action_rationale: Construction of metabolite-responsive dynamic regulation components (sensor-regulator).
ddr_annotation.trigger_observation: Few biosensors exist for central glycolytic metabolites; glycolysis flux imbalance (overflow at high flux, poor growth at low flux) lacks autonomous regulation systems.
ddr_annotation.evidence_grading_rationale: Dose-response curves measured in vivo and Hill-fitted (Fig. 2A,C,E).
ddr_annotation.reason_nature_rationale: Design based on stated transcription-regulation equilibrium among FBP, Cra and operator DNA (4_discussion_p004), i.e., explicit mechanistic basis.
ddr_annotation.generalizable_rule: When building an FBP/Cra-based glycolysis-flux sensor in E. coli, tune core promoter strength, TFBS position and Cra-box affinity so the sensor threshold and dynamic range span the physiological intracellular FBP range, because sensor output is set by the FBP-Cra-DNA equilibrium. (Validated only for Cra/FBP biosensors in E. coli in this paper.)

interventions.description: Tuning by Cra overexpression and by mutating Cra ligand-binding affinity (positive-response branch, Fig. 2B).

ddr_annotation.decision_type_rationale: Deliberate modification of regulator level/affinity to shift sensor response; informs tunability claims.
ddr_annotation.design_action_rationale: Regulator-level tuning of the dynamic control circuit.
ddr_annotation.trigger_observation: Initial promoter variants did not cover desired thresholds/dynamic ranges (implied by need for further tuning axes).
ddr_annotation.evidence_grading_rationale: Resulting sensors characterized by measured dose-response (Fig. 2C,E).
ddr_annotation.reason_nature_rationale: Affinity/expression-level changes act on the Cra-FBP-DNA equilibrium, as explicitly reasoned in Discussion.
ddr_annotation.generalizable_rule: When a TF-based metabolite sensor's threshold is mismatched to the in vivo effector range in E. coli, adjust regulator expression level or ligand-binding affinity of the TF, because both shift the occupancy equilibrium of the operator. (Validated for Cra/FBP in E. coli only.)
alternatives_considered: Cra-overexpressing plasmid sensors were later excluded from application cases because of Cra's global regulatory impact (4_discussion_p004).

experiments.purpose: Replace static pfkA knockout in the EP-bifido pathway with FBP-responsive dynamic repression to resolve growth/production trade-off and maximize MVA.

interventions.description: Genomic replacement of the zwf promoter with the stronger P23109 promoter (strain BW-Pzwf::P23109).

ddr_annotation.decision_type_rationale: Q1 yes (promoter replacement this study), Q2 yes (performed here on the EP-bifido background), Q3 yes (creates the base strain onto which dynamic pfkA control is layered).
ddr_annotation.design_action_rationale: Enhancing PP pathway entry (G6P dehydrogenase, Zwf) to supply fructose-6-phosphate and NADPH for the EP-bifido route.
ddr_annotation.trigger_observation: Prior EP-bifido design (Wang et al. 2019) requires sufficient F6P and NADPH supply from the PP pathway; natural glycolysis was previously blocked by permanent pfkA deletion.
ddr_annotation.evidence_grading_rationale: Resulting strain phenotypes (growth, glucose uptake, MVA) measured in this study.
ddr_annotation.reason_nature_rationale: Rationale explicitly stated: stronger zwf promoter enhances PP pathway flux for F6P/NADPH supply (stoichiometric/pathway mechanism).
ddr_annotation.generalizable_rule: When an EP-bifido-type acetyl-CoA/F6P supply pathway in E. coli is limited by PP pathway throughput, up-regulate zwf via a stronger constitutive promoter, because Zwf controls carbon entry into the PP pathway that delivers F6P and NADPH. (Validated for MVA production in this E. coli EP-bifido system.)

interventions.description: Genomic replacement of the pfkA promoter with negative-response biosensor promoters Ppam (pL19) or Ppar (pL25), yielding BW-PMT and BW-PR (dynamic EP-bifido pathway).

ddr_annotation.decision_type_rationale: Q1 yes (genomic promoter replacement), Q2 yes (this study), Q3 yes (two thresholds compared; Ppar selected as superior, guiding the final strain).
ddr_annotation.design_action_rationale: Metabolite-responsive dynamic down-regulation of a competing glycolysis step.
ddr_annotation.trigger_observation: Permanent pfkA deletion severely suppressed growth and glucose uptake, capping MVA at 11.02 g/L despite 64.3 mol% yield - a measured growth/production trade-off demanding dynamic instead of static control.
ddr_annotation.evidence_grading_rationale: Measured titers, growth, mRNA and FBP time courses for BW-PMT/BW-PR vs non-regulated control.
ddr_annotation.reason_nature_rationale: Mechanistic logic explicit: sense FBP (flux proxy) to repress pfkA only after growth phase, switching flux into EP-bifido and uncoupling growth from production.
ddr_annotation.generalizable_rule: When static knockout of an essential glycolytic step (e.g., pfkA) in E. coli collapses growth and substrate uptake, replace the native promoter with a biosensor promoter negatively responsive to intracellular FBP, because FBP reports glycolytic flux and enables automatic growth-then-production switching. (Validated for MVA via EP-bifido in E. coli; extended to GlcNAc in EXP5.)
alternatives_considered: IPTG-induced CRISPRi repression of pfkA (Li et al. 2021) - external-inducer strategy; yielded only 8.53 g/L MVA (0.12x of BW-PR) and requires inducer timing; cited as inferior benchmark (background_citation).

experiments.purpose: Balance glycolysis and GlcNAc biosynthesis at the F6P node by dynamically repressing pfkA and/or activating glmS.
experiments.host: E. coli DN5 (DH5alpha derivative, delta-nag delta-ackA delta-poxB delta-ldhA delta-nan; constructed in previous studies - background)

interventions.description: Genomic replacement of pfkA promoter in DN5 with Ppam (pL19) or Ppar (pL25), yielding DN5-IM and DN5-PM.

ddr_annotation.decision_type_rationale: Q1 yes, Q2 yes, Q3 yes (two promoter strengths compared for this second product context).
ddr_annotation.design_action_rationale: Same dynamic-control strategy transferred to a second pathway context.
ddr_annotation.trigger_observation: Lower glycolysis is a competitive pathway for GlcNAc synthesis from glucose; F6P is the shared precursor, so pfkA must be down-regulated.
ddr_annotation.evidence_grading_rationale: Measured GlcNAc titers, growth and glucose consumption for DN5-IM/DN5-PM vs DN5.
ddr_annotation.reason_nature_rationale: Explicit node-competition mechanism stated for F6P between glycolysis and GlcNAc pathway.
ddr_annotation.generalizable_rule: When a product draws fructose-6-phosphate as precursor in glucose-grown E. coli, dynamically repress pfkA with an FBP-negative-response promoter, because this diverts F6P from lower glycolysis to the product while preserving early growth. (Validated for GlcNAc in the DN5 background.)

interventions.description: Plasmid-based dynamic activation of glmS using positive-response promoters PM23107 (pBacm) and PR23107-cra plus cra/P23102 (pBacar), transformed into DN5 to give DN5-GM and DN5-GAR.

ddr_annotation.decision_type_rationale: Q1 yes, Q2 yes, Q3 yes (two activation architectures compared; FBP-responsiveness of glmS activation verified).
ddr_annotation.design_action_rationale: Metabolite-responsive up-regulation of the product-forming enzyme (F6P aminotransferase).
ddr_annotation.trigger_observation: glmS needs up-regulation for GlcNAc overproduction, but early-stage overexpression may cause bacterial lysis and growth inhibition (Deng et al. 2005), so constitutive strong expression is unsuitable.
ddr_annotation.evidence_grading_rationale: Measured GlcNAc titers for DN5-GM (6.33 g/L) and DN5-GAR (7.98 g/L) vs DN5 (0.46 g/L).
ddr_annotation.reason_nature_rationale: Mechanistic need (F6P aminotransferase flux) combined with explicit literature-based toxicity concern (Deng et al. 2005) motivating timed activation.
ddr_annotation.generalizable_rule: When overexpression of a product-pathway enzyme is toxic in early growth (e.g., glmS in E. coli), drive it with a positive-response biosensor promoter activated as FBP accumulates, because induction is delayed until the production phase, avoiding lysis. (Validated for GlcNAc in DN5.)

interventions.description: Simultaneous dynamic repression of pfkA and activation of glmS (pBacm or pBacar into DN5-IM), yielding DN5-IMM and DN5-IMAR.

ddr_annotation.decision_type_rationale: Q1 yes, Q2 yes, Q3 yes (tests whether dual control exceeds single regulation - a design-relevant negative/comparative result).
ddr_annotation.design_action_rationale: Layered dual dynamic regulation at one metabolic node.
ddr_annotation.trigger_observation: Hypothesis that combining both arms of node control (repress competitor + activate product path) would further raise GlcNAc titer.
ddr_annotation.evidence_grading_rationale: Measured titer DN5-IMM 8.63 g/L vs single-regulation strains; FBP levels measured in DN5/DN5-IM/DN5-GAR/DN5-IMM.
ddr_annotation.reason_nature_rationale: Push-pull node engineering rationale explicitly described in Fig. 6A narrative.
ddr_annotation.generalizable_rule: When single dynamic repression of pfkA already restores most of the achievable F6P-to-GlcNAc flux in E. coli DN5, adding dynamic glmS activation on top gives no obvious further titer gain, because the node flux is already saturated by competitor repression. (Observed only in this DN5/GlcNAc context; do not generalize.)

EV01.excerpt: Here, we designed and constructed a bifunctional glycolysis flux biosensor ... applied for fine-tuning glycolysis flux to effectively balance the biosynthesis of two chemicals: mevalonate and N-acetylglucosamine.

EV02.excerpt: it regulates the lower glycolysis flux through the allosteric activation of pyruvate kinase ... creating linear relationships between the glycolysis flux and FBP pool in Escherichia coli (Kochanowski et al., 2013)

EV03.excerpt: DN5, a modified DH5alpha strain, which knockout the gene nag, ackA, poxB, ldhA and nan, was constructed by our laboratory in previous studies.

EV04.excerpt: Fig. 2 ... (A) The promoter architecture and characterization of the constructed positive-response biosensors pL01-pL10. (B) Tuning biosensors through the overexpression of Cra and modifying the metabolite-binding affinity of Cra ... (D) ... (CK-, no plasmid pL18; CK, 0 g/L acetate and 0 mM FBP; ... 0.001-400, 10 g/L acetate and 0.001-400 mM FBP). (E) ... dynamic range and threshold EC50.

EV05.excerpt: the fluorescence value of BW-pfkA, BW-ptsG, and BW-pykF at 18h were 11.32, 7.13, and 1.11 times higher than that of the control BW25113 ... linear detection range of intracellular FBP with biosensor pL19 is about 0-50 mmol g-1 dry cell weight ... generally 0-31 mM g-1 dry cell weight

EV06.excerpt: The highest MVA production was obtained by strain BW-PR, which produced 73.31 g/L MVA, and the carbon yield reached 63.00 mol% ... a 111.3 g/L MVA was produced after 120 h cultivation and no by-products were produced.

EV07.excerpt: A previous work indicated the IPTG induced CRISPRi suppression on pfkA gene in the EP-bifido strain only yield 8.53 g/L MVA (Li et al., 2021), 0.12 times of the MVA titer in BW-PR (73.31 g/L).

EV08.excerpt: we tuned the biosensors in the following aspects: (1) the strength of the core promoters ... (2) the position of TFBS ... (3) the affinity of Cra-box ... (4) the expression level of Cra, and (5) the affinity of Cra with small-molecule FBP ... we didn't use those biosensors with overexpression of Cra or its mutants on plasmids for the practical application cases.

EV09.excerpt: strain DN5-IM finally produced 8.65 g/L GlcNAc, whereas the control strain DN5 only produced 0.46 g/L ... DN5-GM and DN5-GAR produced 6.33 and 7.98 g/L ... Strain DN5-IMM produced 8.63 g/L ... did not exhibit an obviously higher titer compared with that of pfkA or glmS single regulation.

EV10.excerpt: Fig. 6 ... (C-H) The cell growth ... GlcNAc production of engineered E. coli strains DN5, DN5-PM, DN5-IM, DN5-GM, DN5-GAR, DN5-IMM, and DN5-IMAR.

unsupported_values: Develop a rapid CRISPRi-based combinatorial repression system for multiple genes in E. coli by expressing different sgRNAs from orthogonal low-leakage inducible promoters (PlacO1, PLtetO-1, ParaBAD) on a single plasmid (p3gRNA-LTA), so that repression combinations are generated by adding inducers instead of building many sgRNA plasmids; demonstrate it on NeuAc biosynthesis.

Using orthogonal inducible promoters with low background leakage plus sgRNA handle mutations that reduce dCas9 affinity can mitigate leaky CRISPRi repression, enabling rigorous, independently inducible multi-gene repression; repressing PEP-consuming genes (pta, ptsI, pykA) should redirect PEP toward NeuAc biosynthesis.

E. coli DH5alpha (cloning host); E. coli BW25113 and MG1655 (system characterization); E. coli MG1655RFP (reporter strain constructed in this study); E. coli DH5alpha-derived DN5 carrying plasmid pB3 (NeuAc fermentation; DN5 and pB3 constructed in previous studies).

MG1655RFP: lacI and gusR knocked out; native lacZ and gusA promoters replaced with constitutive promoters; rfp integrated into genome for constitutive expression. DN5: delta-nanATEK, delta-nagEBAC, delta-ldhA, delta-poxB, delta-ackA (prior work). Plasmids: p3gRNA-LTA (three sgRNA expression cassettes under PlacO1/PLtetO-1/ParaBAD with BbsI/BsaI/SapI sites); pdCas9-3TFs (dCas9 plus lacI-AM, tetR, araC).

CRISPR interference (dCas9) with three orthogonal inducible promoters driving three sgRNAs; modified one-step/one-pot Golden Gate Assembly (sequential BbsI, BsaI, SapI Type IIS ligations in one reaction) to build three-sgRNA plasmid p3gRNA-LTA; sgRNA handle sequence mutation (#3 for PlacO1, #5 for PLtetO-1 and ParaBAD) to reduce leaky repression; combinatorial repression achieved by mixing inducers (IPTG, aTc, arabinose).

(1) Promoter screen: 8 inducible promoters expressing mKate, with/without cognate inducer. (2) Orthogonality test: 4 promoters x 4 inducers. (3) Glucose effect: PrhaBAD +/- 10 g/L glucose. (4) sgRNA handle mutant screen: 7 mutants (#1-#7) with lacZ reporter under each of 3 promoters. (5) Spacer target-site (3 lacZ, 3 gusA spacers) and spacer-length (17/22/24/27 bp) tests. (6) System characterization in MG1655RFP: all 8 inducer combinations targeting gusA/rfp/lacZ. (7) NeuAc fermentation: DN5/pB3/p3gRNA-LTA with 7 inducer combinations (single, double, triple repression of pta/ptsI/pykA).

Fig 4: strain constitutively expressing fluorescent protein without CRISPRi as control. Fig 5 and Fig 6: strains carrying the system without sgRNA targeting any gene as controls (control enzyme activity/fluorescence normalized to 1); no-inducer conditions as baseline for leakage assessment.

Cloning/characterization strains: LB, 37 C, aeration. Fluorescence assay: 2% inoculum into 2 mL LB in 24-well plates, 37 C, high-speed shaking, 18 h. Enzyme assays: 2% inoculum, 2 mL LB, 37 C, 400 rpm, 18 h. NeuAc fermentation: seed in LB+ampicillin (5 mL overnight, then 50 mL at 2% for 12 h), 4% inoculum into 50 mL MTB + 30 g/L glucose, 30 C, 220 rpm; induction at OD600 0.4-0.6; pH held ~7.0 with 30% NH4OH; 48 h total.

LB (cloning, characterization, reporter assays); MTB: 12 g/L tryptone, 24 g/L yeast extract, 5 g/L NaCl, supplemented with 30 g/L glucose for NeuAc fermentation; LB agar + 25 ug/mL spectinomycin for transformant selection after Golden Gate assembly.

Promoter screen inducers (Fig 2A): 0.5 mM IPTG, 4.3 uM aTc, 13.3 mM arabinose, 121.8 uM L-rhamnose monohydrate, 100 uM cuminic acid, 10 uM OC6, 100 uM sodium salicylate, 10 uM OHC14. Fig 4 repression assays: 0.5 mM IPTG, 4.3 uM aTc, 13.3 mM Ara. Fermentation: 200 uM IPTG; aTc/Ara doses for fermentation given only via Table S4 (requires_supplement).

Fluorescence/OD600 measured every 15 min for 18 h; enzyme reporter assays after 18 h induction; Golden Gate thermocycling 37 C 5 min / 25 C 15 min x 10 cycles per ligation round; fermentation seed 12 h, fermentation 48 h with sampling every 6-12 h.
Fig 5 and Fig 6: means (+- s.d.) from three independent experiments. Replicate counts/types for Fig 2, Fig 4, spacer tests (Figures S4-S6) not stated in main text.

mKate/rfp fluorescence (excitation 590 nm, emission 640 nm) with OD600; beta-galactosidase (lacZ) activity via ONPG hydrolysis, absorbance 420 nm; beta-glucuronidase (gusA) activity via 4-NPG, absorbance 405 nm; extracellular metabolites (glucose, NeuAc, acetate, ethanol, formate, pyruvate, GlcNAc, ManNAc) by HPLC-RID; Sanger sequencing of assembled clones.

BioTek microplate reader; Shimadzu spectrophotometer (OD600); HPLC (Shimadzu) with RID-10A refractive index detector and Aminex HPX-87H ion exclusion column (Bio-Rad), 5 mM sulfuric acid mobile phase, 1 mL/min; Biosensors Analyzer (Jinan) for glucose.

Fold-change of fluorescence with/without inducer; percent repression relative to control; normalization of control enzyme activity/fluorescence to 1; means +- s.d. of three independent experiments; HPLC quantification of titers and by-products; comparison of NeuAc titers as % of control across repression combinations.

4 low-leakage promoters selected (PlacO1, PLtetO-1, ParaBAD, PrhaBAD); PrhaBAD excluded due to glucose abolishing induction; final 3 promoters orthogonal. One-pot assembly: 5/7 sequenced clones carried all three sgRNAs, 2/7 carried the first two. sgRNA handle #3 (PlacO1) and #5 (PLtetO-1, ParaBAD) nearly eliminated leaky repression (leakage reduced from up to ~90% to ~20% for PLtetO-1/ParaBAD; nearly intact lacZ without inducer for PlacO1). Spacers 17-27 bp equally effective; sites closer to start codon repress better. System characterization: each inducer primarily repressed its target (gusA -48.3% with IPTG alone; RFP -74% with aTc alone; lacZ -32.4% with Ara alone; residual PLtetO-1 leakage -22.2% RFP). NeuAc: ptsI repression alone gave highest titer 2.62 g/L (240.8% of control); ptsI/pykA 2.22 g/L (203.7%); pta/ptsI/pykA 1.91 g/L (176%); pta/ptsI 121.2%; pta 126.5%; pykA 144.2%; pta/pykA 81.6%. ptsI repression raised GlcNAc +83.2% and ManNAc +63.2%, lowered pyruvate -68%; OD600 unchanged (Figure S7).

conflicts.prose_interpretation: Abstract: 'the optimal combinatorial inhibition of the pta, ptsI, and pykA genes resulted in a 2.4-fold increase in NeuAc yield compared to the control' - implies a multi-gene combination gave 2.4-fold.
conflicts.equation_or_figure_interpretation: Results/Fig 6B: ptsI single-gene repression gave 240.8% of control (2.62 g/L, the 2.4-fold); triple repression pta/ptsI/pykA gave only 176% (1.91 g/L); text states multi-gene repression was NOT superior to ptsI alone.
conflicts.impact: Abstract wording misattributes the best result to combinatorial repression of all three genes; downstream use should cite ptsI single repression as the best condition.

conflicts.topic: Inducer addition timing in NeuAc fermentation
conflicts.prose_interpretation: Methods: 'Then 200 uM IPTG was added for fermentation' after reaching OD600 0.4-0.6 - reads as if only IPTG is added at induction.
conflicts.equation_or_figure_interpretation: Fig 6 caption: 'Different combinations of inducers were added when the strain was transferred to the shake flask' - implies aTc/Ara/IPTG combinations added earlier, at transfer.
conflicts.impact: Exact timing/doses of aTc and Ara during fermentation are ambiguous without Table S4; blocks exact protocol reproduction.

conflicts.prose_interpretation: Text annotates pykA as 'encoding pyruvate carboxykinase'.
conflicts.equation_or_figure_interpretation: Standard E. coli annotation: pykA encodes pyruvate kinase II (pyruvate-forming), consistent with Fig 6 pathway and the observed pyruvate decrease upon pykA repression; 'pyruvate carboxykinase' appears to be a paper annotation error.
conflicts.impact: Low for extraction (role as PEP-consuming gene is clear); flagged for accuracy.

System characterization: each inducer primarily repressed its target (gusA -48.3% with IPTG alone; RFP -74% with aTc alone; lacZ -32.4% with Ara alone; residual PLtetO-1 leakage -22.2% RFP). NeuAc: ptsI repression alone gave highest titer 2.62 g/L (240.8% of control); ptsI/pykA 2.22 g/L (203.7%); pta/ptsI/pykA 1.91 g/L (176%); pta/ptsI 121.2%; pta 126.5%; pykA 144.2%; pta/pykA 81.6%. ptsI repression raised GlcNAc +83.2% and ManNAc +63.2%, lowered pyruvate -68%; OD600 unchanged (Figure S7).

objective.value: Develop a rapid CRISPRi-based combinatorial repression system for multiple genes in E. coli by expressing different sgRNAs from orthogonal low-leakage inducible promoters (PlacO1, PLtetO-1, ParaBAD) on a single plasmid (p3gRNA-LTA), so that repression combinations are generated by adding inducers instead of building many sgRNA plasmids; demonstrate it on NeuAc biosynthesis.
objective.notes: Primary research; system development plus one application case (NeuAc).

hypothesis.value: Using orthogonal inducible promoters with low background leakage plus sgRNA handle mutations that reduce dCas9 affinity can mitigate leaky CRISPRi repression, enabling rigorous, independently inducible multi-gene repression; repressing PEP-consuming genes (pta, ptsI, pykA) should redirect PEP toward NeuAc biosynthesis.
hypothesis.notes: Leakage hypothesis stated explicitly ('We hypothesized that it was likely to reduce the background leakage of CRISPRi'); PEP hypothesis stated as author reasoning from precursor accumulation data.

strain.value: E. coli DH5alpha (cloning host); E. coli BW25113 and MG1655 (system characterization); E. coli MG1655RFP (reporter strain constructed in this study); E. coli DH5alpha-derived DN5 carrying plasmid pB3 (NeuAc fermentation; DN5 and pB3 constructed in previous studies).
strain.notes: DN5 genotype: deletions of nan operon (nanATEK), nag operon (nagEBAC), ldhA, poxB, ackA - previously constructed [29]. pB3 contains neuB, slr1975, GNA1, feedback-resistant glmS - from [30]. Full strain/plasmid list in Table S1 (requires_supplement).

genotype.value: MG1655RFP: lacI and gusR knocked out; native lacZ and gusA promoters replaced with constitutive promoters; rfp integrated into genome for constitutive expression. DN5: delta-nanATEK, delta-nagEBAC, delta-ldhA, delta-poxB, delta-ackA (prior work). Plasmids: p3gRNA-LTA (three sgRNA expression cassettes under PlacO1/PLtetO-1/ParaBAD with BbsI/BsaI/SapI sites); pdCas9-3TFs (dCas9 plus lacI-AM, tetR, araC).
genotype.notes: Exact sequences, spacer sequences and constitutive promoter identity in Tables S2/S3/S6 (requires_supplement).

engineering_method.value: CRISPR interference (dCas9) with three orthogonal inducible promoters driving three sgRNAs; modified one-step/one-pot Golden Gate Assembly (sequential BbsI, BsaI, SapI Type IIS ligations in one reaction) to build three-sgRNA plasmid p3gRNA-LTA; sgRNA handle sequence mutation (#3 for PlacO1, #5 for PLtetO-1 and ParaBAD) to reduce leaky repression; combinatorial repression achieved by mixing inducers (IPTG, aTc, arabinose).

experimental_groups.value: (1) Promoter screen: 8 inducible promoters expressing mKate, with/without cognate inducer. (2) Orthogonality test: 4 promoters x 4 inducers. (5) Spacer target-site (3 lacZ, 3 gusA spacers) and spacer-length (17/22/24/27 bp) tests. (6) System characterization in MG1655RFP: all 8 inducer combinations targeting gusA/rfp/lacZ. ddr_annotation.generalizable_rule: When many multi-sgRNA plasmid variants must be built for combinatorial CRISPRi screening in E. coli, apply a one-pot sequential Type IIS (Golden Gate) ligation with distinct enzyme pairs per insertion site, because orthogonal sticky ends allow successive spacer insertion in a single reaction mixture.
alternatives_considered: Conventional sgRNA array plasmid per combination - rejected as time- and labor-intensive

experiments.purpose: Reduce leaky (inducer-independent) repression of the CRISPRi system
experiments.host: E. coli (characterization strains; reporter rfp, then lacZ)
experiments.intervention: Test 7 sgRNA handle mutants (#1-#7, from Reis et al. [28]) under each of the 3 promoters; select handle #3 for PlacO1 and #5 for PLtetO-1/ParaBAD; rebuild p3gRNA-LTA
experiments.conditions: LB, 37 C, 18 h induction; inducers 0.5 mM IPTG / 4.3 uM aTc / 13.3 mM Ara
experiments.control: Strain constitutively expressing fluorescent protein without CRISPRi; no-inducer condition
experiments.readout: rfp fluorescence; lacZ beta-galactosidase activity (ONPG, 420 nm)
experiments.analysis: % repression with inducer vs % leaky repression without inducer
experiments.outcome: Wild-type handle leakage: 21.8%/74.9%/37.5% repression without inducer. Handle #3: lacZ nearly intact uninduced, 84.5% repressed induced (PlacO1). Handle #5: low leakage for PLtetO-1/ParaBAD (leakage reduced from ~90% to ~20% per Discussion).

ddr_annotation.decision_type_rationale: Handle mutation is an active design change that fixed the leakage problem and defined the final plasmid.
ddr_annotation.design_action_rationale: Tuning sgRNA-dCas9 affinity to rebalance on-target repression vs background expression.
ddr_annotation.trigger_observation: All three promoters showed substantial leaky repression without inducer (rfp reduced 21.8-74.9%), which would confound combinatorial control.
ddr_annotation.evidence_grading_rationale: Leakage and repression directly measured via fluorescence and enzyme activity for each mutant.
ddr_annotation.reason_nature_rationale: Paper explicitly bases the handle-mutation strategy on Reis et al. [28], who reported handle mutations with reduced dCas9 affinity; selection among the 7 mutants was then empirical.
ddr_annotation.generalizable_rule: When inducible-promoter CRISPRi in E. coli shows leaky repression that corrupts combinatorial control, apply sgRNA handle mutations that modestly reduce dCas9 affinity, because lower affinity raises the sgRNA expression threshold needed for repression while preserving inducer-dependent knockdown.
alternatives_considered: crRNA mismatches, decoy crRNA binding sites, feedback control of crRNA expression (Hove et al. [42]) - not adopted; handle mutation requires only a fixed handle swap with no extra design

ddr_annotation.decision_type_rationale: Q1: active intervention (CRISPRi repression of 3 chosen genes); Q2: performed in this study (only the DN5 chassis and pB3 are prior work); Q3: results directly informed which gene(s) to repress and revealed combination effects.
ddr_annotation.design_action_rationale: Blocking PEP dissipation to enhance supply of the limiting precursor PEP for NeuAc synthesis.
ddr_annotation.trigger_observation: DN5/pB3 accumulated large amounts of ManNAc (direct NeuAc precursor) while PEP showed no accumulation, indicating PEP was limiting relative to ManNAc.
ddr_annotation.evidence_grading_rationale: Precursor accumulation measured by HPLC; intervention outcomes measured as NeuAc titers across all combinations in triplicate.
ddr_annotation.reason_nature_rationale: Paper explicitly reasons that PEP is consumed by conversion to acetyl-CoA/pyruvate (pykA, pta) and the PTS glucose-uptake system (ptsI), so repressing these three genes should conserve PEP for NeuAc synthesis.
ddr_annotation.generalizable_rule: When one precursor (PEP) is limiting relative to a co-substrate (ManNAc) in E. coli NeuAc biosynthesis, repress PEP-dissipating reactions (PTS component ptsI, pyruvate kinase pykA) rather than only pushing the downstream pathway, because conserving the limiting precursor redirects flux toward product formation; note single-node repression (ptsI) outperformed combinations here, so combinations must be tested rather than assumed additive.

conflicts.prose_interpretation: Abstract: 'the optimal combinatorial inhibition of the pta, ptsI, and pykA genes resulted in a 2.4-fold increase in NeuAc yield compared to the control' - implies a multi-gene combination gave 2.4-fold.
conflicts.equation_or_figure_interpretation: Results/Fig 6B: ptsI single-gene repression gave 240.8% of control (2.62 g/L, the 2.4-fold); triple repression pta/ptsI/pykA gave only 176% (1.91 g/L); text states multi-gene repression was NOT superior to ptsI alone.
conflicts.impact: Abstract wording misattributes the best result to combinatorial repression of all three genes; downstream use should cite ptsI single repression as the best condition.

conflicts.topic: Inducer addition timing in NeuAc fermentation
conflicts.prose_interpretation: Methods: 'Then 200 uM IPTG was added for fermentation' after reaching OD600 0.4-0.6 - reads as if only IPTG is added at induction.
conflicts.equation_or_figure_interpretation: Fig 6 caption: 'Different combinations of inducers were added when the strain was transferred to the shake flask' - implies aTc/Ara/IPTG combinations added earlier, at transfer.
conflicts.impact: Exact timing/doses of aTc and Ara during fermentation are ambiguous without Table S4; blocks exact protocol reproduction.

conflicts.prose_interpretation: Text annotates pykA as 'encoding pyruvate carboxykinase'.
conflicts.equation_or_figure_interpretation: Standard E. coli annotation: pykA encodes pyruvate kinase II (pyruvate-forming), consistent with Fig 6 pathway and the observed pyruvate decrease upon pykA repression; 'pyruvate carboxykinase' appears to be a paper annotation error.
conflicts.impact: Low for extraction (role as PEP-consuming gene is clear); flagged for accuracy.

objective.value: Develop a rapid CRISPRi-based combinatorial repression system for multiple genes in E. coli by expressing different sgRNAs from orthogonal low-leakage inducible promoters (PlacO1, PLtetO-1, ParaBAD) on a single plasmid (p3gRNA-LTA), so that repression combinations are generated by adding inducers instead of building many sgRNA plasmids; demonstrate it on NeuAc biosynthesis.
objective.notes: Primary research; system development plus one application case (NeuAc).

hypothesis.value: Using orthogonal inducible promoters with low background leakage plus sgRNA handle mutations that reduce dCas9 affinity can mitigate leaky CRISPRi repression, enabling rigorous, independently inducible multi-gene repression; repressing PEP-consuming genes (pta, ptsI, pykA) should redirect PEP toward NeuAc biosynthesis.
hypothesis.notes: Leakage hypothesis stated explicitly ('We hypothesized that it was likely to reduce the background leakage of CRISPRi'); PEP hypothesis stated as author reasoning from precursor accumulation data.

strain.value: E. coli DH5alpha (cloning host); E. coli BW25113 and MG1655 (system characterization); E. coli MG1655RFP (reporter strain constructed in this study); E. coli DH5alpha-derived DN5 carrying plasmid pB3 (NeuAc fermentation; DN5 and pB3 constructed in previous studies).
strain.notes: DN5 genotype: deletions of nan operon (nanATEK), nag operon (nagEBAC), ldhA, poxB, ackA - previously constructed [29]. pB3 contains neuB, slr1975, GNA1, feedback-resistant glmS - from [30]. Full strain/plasmid list in Table S1 (requires_supplement).

genotype.value: MG1655RFP: lacI and gusR knocked out; native lacZ and gusA promoters replaced with constitutive promoters; rfp integrated into genome for constitutive expression. DN5: delta-nanATEK, delta-nagEBAC, delta-ldhA, delta-poxB, delta-ackA (prior work). Plasmids: p3gRNA-LTA (three sgRNA expression cassettes under PlacO1/PLtetO-1/ParaBAD with BbsI/BsaI/SapI sites); pdCas9-3TFs (dCas9 plus lacI-AM, tetR, araC).
genotype.notes: Exact sequences, spacer sequences and constitutive promoter identity in Tables S2/S3/S6 (requires_supplement).

engineering_method.value: CRISPR interference (dCas9) with three orthogonal inducible promoters driving three sgRNAs; modified one-step/one-pot Golden Gate Assembly (sequential BbsI, BsaI, SapI Type IIS ligations in one reaction) to build three-sgRNA plasmid p3gRNA-LTA; sgRNA handle sequence mutation (#3 for PlacO1, #5 for PLtetO-1 and ParaBAD) to reduce leaky repression; combinatorial repression achieved by mixing inducers (IPTG, aTc, arabinose).
engineering_method.notes: Base plasmid construction by Gibson assembly [21].

experimental_groups.value: (1) Promoter screen: 8 inducible promoters expressing mKate, with/without cognate inducer. (2) Orthogonality test: 4 promoters x 4 inducers. (3) Glucose effect: PrhaBAD +/- 10 g/L glucose. (4) sgRNA handle mutant screen: 7 mutants (#1-#7) with lacZ reporter under each of 3 promoters. (5) Spacer target-site (3 lacZ, 3 gusA spacers) and spacer-length (17/22/24/27 bp) tests. (6) System characterization in MG1655RFP: all 8 inducer combinations targeting gusA/rfp/lacZ. (7) NeuAc fermentation: DN5/pB3/p3gRNA-LTA with 7 inducer combinations (single, double, triple repression of pta/ptsI/pykA).
experimental_groups.notes: Inducer-to-group assignment for fluorescence/repression assays detailed in Table S4 (requires_supplement).

controls.value: Fig 4: strain constitutively expressing fluorescent protein without CRISPRi as control. Fig 5 and Fig 6: strains carrying the system without sgRNA targeting any gene as controls (control enzyme activity/fluorescence normalized to 1); no-inducer conditions as baseline for leakage assessment.
controls.notes: Controls instantiated per experiment; no single universal control.

culture_conditions.value: Cloning/characterization strains: LB, 37 C, aeration. Fluorescence assay: 2% inoculum into 2 mL LB in 24-well plates, 37 C, high-speed shaking, 18 h. Enzyme assays: 2% inoculum, 2 mL LB, 37 C, 400 rpm, 18 h. NeuAc fermentation: seed in LB+ampicillin (5 mL overnight, then 50 mL at 2% for 12 h), 4% inoculum into 50 mL MTB + 30 g/L glucose, 30 C, 220 rpm; induction at OD600 0.4-0.6; pH held ~7.0 with 30% NH4OH; 48 h total.
culture_conditions.notes: NeuAc fermentation inducer addition timing: 'added when the strain was transferred to the shake flask' per Fig 6 caption; Methods state 200 uM IPTG added at OD600 0.4-0.6 - see conflicts.

medium.value: LB (cloning, characterization, reporter assays); MTB: 12 g/L tryptone, 24 g/L yeast extract, 5 g/L NaCl, supplemented with 30 g/L glucose for NeuAc fermentation; LB agar + 25 ug/mL spectinomycin for transformant selection after Golden Gate assembly.
medium.notes: Antibiotics: ampicillin 100 ug/mL, kanamycin 25 ug/mL, chloramphenicol 17 ug/mL, spectinomycin 100 ug/mL.

dosage.value: Promoter screen inducers (Fig 2A): 0.5 mM IPTG, 4.3 uM aTc, 13.3 mM arabinose, 121.8 uM L-rhamnose monohydrate, 100 uM cuminic acid, 10 uM OC6, 100 uM sodium salicylate, 10 uM OHC14. Fig 4 repression assays: 0.5 mM IPTG, 4.3 uM aTc, 13.3 mM Ara. Fermentation: 200 uM IPTG; aTc/Ara doses for fermentation given only via Table S4 (requires_supplement).
dosage.notes: Inducer dosing matrix for characterization/fermentation experiments is in Table S4, not available in main text.

time.value: Fluorescence/OD600 measured every 15 min for 18 h; enzyme reporter assays after 18 h induction; Golden Gate thermocycling 37 C 5 min / 25 C 15 min x 10 cycles per ligation round; fermentation seed 12 h, fermentation 48 h with sampling every 6-12 h.

replicates.value: Fig 5 and Fig 6: means (+- s.d.) from three independent experiments. Replicate counts/types for Fig 2, Fig 4, spacer tests (Figures S4-S6) not stated in main text.
replicates.notes: 'three independent experiments' - likely independent culture replicates; exact replicate_type for other assays unknown (requires_supplement or methods clarification).

assay.value: mKate/rfp fluorescence (excitation 590 nm, emission 640 nm) with OD600; beta-galactosidase (lacZ) activity via ONPG hydrolysis, absorbance 420 nm; beta-glucuronidase (gusA) activity via 4-NPG, absorbance 405 nm; extracellular metabolites (glucose, NeuAc, acetate, ethanol, formate, pyruvate, GlcNAc, ManNAc) by HPLC-RID; Sanger sequencing of assembled clones.
assay.notes: Enzyme assays adapted from OpenWetWare protocols; permeabilization with CTAB/sodium deoxycholate.

instruments.value: BioTek microplate reader; Shimadzu spectrophotometer (OD600); HPLC (Shimadzu) with RID-10A refractive index detector and Aminex HPX-87H ion exclusion column (Bio-Rad), 5 mM sulfuric acid mobile phase, 1 mL/min; Biosensors Analyzer (Jinan) for glucose.

analysis_methods.value: Fold-change of fluorescence with/without inducer; percent repression relative to control; normalization of control enzyme activity/fluorescence to 1; means +- s.d. of three independent experiments; HPLC quantification of titers and by-products; comparison of NeuAc titers as % of control across repression combinations.
analysis_methods.notes: No formal statistical hypothesis tests reported in main text.

outcomes.value: 4 low-leakage promoters selected (PlacO1, PLtetO-1, ParaBAD, PrhaBAD); PrhaBAD excluded due to glucose abolishing induction; final 3 promoters orthogonal. One-pot assembly: 5/7 sequenced clones carried all three sgRNAs, 2/7 carried the first two. sgRNA handle #3 (PlacO1) and #5 (PLtetO-1, ParaBAD) nearly eliminated leaky repression (leakage reduced from up to ~90% to ~20% for PLtetO-1/ParaBAD; nearly intact lacZ without inducer for PlacO1). Spacers 17-27 bp equally effective; sites closer to start codon repress better. System characterization: each inducer primarily repressed its target (gusA -48.3% with IPTG alone; RFP -74% with aTc alone; lacZ -32.4% with Ara alone; residual PLtetO-1 leakage -22.2% RFP). NeuAc: ptsI repression alone gave highest titer 2.62 g/L (240.8% of control); ptsI/pykA 2.22 g/L (203.7%); pta/ptsI/pykA 1.91 g/L (176%); pta/ptsI 121.2%; pta 126.5%; pykA 144.2%; pta/pykA 81.6%. ptsI repression raised GlcNAc +83.2% and ManNAc +63.2%, lowered pyruvate -68%; OD600 unchanged (Figure S7).
outcomes.notes: Multi-gene repression was NOT superior to ptsI single repression - authors explicitly state this.

experiments.purpose: Identify inducible promoters with low background leakage and high induced expression for sgRNA expression
experiments.intervention: Express mKate reporter from 8 candidate inducible promoters (PlacO1, PLtetO-1, ParaBAD, PrhaBAD, PCymRC, PLuxB, PsalTTC, PCin) with/without cognate inducer
experiments.conditions: LB, 24-well plates, 37 C, 18 h, inducer panel per Fig 2A
experiments.readout: mKate fluorescence (590/640 nm) and OD600 every 15 min
experiments.analysis: Induced intensity, background leakage, fold-change
experiments.outcome: PrhaBAD, ParaBAD, PLtetO-1, PlacO1 selected (leakage 27/31/40/48 RFU; induction 176.3/107.8/43.3/7.4-fold); PLuxB, PCin, PsalTTC, PCymRC excluded for high leakage

ddr_annotation.decision_type_rationale: Q1 pass: authors actively screened and selected promoter components; Q2 pass: characterization done in this study; Q3 pass: selection determined the final 3-promoter system architecture.
ddr_annotation.design_action_rationale: Selection of expression-control components to balance tightness (low leakage) vs dynamic range for multi-sgRNA expression.
ddr_annotation.trigger_observation: CRISPRi is functional immediately upon sgRNA transcription, so even weak promoter leakage causes undesired repression; needed independently controllable, low-leakage promoters.
ddr_annotation.evidence_grading_rationale: Direct fluorescence measurements of all 8 promoters with/without inducers.
ddr_annotation.reason_nature_rationale: Final promoters chosen by empirical screening of 8 candidates, not from mechanistic prediction.
alternatives_considered: PrhaBAD - excluded because 10 g/L glucose abolished Rha induction, incompatible with glucose-based fermentation
PLuxB, PCin, PsalTTC, PCymRC - excluded for significant background leakage

experiments.conditions: LB, 37 C, 18 h microplate assay
experiments.readout: mKate fluorescence
experiments.analysis: Cross-reactivity comparison; expression levels 354-4760 RFU
experiments.outcome: Each inducer activated only its cognate promoter; PrhaBAD excluded (glucose catabolite effect); final set = PlacO1, PLtetO-1, ParaBAD

ddr_annotation.decision_type_rationale: Component exclusion (PrhaBAD) changed the final system design for glucose-based fermentation use.
ddr_annotation.design_action_rationale: Choosing expression-control parts compatible with the intended process carbon source.
ddr_annotation.trigger_observation: Rha lost the ability to activate PrhaBAD in the presence of 10 g/L glucose (Figure S2).

experiments.purpose: Enable rapid construction of a three-sgRNA expression plasmid without building separate plasmids per combination
experiments.intervention: Build p3gRNA-LTA with three sgRNA insertion sites flanked by paired BbsI/BsaI/SapI Type IIS sites; one-pot sequential ligation of three annealed spacer fragments (37 C 5 min / 25 C 15 min, 10 cycles per round, reagents added successively)
experiments.conditions: 20 uL Golden Gate reactions; transformants selected on LB + 25 ug/mL spectinomycin
experiments.replicates: 7 clones randomly picked for sequencing from thousands of transformants
experiments.readout: Sanger sequencing of inserted spacers
experiments.analysis: Count of clones with all three vs two spacers
experiments.outcome: 5/7 clones correctly assembled all three sgRNAs; 2/7 contained only the first two spacers

ddr_annotation.decision_type_rationale: Q1: new assembly method designed; Q2: developed in this paper; Q3: defines the retargeting workflow of the whole system.
ddr_annotation.design_action_rationale: Integrated construction strategy enabling rapid re-targeting and combinatorial screening.
ddr_annotation.trigger_observation: Covering all repression combinations of n genes requires 2^n - 1 sgRNA plasmids with conventional arrays - labor-intensive and inefficient.
ddr_annotation.evidence_grading_rationale: Assembly success directly verified by sequencing 7 clones.
ddr_annotation.reason_nature_rationale: Explicitly a modification of published Golden Gate Assembly [22]; the novelty (one-pot sequential addition of enzymes/fragments) is an adaptation of that method.
ddr_annotation.generalizable_rule: When many multi-sgRNA plasmid variants must be built for combinatorial CRISPRi screening in E. coli, apply a one-pot sequential Type IIS (Golden Gate) ligation with distinct enzyme pairs per insertion site, because orthogonal sticky ends allow successive spacer insertion in a single reaction mixture.
alternatives_considered: Conventional sgRNA array plasmid per combination - rejected as time- and labor-intensive

experiments.purpose: Reduce leaky (inducer-independent) repression of the CRISPRi system
experiments.host: E. coli (characterization strains; reporter rfp, then lacZ)
experiments.intervention: Test 7 sgRNA handle mutants (#1-#7, from Reis et al. [28]) under each of the 3 promoters; select handle #3 for PlacO1 and #5 for PLtetO-1/ParaBAD; rebuild p3gRNA-LTA
experiments.conditions: LB, 37 C, 18 h induction; inducers 0.5 mM IPTG / 4.3 uM aTc / 13.3 mM Ara
experiments.control: Strain constitutively expressing fluorescent protein without CRISPRi; no-inducer condition
experiments.readout: rfp fluorescence; lacZ beta-galactosidase activity (ONPG, 420 nm)
experiments.analysis: % repression with inducer vs % leaky repression without inducer
experiments.outcome: Wild-type handle leakage: 21.8%/74.9%/37.5% repression without inducer. Handle #3: lacZ nearly intact uninduced, 84.5% repressed induced (PlacO1). Handle #5: low leakage for PLtetO-1/ParaBAD (leakage reduced from ~90% to ~20% per Discussion).

ddr_annotation.decision_type_rationale: Handle mutation is an active design change that fixed the leakage problem and defined the final plasmid.
ddr_annotation.design_action_rationale: Tuning sgRNA-dCas9 affinity to rebalance on-target repression vs background expression.
ddr_annotation.trigger_observation: All three promoters showed substantial leaky repression without inducer (rfp reduced 21.8-74.9%), which would confound combinatorial control.
ddr_annotation.evidence_grading_rationale: Leakage and repression directly measured via fluorescence and enzyme activity for each mutant.
ddr_annotation.reason_nature_rationale: Paper explicitly bases the handle-mutation strategy on Reis et al. [28], who reported handle mutations with reduced dCas9 affinity; selection among the 7 mutants was then empirical.
ddr_annotation.generalizable_rule: When inducible-promoter CRISPRi in E. coli shows leaky repression that corrupts combinatorial control, apply sgRNA handle mutations that modestly reduce dCas9 affinity, because lower affinity raises the sgRNA expression threshold needed for repression while preserving inducer-dependent knockdown.
alternatives_considered: crRNA mismatches, decoy crRNA binding sites, feedback control of crRNA expression (Hove et al. [42]) - not adopted; handle mutation requires only a fixed handle swap with no extra design

experiments.purpose: Assess effect of sgRNA target position and spacer length on repression
experiments.intervention: Express 3 lacZ-targeting and 3 gusA-targeting spacers from ParaBAD; test 17/22/24/27 bp spacers at lacZ1 site
experiments.conditions: LB, 37 C, 18 h
experiments.readout: lacZ/gusA enzyme activity
experiments.analysis: % repression per site/length
experiments.outcome: Sites nearer the start codon repress more strongly (lacZ1, gusA1 best); 17-27 bp spacers gave 70.4-79.4% repression with no significant length effect

ddr_annotation.decision_type_rationale: Fails Q3: characterization of spacer position/length effects produced design knowledge but did not itself change a construct in this paper; it validates spacer choice rules.

experiments.purpose: Characterize independent multi-gene control of the optimized system on genomic and plasmid reporters
experiments.host: E. coli MG1655RFP (constructed here: delta-lacI, delta-gusR, constitutive lacZ/gusA promoters, genomically integrated constitutive rfp)
experiments.intervention: Co-transform p3gRNA-LTA (sgRNAs targeting gusA via PlacO1, rfp via PLtetO-1, lacZ via ParaBAD) with pdCas9-3TFs; apply all 8 inducer combinations
experiments.conditions: LB, 37 C, 18 h
experiments.readout: gusA activity, RFP fluorescence, lacZ activity
experiments.analysis: % inhibition per inducer combination
experiments.outcome: IPTG-only: gusA -48.3%; aTc-only: RFP -74%; Ara-only: lacZ -32.4%; targets stayed repressed (41-72%) when other inducers added; residual PLtetO-1 leakage (RFP -22.2% uninduced)

ddr_annotation.decision_type_rationale: Construction of the dedicated MG1655RFP reporter chassis (knockouts + promoter replacement + genomic rfp) is an active design action enabling the multi-reporter readout.
ddr_annotation.design_action_rationale: Building an integrated reporter strain to characterize a multi-channel regulation system.
ddr_annotation.trigger_observation: Need to test simultaneous independent repression of three genes distinguished by orthogonal readouts; native lacZ/gusA are under endogenous regulation that would confound readouts.
ddr_annotation.evidence_grading_rationale: Reporter responses directly measured across all 8 inducer combinations in triplicate.
ddr_annotation.reason_nature_rationale: The paper states lacI and gusR were knocked out because they regulate lacZ/gusA, and native promoters were replaced with constitutive promoters - explicit regulatory-logic reasoning to decouple reporters from native control.
ddr_annotation.generalizable_rule: When benchmarking a multi-channel CRISPRi system on native genomic reporters in E. coli, delete the endogenous regulators (e.g., lacI, gusR) and drive the reporters from constitutive promoters, because otherwise native regulation confounds the CRISPRi-specific repression readout.

experiments.purpose: Demonstrate the system by optimizing NeuAc biosynthesis through combinatorial repression of PEP-consuming genes
experiments.host: E. coli DN5/pB3 (DN5 = DH5alpha derivative with delta-nanATEK, delta-nagEBAC, delta-ldhA, delta-poxB, delta-ackA from prior work [29]; pB3 carries neuB, slr1975, GNA1, glmS-fbr [30])
experiments.intervention: Introduce p3gRNA-LTA with sgRNAs targeting pta (PlacO1), ptsI (PLtetO-1), pykA (ParaBAD); apply 7 inducer combinations during shake-flask fermentation
experiments.conditions: 50 mL MTB + 30 g/L glucose + ampicillin, 4% inoculum, 30 C, 220 rpm, inducers added at transfer to shake flask; 200 uM IPTG at OD600 0.4-0.6 per Methods; pH ~7.0 via 30% NH4OH; 48 h; sampling every 6-12 h
experiments.control: DN5/pB3 with plasmid lacking gene-targeting sgRNA
experiments.readout: NeuAc titer; by-products GlcNAc, ManNAc, pyruvate, acetate (HPLC); OD600
experiments.analysis: Titer as % of control across the 7 repression combinations
experiments.outcome: ptsI single repression best: 2.62 g/L (240.8% of control); ptsI/pykA 2.22 g/L (203.7%); pta/ptsI/pykA 1.91 g/L (176%); multi-gene repression NOT superior to ptsI alone; ptsI repression raised GlcNAc +83.2%, ManNAc +63.2%, pyruvate -68%; OD600 unaffected

ddr_annotation.decision_type_rationale: Q1: active intervention (CRISPRi repression of 3 chosen genes); Q2: performed in this study (only the DN5 chassis and pB3 are prior work); Q3: results directly informed which gene(s) to repress and revealed combination effects.
ddr_annotation.design_action_rationale: Blocking PEP dissipation to enhance supply of the limiting precursor PEP for NeuAc synthesis.
ddr_annotation.trigger_observation: DN5/pB3 accumulated large amounts of ManNAc (direct NeuAc precursor) while PEP showed no accumulation, indicating PEP was limiting relative to ManNAc.
ddr_annotation.evidence_grading_rationale: Precursor accumulation measured by HPLC; intervention outcomes measured as NeuAc titers across all combinations in triplicate.
ddr_annotation.reason_nature_rationale: Paper explicitly reasons that PEP is consumed by conversion to acetyl-CoA/pyruvate (pykA, pta) and the PTS glucose-uptake system (ptsI), so repressing these three genes should conserve PEP for NeuAc synthesis.
ddr_annotation.generalizable_rule: When one precursor (PEP) is limiting relative to a co-substrate (ManNAc) in E. coli NeuAc biosynthesis, repress PEP-dissipating reactions (PTS component ptsI, pyruvate kinase pykA) rather than only pushing the downstream pathway, because conserving the limiting precursor redirects flux toward product formation; note single-node repression (ptsI) outperformed combinations here, so combinations must be tested rather than assumed additive.

unsupported_values: Test whether E. coli can optimally utilize multiple alternative carbon sources via serial adaptive laboratory evolution (ALE) first in L-lactate then glycerol and vice versa; elucidate the genetic and transcriptomic basis of serial adaptation; and assess serial-ALE strains for acetoin bioproduction under single and mixed-carbon conditions.

Serial (sequential single-carbon) ALE across two fitness landscapes yields a single dominant generalist lineage with universal growth advantage on both carbon sources and their mixture, avoiding the fitness trade-offs or specialist subpopulations seen in mixed-carbon ALE, and the resulting rewired physiology improves bioproduction of a value-added product (acetoin).

Escherichia coli K-12 MG1655 wild-type (parental/ancestor); phase-1 evolved strains LA (lactate-adapted) and GL (glycerol-adapted); serial-ALE end-point strains LA-GL and GL-LA; LA and LA-GL derivatives with mutT and dam restored at the lacZ locus (used as acetoin production hosts); reconstructed single/sequential mutants in MG1655 background.

Adaptive mutations tracked by WGS: LA lineage - rph-pyrE 69 bp deletion (rph 619del69, E207fs; first fixed by generation 50), hfq (142 A>T), cyaA (reported as 2336 T>G in 2.2 and 2236 T>G in 2.4 - unresolved), ppsA (72 T>G), ydcI (5 A>C); GL lineage - rpoC (3610del9, V1204fs), glpK (694 G>T, G232C); second phase added ppsA (13 G>T, G5R), ydcI (686-7insG, G229fs), hdfR (463 G>T, E155*), glpK (189 A>C); mutator phenotypes of LA and LA-GL attributed to mutT and dam mutations, restored with wild-type mutT and dam at lacZ. rpoC mutant excluded from reverse engineering (essential gene difficulty).

Two-phase serial adaptive laboratory evolution (serial passage at mid-exponential phase, ~800 generations per carbon source, 1400-1600 generations total); lambda-Red one-step inactivation/recombineering (Datsenko-Wanner) with pKD13 kanamycin cassette, overlap-extension PCR and pCP20 marker excision for reverse engineering of single, sequential and double mutants; restoration of mutT/dam at lacZ locus; episomal heterologous expression of Bacillus subtilis alsS and Aeromonas hydrophila alsD from plasmid pTrcHis2A-alsSD (IPTG-inducible).

ALE: three independent populations per lineage direction (LA->LA-GL and GL->GL-LA). Phenotyping: WT, LA, GL, LA-GL, GL-LA each in M9 glycerol, M9 lactate, and M9 mix; also acetate, D-xylose, D-glucose, LB, TB. Reverse engineering: 11 single/sequential mutants from LA-GL mutation set and 7 from GL-LA set in WT background, assayed in glycerol, lactate, and mixed conditions; double mutants glpK(694G>T)-rph-pyrE(del) and ppsA(13G>T)-rph-pyrE(del). Transcriptomics: WT and end-point strains in respective evolutionary media and mixed-carbon (10 datasets, 1205 DEGs). Biolog PM1/PM2A respiration profiling. Acetoin production: WT, GL, GL-LA carrying pTrcHis2A-alsSD in M9 glycerol, M9 lactate, M9 mix with casamino acids.

E. coli MG1655 wild-type as ancestral/unevolved comparator in all growth, uptake, transcriptome, cAMP, Biolog and acetoin assays; single-ALE ancestors LA and GL as comparators for serial-ALE end-point strains; negative-control wells (AUC baseline) in Biolog phenotype microarray to discriminate false-negative growth; 'control__wt_glc' sample used as baseline control for iModulon ICA against the PRECISE compendium.

30 C, oxic. ALE: 60 mL M9 minimal in 300 mL Erlenmeyer flasks, 200 rpm shaking, serial transfer twice daily at OD600 0.4-0.6 (mid-exponential), initial OD adjusted downward as growth improved. Plate-reader growth assays: 48-well, 300 uL working volume, 807 rpm double orbital, 30 C, 24 h, OD600 every 30 min. Biolog: 30 C, 48 h on OmniLog. Acetoin batch production: 60 mL, 30 C with shaking, 24 h, supernatant sampled every 2 h. Pre-cultures: 3 mL M9 with matched carbon source.

M9 minimal medium (M9 salts, 2 mM MgSO4, 0.1 mM CaCl2) with either 0.2% (v/v) L-lactate or 0.2% (v/v) glycerol as sole carbon source; M9 mix (0.1% v/v each of glycerol and L-lactate); acetoin production media: M9 glycerol / M9 lactate / M9 mix each supplemented with 0.2% Casamino Acids and 100 ug/mL ampicillin; LB agar with 50 ug/mL kanamycin for recombineering selection; LB for pCP20 curing at 42 C; enriched LB and Terrific Broth for non-adaptive growth profiling; Biolog IF-0a GN/GP inoculating fluid with PM1/PM2A plates.

Carbon sources: 0.2% v/v L-lactate or glycerol (single), 0.1% v/v each (mix); non-adaptive carbons: sodium acetate 0.2% v/v, D-xylose 0.2% w/v, D-glucose 0.2% w/v; kanamycin 50 ug/mL; ampicillin 100 ug/mL; IPTG 10 uM added 2 h post-inoculation; Casamino Acids 0.2%; Biolog inoculum OD600 = 0.05; cAMP assay cell input ~20 mL of OD600 = 1.0 culture.

ALE: ~800 generations phase 1, then 600-800 generations phase 2 (1400-1600 total); WGS sampling every 50 generations; growth assays 24 h with OD600 at 30-min intervals; Biolog respiration 48 h; acetoin batch 24 h with supernatant sampling at 2 h intervals; IPTG induction at 2 h post-inoculation; RNASnap lysis 95 C 7 min; cAMP lysis 20 min at room temperature.

Three independent ALE populations per lineage direction (independent_culture_replicates, biological_independence=likely); growth/fitness assays and SGR/CUR comparisons: biological triplicates (Fig. 1 and Fig. 2 captions, SD error bars); acetoin production: three biological replicates (Fig. 4 caption); Biolog PM: biological triplicates; cAMP ELISA: each sample assayed in duplicates (technical replicates); RNA-seq replicate counts not stated in main text (requires supplement).

Doubling time per passage from initial/final OD of serial transfers (fitness trajectory); specific growth rate (SGR) from OD600 time series; specific carbon uptake rate (CUR) by HPLC of spent media; whole-genome resequencing for mutation trajectories; reconstructed-mutant fitness assay (percent contribution = mutant SGR relative to end-point strain SGR); RNA-seq transcriptomics with PCA, DEG and iModulon/ICA analysis; intracellular cAMP ELISA (colorimetric, non-acetylation protocol); Biolog PM1/PM2A specific respiration rates (AUC); maximum acetoin specific productivity from HPLC time courses.

BioTek Epoch2 / Synergy HT plate readers; Shimadzu Nexera LC-40 HPLC with RID-20A RI detector and Agilent MetaCarb 87H column (0.007 N H2SO4, 0.6 mL/min, 50 C or 65 C for mixed-carbon); Covaris S220 ultrasonicator; Qubit 2.0 fluorometer; Illumina HiSeq 2500 (50-cycle SE, WGS) and HiSeq X Ten (150-cycle PE, RNA-seq); TapeStation 2200 with High Sensitivity D1000; Bio-Rad MicroPulser electroporator; Biolog OmniLog.

CLC Genomics Workbench read trimming/mapping to NC_000913.3 (mismatch cost 2, indel cost 3, length/similarity 0.9); Quality-based Variant Detection (min coverage 10, min variant frequency 10%); mutation causality triangulation via recurrence across ALE studies and ALEdb; DESeq2 normalization and fold-change; hierarchical clustering (Euclidean, complete); PCA; OptICA/iModulon analysis against PRECISE 278-dataset compendium (100 iterations, 1e-7 tolerance, DBSCAN robust components); student's independent t-test for Biolog AUC; pairwise significance testing with P<0.05/0.01/0.001 thresholds (full matrix in Table S3).

Serial-ALE end-point strains (LA-GL, GL-LA) showed generalist phenotype with significantly improved SGR/CUR in both glycerol and lactate and in the mixture without trade-offs on the first carbon (e.g., GL-LA +1.89x SGR, +1.73x CUR vs GL); mixed-carbon growth advantages 1.38-2.15x over WT. Four variants (glpK, ppsA, ydcI, rph-pyrE) accounted for >80% of end-point strain fitness; glpK/ppsA specialist effects vanished in mixed carbon and were rescued/strengthened by rph-pyrE(del) (double mutants: ~2x rph-pyrE single-mutant contribution for glpK pair, >=+8% for ppsA pair). Transcriptomes diverged lineage-specifically despite fitness convergence; RpoS/GadW iModulons decreased in all evolved strains; GlpR/LldR/Zur/Crp-2 activities condition-specific. glpK-mutant strains had up to 38% lower intracellular cAMP. 82 carbons with increased respiration in >=1 evolved strain, 36 concordant across all; evolved strains grew faster on acetate/xylose/glucose but showed fitness deficits in LB/TB. Acetoin: GL-LA specific productivity highest in all conditions; ~3.7x (GL-LA) and 2.9x (GL) vs WT in glycerol; GL-LA 1.3x over GL (glycerol), 1.6x/1.4x over WT/GL in lactate; superior in mixed condition.

objective.value: Test whether E. coli can optimally utilize multiple alternative carbon sources via serial adaptive laboratory evolution (ALE) first in L-lactate then glycerol and vice versa; elucidate the genetic and transcriptomic basis of serial adaptation; and assess serial-ALE strains for acetoin bioproduction under single and mixed-carbon conditions.
objective.notes: Abstract and Introduction final paragraph state the objective directly.

hypothesis.value: Serial (sequential single-carbon) ALE across two fitness landscapes yields a single dominant generalist lineage with universal growth advantage on both carbon sources and their mixture, avoiding the fitness trade-offs or specialist subpopulations seen in mixed-carbon ALE, and the resulting rewired physiology improves bioproduction of a value-added product (acetoin).

inference.rationale: No explicit formal hypothesis statement; inferred from 'To test whether a bacterial strain can optimally utilize multiple carbon sources' (abstract) and Discussion statement that serial ALE is expected to enable evolution of a single dominant generalist instead of co-existing sub-populations.

hypothesis.notes: Authors frame expectations but do not label a formal hypothesis.

strain.value: Escherichia coli K-12 MG1655 wild-type (parental/ancestor); phase-1 evolved strains LA (lactate-adapted) and GL (glycerol-adapted); serial-ALE end-point strains LA-GL and GL-LA; LA and LA-GL derivatives with mutT and dam restored at the lacZ locus (used as acetoin production hosts); reconstructed single/sequential mutants in MG1655 background.
strain.notes: Strain list and plasmids deferred to Supplementary Table S1 (not available); lineage nomenclature LA/GL/LA-GL/GL-LA defined in Results 2.1. 'wild type' paper label corresponds to standard lab strain MG1655, not a natural isolate.

genotype.value: Adaptive mutations tracked by WGS: LA lineage - rph-pyrE 69 bp deletion (rph 619del69, E207fs; first fixed by generation 50), hfq (142 A>T), cyaA (reported as 2336 T>G in 2.2 and 2236 T>G in 2.4 - unresolved), ppsA (72 T>G), ydcI (5 A>C); GL lineage - rpoC (3610del9, V1204fs), glpK (694 G>T, G232C); second phase added ppsA (13 G>T, G5R), ydcI (686-7insG, G229fs), hdfR (463 G>T, E155*), glpK (189 A>C); mutator phenotypes of LA and LA-GL attributed to mutT and dam mutations, restored with wild-type mutT and dam at lacZ. rpoC mutant excluded from reverse engineering (essential gene difficulty).
genotype.notes: Fig. 1D table in extracted markdown has empty frequency cells; exact allele-frequency trajectories require figure rendering/supplement. cyaA nucleotide-change notation inconsistent between sections (see conflicts).

engineering_method.value: Two-phase serial adaptive laboratory evolution (serial passage at mid-exponential phase, ~800 generations per carbon source, 1400-1600 generations total); lambda-Red one-step inactivation/recombineering (Datsenko-Wanner) with pKD13 kanamycin cassette, overlap-extension PCR and pCP20 marker excision for reverse engineering of single, sequential and double mutants; restoration of mutT/dam at lacZ locus; episomal heterologous expression of Bacillus subtilis alsS and Aeromonas hydrophila alsD from plasmid pTrcHis2A-alsSD (IPTG-inducible).
engineering_method.notes: pTrcHis2A-alsSD was constructed in a previous study (Choe et al., 2022) - background element, not a design decision of this paper.

experimental_groups.value: ALE: three independent populations per lineage direction (LA->LA-GL and GL->GL-LA). Phenotyping: WT, LA, GL, LA-GL, GL-LA each in M9 glycerol, M9 lactate, and M9 mix; also acetate, D-xylose, D-glucose, LB, TB. Reverse engineering: 11 single/sequential mutants from LA-GL mutation set and 7 from GL-LA set in WT background, assayed in glycerol, lactate, and mixed conditions; double mutants glpK(694G>T)-rph-pyrE(del) and ppsA(13G>T)-rph-pyrE(del). Transcriptomics: WT and end-point strains in respective evolutionary media and mixed-carbon (10 datasets, 1205 DEGs). Biolog PM1/PM2A respiration profiling. Acetoin production: WT, GL, GL-LA carrying pTrcHis2A-alsSD in M9 glycerol, M9 lactate, M9 mix with casamino acids.
experimental_groups.notes: Methods 4.2 says 'Two independent lineages' (the two lineage directions), Results 2.1 says 'Three independent populations' were serially passaged - recorded as minor ambiguity, interpreted as 3 populations per direction.

controls.value: E. coli MG1655 wild-type as ancestral/unevolved comparator in all growth, uptake, transcriptome, cAMP, Biolog and acetoin assays; single-ALE ancestors LA and GL as comparators for serial-ALE end-point strains; negative-control wells (AUC baseline) in Biolog phenotype microarray to discriminate false-negative growth; 'control__wt_glc' sample used as baseline control for iModulon ICA against the PRECISE compendium.
controls.notes: No empty-plasmid/no-pathway negative control for acetoin production is reported in the main text.

culture_conditions.value: 30 C, oxic. ALE: 60 mL M9 minimal in 300 mL Erlenmeyer flasks, 200 rpm shaking, serial transfer twice daily at OD600 0.4-0.6 (mid-exponential), initial OD adjusted downward as growth improved. Plate-reader growth assays: 48-well, 300 uL working volume, 807 rpm double orbital, 30 C, 24 h, OD600 every 30 min. Biolog: 30 C, 48 h on OmniLog. Acetoin batch production: 60 mL, 30 C with shaking, 24 h, supernatant sampled every 2 h. Pre-cultures: 3 mL M9 with matched carbon source.
culture_conditions.notes: Cell-stock temperature printed as '80 C glycerol cell stocks' - minus sign lost in parsing; physically implies -80 C (see conflicts).

medium.value: M9 minimal medium (M9 salts, 2 mM MgSO4, 0.1 mM CaCl2) with either 0.2% (v/v) L-lactate or 0.2% (v/v) glycerol as sole carbon source; M9 mix (0.1% v/v each of glycerol and L-lactate); acetoin production media: M9 glycerol / M9 lactate / M9 mix each supplemented with 0.2% Casamino Acids and 100 ug/mL ampicillin; LB agar with 50 ug/mL kanamycin for recombineering selection; LB for pCP20 curing at 42 C; enriched LB and Terrific Broth for non-adaptive growth profiling; Biolog IF-0a GN/GP inoculating fluid with PM1/PM2A plates.
medium.notes: Only L-lactate (not D/DL mixtures) used unless stated otherwise.

dosage.value: Carbon sources: 0.2% v/v L-lactate or glycerol (single), 0.1% v/v each (mix); non-adaptive carbons: sodium acetate 0.2% v/v, D-xylose 0.2% w/v, D-glucose 0.2% w/v; kanamycin 50 ug/mL; ampicillin 100 ug/mL; IPTG 10 uM added 2 h post-inoculation; Casamino Acids 0.2%; Biolog inoculum OD600 = 0.05; cAMP assay cell input ~20 mL of OD600 = 1.0 culture.
dosage.notes: Methods 4.13 prints 'M9 lactate (0.2 v/v L-lactate)' with missing % sign (typo).

time.value: ALE: ~800 generations phase 1, then 600-800 generations phase 2 (1400-1600 total); WGS sampling every 50 generations; growth assays 24 h with OD600 at 30-min intervals; Biolog respiration 48 h; acetoin batch 24 h with supernatant sampling at 2 h intervals; IPTG induction at 2 h post-inoculation; RNASnap lysis 95 C 7 min; cAMP lysis 20 min at room temperature.
time.notes: ALE duration expressed in generations, not calendar time; per-passage wall time not reported.

replicates.value: Three independent ALE populations per lineage direction (independent_culture_replicates, biological_independence=likely); growth/fitness assays and SGR/CUR comparisons: biological triplicates (Fig. 1 and Fig. 2 captions, SD error bars); acetoin production: three biological replicates (Fig. 4 caption); Biolog PM: biological triplicates; cAMP ELISA: each sample assayed in duplicates (technical replicates); RNA-seq replicate counts not stated in main text (requires supplement).
replicates.notes: RNA-seq replicate structure and per-mutant growth-assay replicate counts not visible in main text - requires_supplement.

assay.value: Doubling time per passage from initial/final OD of serial transfers (fitness trajectory); specific growth rate (SGR) from OD600 time series; specific carbon uptake rate (CUR) by HPLC of spent media; whole-genome resequencing for mutation trajectories; reconstructed-mutant fitness assay (percent contribution = mutant SGR relative to end-point strain SGR); RNA-seq transcriptomics with PCA, DEG and iModulon/ICA analysis; intracellular cAMP ELISA (colorimetric, non-acetylation protocol); Biolog PM1/PM2A specific respiration rates (AUC); maximum acetoin specific productivity from HPLC time courses.

instruments.value: BioTek Epoch2 / Synergy HT plate readers; Shimadzu Nexera LC-40 HPLC with RID-20A RI detector and Agilent MetaCarb 87H column (0.007 N H2SO4, 0.6 mL/min, 50 C or 65 C for mixed-carbon); Covaris S220 ultrasonicator; Qubit 2.0 fluorometer; Illumina HiSeq 2500 (50-cycle SE, WGS) and HiSeq X Ten (150-cycle PE, RNA-seq); TapeStation 2200 with High Sensitivity D1000; Bio-Rad MicroPulser electroporator; Biolog OmniLog.

analysis_methods.value: CLC Genomics Workbench read trimming/mapping to NC_000913.3 (mismatch cost 2, indel cost 3, length/similarity 0.9); Quality-based Variant Detection (min coverage 10, min variant frequency 10%); mutation causality triangulation via recurrence across ALE studies and ALEdb; DESeq2 normalization and fold-change; hierarchical clustering (Euclidean, complete); PCA; OptICA/iModulon analysis against PRECISE 278-dataset compendium (100 iterations, 1e-7 tolerance, DBSCAN robust components); student's independent t-test for Biolog AUC; pairwise significance testing with P<0.05/0.01/0.001 thresholds (full matrix in Table S3).
analysis_methods.notes: Abstract calls iModulon/ICA 'machine learning analysis'. Statistical test used for SGR/CUR/productivity comparisons not specified in main text (Table S3 in supplement).

outcomes.value: Serial-ALE end-point strains (LA-GL, GL-LA) showed generalist phenotype with significantly improved SGR/CUR in both glycerol and lactate and in the mixture without trade-offs on the first carbon (e.g., GL-LA +1.89x SGR, +1.73x CUR vs GL); mixed-carbon growth advantages 1.38-2.15x over WT. Four variants (glpK, ppsA, ydcI, rph-pyrE) accounted for >80% of end-point strain fitness; glpK/ppsA specialist effects vanished in mixed carbon and were rescued/strengthened by rph-pyrE(del) (double mutants: ~2x rph-pyrE single-mutant contribution for glpK pair, >=+8% for ppsA pair). Transcriptomes diverged lineage-specifically despite fitness convergence; RpoS/GadW iModulons decreased in all evolved strains; GlpR/LldR/Zur/Crp-2 activities condition-specific. glpK-mutant strains had up to 38% lower intracellular cAMP. 82 carbons with increased respiration in >=1 evolved strain, 36 concordant across all; evolved strains grew faster on acetate/xylose/glucose but showed fitness deficits in LB/TB. Acetoin: GL-LA specific productivity highest in all conditions; ~3.7x (GL-LA) and 2.9x (GL) vs WT in glycerol; GL-LA 1.3x over GL (glycerol), 1.6x/1.4x over WT/GL in lactate; superior in mixed condition.
outcomes.notes: Exact SGR/CUR/productivity values, error bars and full statistics reside in Table S3 / Supplementary Figs (requires_supplement); mechanism of rph-pyrE epistasis stated by authors as elusive - interpretation, not validated causality.

experimental_design_object.purpose: Evolve E. coli MG1655 sequentially on two alternative carbon sources to obtain generalist end-point strains and test serial-ALE as a strain-optimization scheme.
experimental_design_object.host: E. coli K-12 MG1655 (clonal ancestral population)
experimental_design_object.intervention: Two-phase serial ALE: phase 1 ~800 generations on M9+lactate (LA) or M9+glycerol (GL); carbon switch at fitness plateau; phase 2 600-800 generations on the other carbon (LA-GL, GL-LA); 60 mL M9 in 300 mL flasks, 30 C, 200 rpm, transfer twice daily at OD600 0.4-0.6.

conditions.medium: M9 minimal + 0.2% v/v single carbon per phase
conditions.selection: fastest-growing progeny via mid-exponential serial transfer

experimental_design_object.control: Wild-type MG1655 (fitness baseline); phase-1 ancestors LA/GL as comparators for end-point strains
experimental_design_object.readout: Doubling time per passage vs cumulative generation; end-point SGR and CUR in each carbon source
experimental_design_object.analysis: Fitness trajectory plateau detection; pairwise significance vs WT (Table S3)
experimental_design_object.outcome: End-point strains LA-GL and GL-LA acquired universal growth advantage on both single and mixed carbon sources without trade-off on the first carbon; GL showed trade-off in lactate (single-ALE specialist).

ddr_annotation.decision_type_rationale: Q1: deliberate initiation of an ALE/selection campaign; Q2: performed in this study; Q3: produced the chassis later chosen (GL-LA) for bioproduction, changing subsequent design choices.
ddr_annotation.design_action_rationale: Integrated evolution/screening campaign generating strain variants rather than targeting a pre-specified genetic change.
ddr_annotation.trigger_observation: E. coli K-12 exhibits suboptimal fitness on glycerol and lactate, and prior single-carbon ALE studies showed such phenotypes can be reconfigured by evolution; whether sequential adaptation across two landscapes works was seldom explored.
ddr_annotation.evidence_grading_rationale: Outcome measured directly (growth rates, uptake rates, WGS of evolving populations).
ddr_annotation.reason_nature_rationale: Choice of ALE and the 800-generation timescale explicitly built on prior studies (Ibarra 2002, Kang 2019, Sandberg 2019) rather than a newly derived mechanistic argument; sequential single-carbon design contrasted against prior mixed-carbon ALE (Sandberg 2017).
ddr_annotation.generalizable_rule: When optimizing E. coli for utilization of multiple metabolically related alternative carbon sources (e.g., gluconeogenic glycerol and L-lactate), apply serial single-carbon ALE phases (~800 generations each to fitness plateau) instead of simultaneous mixed-carbon evolution, because sequential adaptation fixed carbon-specialist plus generalist mutations and avoided fitness trade-offs and specialist subpopulation splitting in the tested two-carbon system.
alternatives_considered: Simultaneous mixed-carbon ALE (contrasted with Sandberg et al., 2017; avoided to evade trade-offs/bet-hedging)

ddr_annotation.reason_nature_rationale: Paper explicitly attributes the mutator phenotype to mutT (8-oxo-dGTP diphosphatase) and dam (DNA adenine methyltransferase) defects; restoring wild-type alleles acts on a well-defined DNA-repair mechanism.
ddr_annotation.generalizable_rule: When deploying ALE-derived E. coli lineages as production hosts, check and restore DNA-repair defects (e.g., mutT/dam mutator alleles) before pathway introduction, because mutator backgrounds accumulated during evolution destabilize the production genotype - validated here only for lactate/glycerol-evolved MG1655 lineages used for acetoin production.
