experiments.purpose: Adapt E. coli W to glycerol limitation to improve glycerol utilization and growth as a chassis for growth-coupled GABA production.
experiments.intervention: Serial-batch adaptive laboratory evolution in M9 + 0.2% (v/v) glycerol; 50 mL / 250 mL flask, 37 C, agitation; transfer every 12 h; initial OD600 stepped down 0.0008 -> 0.0004 -> 0.00016; ~1300 generations; single clone CY02 isolated from fittest endpoint lineage on M9-glycerol agar.
experiments.conditions: M9 minimal, glycerol sole carbon, 37 C, 200 rpm.
experiments.control: Parental E. coli W grown in parallel assays (growth-rate and glycerol-consumption comparison, incl. M9-glucose reference).
experiments.replicates: single evolving lineage; endpoint characterized as single clone (replicate lineages not reported)
experiments.readout: Doubling time/growth rate trajectory (Fig. 1B/C), specific growth rate, glycerol consumption rate (Fig. 1D).
experiments.analysis: Generation number Eq. (1); fold-change comparison to parental strain.
experiments.outcome: Growth rate +~40% (0.67 -> 0.94 /hr); glycerol consumption rate significantly increased; negligible fitness change on glucose (glycerol-specialist adaptation).

ddr_annotation.decision_type_rationale: Q1 pass (ALE campaign initiated by authors); Q2 pass (performed in this study); Q3 pass (produced CY02 chassis that enabled all subsequent engineering choices).
ddr_annotation.design_action_rationale: ALE is an integrated selection/screening campaign enriching beneficial genotypes rather than a single targeted modification.
ddr_annotation.trigger_observation: Glycerol is a non-preferential, low-energy-density carbon source; prior work showed E. coli W among the best GABA producers from glycerol but without optimization (Hou and Kang, 2018).
ddr_annotation.evidence_grading_rationale: Outcome measured directly: growth rates, glycerol uptake rates, WGS mutation profiles.
ddr_annotation.reason_nature_rationale: ALE justified by established precedent of glycerol ALE in E. coli (Ibarra 2002; Fong 2005; Cheng 2014; Herring 2006; Kang 2019) and prior demonstration of E. coli W GABA production; no de novo mechanistic prediction drove the choice.
ddr_annotation.generalizable_rule: When improving an E. coli host for growth-coupled product formation from the low-energy-density feedstock glycerol, apply serial-batch ALE under glycerol limitation (order of 10^3 generations), because selection enriches substrate-uptake/utilization mutations (e.g., glpK, crp) that raise fitness and feedstock conversion, as validated for E. coli W glycerol utilization and GABA production in this study.

experiments.purpose: Identify causal mutations underlying fitness improvement.
experiments.host: Parental E. coli W, endpoint population, CY02
experiments.intervention: Whole-genome resequencing (MiSeq 50-cycle SE); background mutations of lab stock vs NC_017635.1 excluded; shared mutations between population and clone prioritized.
experiments.conditions: gDNA from cultures; TruSeq DNA LT library.
experiments.control: Parental strain sequence as reference baseline.
experiments.readout: Mutation calls: 30 (population) / 28 (CY02) new mutations; shared set incl. glpK T235M, crp R209H, ptsP fs, rsfS Q6*, mglC fs.
experiments.analysis: CLC Genomics Workbench mapping; recurrence-based prioritization against ALE literature.
experiments.outcome: glpK^m and crp^m nominated as key causal mutations; mglC judged hitchhiker (reverse-engineered mutant grew like WT, Fig. S2).

ddr_annotation.decision_type_rationale: Q1 fails: sequencing and mutation identification is measurement/characterization, not an engineering intervention.

experiments.purpose: Test whether glpK^m and crp^m recapitulate fitness benefits in the parental background.
experiments.intervention: Lambda-Red recombineering (Datsenko-Wanner) to construct glpK^m, crp^m singles and glpK^m crp^m double mutant.
experiments.conditions: M9 + 0.2% glycerol, 37 C, 200 rpm.
experiments.readout: Specific growth rate and specific glycerol uptake rate.
experiments.analysis: Independent t-tests; fold-change vs WT.
experiments.outcome: glpK^m +1.45-fold growth (p<0.022), +1.78-fold GUR (p=0.02); double +1.56/+1.70; CY02 +1.63/+1.60; crp^m alone not significant; glpK^m accounts for >90% of CY02 fitness increase (Discussion).

ddr_annotation.decision_type_rationale: Q1 pass (point mutations deliberately introduced); Q2 pass (constructed in this study); Q3 pass (results established glpK^m as the dominant contributor and informed downstream interpretation/engineering).
ddr_annotation.design_action_rationale: glpK encodes the rate-limiting enzyme (pacemaker) of glycerol dissimilation; introducing the T235M variant engineers the rate-limiting step (relief of FBP allosteric inhibition).
ddr_annotation.trigger_observation: WGS found glpK^m and crp^m shared between endpoint population and CY02 and recurrent across published glycerol/nutrient-limitation ALE experiments; mglC failed validation as hitchhiker.
ddr_annotation.evidence_grading_rationale: Fitness and GUR effects measured directly in reconstructed strains; enzyme phenotype confirmed by kinetics (EXP4).
ddr_annotation.reason_nature_rationale: The mutations were discovered by ALE selection and prioritized by recurrence, not rationally designed by the authors; mechanistic understanding (FBP site) was inferred after the fact.
alternatives_considered: ptsP, rsfS and mglC were candidate causal mutations but deprioritized (mglC shown phenotypically neutral; rsfS low recurrence; ptsP role left unresolved)

experiments.purpose: Determine whether T235M alters GlpK catalytic/allosteric properties.
experiments.host: In vitro: purified GlpK^w and GlpK T235M (overexpressed in BL21(DE3), pET28a, Ni-NTA).
experiments.intervention: Coupled PK/LDH kinetic assay; FBP titration 0-10 mM.
experiments.conditions: 50 mM PIPES pH 7.0, 5 mM MgCl2, 20 mM KCl, 2.5 mM ATP, 25 C, A340.
experiments.replicates: six replicates (WT), five (T235M); replicate type undefined
experiments.readout: Vmax, Km_gly, kcat, kcat/Km, FBP K0.5 (Table 2).
experiments.analysis: SigmaPlot 12 fit to Eq. (4) Hill-type inhibition model.
experiments.outcome: Catalytic parameters essentially unchanged; FBP K0.5 386 uM (WT) vs >10,000 uM (T235M): mutant insensitive to FBP inhibition; WT expected maximally inhibited at cytosolic FBP ~5.85 mM.

ddr_annotation.decision_type_rationale: Q1 fails: enzyme kinetics is characterization validating the glpK^m mechanism; no new engineering action.

experiments.purpose: Test whether glycerol adaptation rewires cAMP-CRP signaling.
experiments.host: WT, glpK^m, crp^m, glpK^m crp^m, CY02
experiments.intervention: Intracellular cAMP extraction (65% ethanol) and commercial ELISA (Invitrogen) at exponential phase.
experiments.conditions: M9-glycerol exponential cultures.
experiments.readout: cAMP relative to WT: glpK^m-harboring strains ~2% (98% decrease), CY02 ~20%, crp^m ~36%; all P<0.001.
experiments.analysis: One-way ANOVA + Tukey post hoc.
experiments.outcome: GlpK-driven cAMP depletion confirmed; crp^m unexpectedly lowers cAMP; CY02 intermediate level interpreted as adaptive vs maladaptive extremes of single mutants.

ddr_annotation.decision_type_rationale: Q1 fails: measurement of signaling state; no intervention beyond already-constructed strains.

experiments.purpose: Profile genome-wide expression changes after glycerol adaptation.
experiments.intervention: RNA-seq (RNASnap extraction, RiboZero depletion, TruSeq stranded, HiSeq 50-cycle SE) at OD600 0.4-0.5 in M9 + 2 g/L glycerol.
experiments.conditions: M9 + 2 g/L glycerol, exponential phase.
experiments.readout: 640 DEGs (149 up, 491 down); 181 DEGs are CRP regulons (>2-fold enrichment over genomic ~12%); 148/157 positively CRP-regulated genes downregulated; lower glycolysis up, TCA/respiration/ATP synthase down, pta-ackA up, acs down.
experiments.analysis: CLC mapping; DESeq2 (FC>2, adj P<0.01); CRP regulon annotation via RegulonDB.
experiments.outcome: Transcriptome consistent with cAMP depletion and aerobic acetate overflow phenotype.

ddr_annotation.decision_type_rationale: Q1 fails: transcriptomic measurement supporting mechanism, no engineering action.

experiments.purpose: Verify glpK mRNA downregulation across mutants.
experiments.intervention: RT-qPCR of glpK normalized to rrsA/ihfB.
experiments.conditions: M9-glycerol log-phase RNA.
experiments.readout: glpK expression 3-6% of WT in glpK^m-harboring strains incl. CY02; ~22% in crp^m; < half of glpK^m single in the double.
experiments.analysis: StepOne software v2.3; standard-curve efficiency from 10^1-10^4 gDNA dilutions.
experiments.outcome: Supports G3P-mediated auto-catabolite repression of the glpFKX operon.

ddr_annotation.decision_type_rationale: Q1 fails: targeted transcript measurement.

experiments.purpose: Test whether transcriptomic signs of overflow translate into acetate secretion.
experiments.host: WT, glpK^m, crp^m, glpK^m crp^m, CY02
experiments.intervention: Acetate quantification (Cedex Acetate V2) in exponential M9-glycerol cultures; rate per Eq. (3).

ddr_annotation.decision_type_rationale: Q1 fails: phenotype measurement; it triggers later engineering but is itself not an intervention.

experiments.readout: GABA production capability.
experiments.analysis: n/a

experiments.purpose: Overcome negligible GABA production observed in minimal glycerol medium.
experiments.host: WT, glpK^m, crp^m, glpK^m crp^m, CY02 (lacZ:mtGAD)
experiments.intervention: Switch from M9 + 0.2% glycerol + 50 mg/L yeast extract to amino-acid-rich LB + glycerol; glycerol concentration screen (0-? %; optimum 2% v/v) using growth rate as proxy assuming growth-coupled production; stationary-phase GABA screen of all strains.
experiments.conditions: LB + 2% (v/v) glycerol, 37 C, 200 rpm, 50 mL/250 mL flask.
experiments.readout: Final GABA: minimal medium 0.06 vs 0.06 g/L (WT vs CY02, negligible); LB + 2% glycerol: WT 0.05, crp^m 0.06, glpK^m 0.07, glpK^m crp^m 0.07, CY02 0.17 g/L.
experiments.analysis: Growth-rate proxy screen (Fig. S7); HPLC GABA quantification (medium-specific methods).

ddr_annotation.decision_type_rationale: Q1 pass (deliberate fermentation-condition change); Q2 pass (done in this study); Q3 pass (enabled all subsequent production gains and defined the assay medium for engineering).
ddr_annotation.design_action_rationale: Fermentation/process-level optimization of medium composition and substrate concentration.
ddr_annotation.trigger_observation: Final GABA titers in minimal glycerol medium were negligible and identical between WT and CY02 (0.06 g/L), despite improved glycerol uptake.
ddr_annotation.evidence_grading_rationale: Decisions followed measured titers and measured growth-rate optima (Fig. S7).
ddr_annotation.reason_nature_rationale: Amino-acid supplementation to restore growth efficiency and >=1% carbon feed are adopted from cited literature (Prensky 2021; Russell 1995; Waschina 2016; prior GABA studies); the growth-coupling assumption is an assumption, and the metabolic-cost argument is literature-sourced mechanism rather than mechanism demonstrated in this paper.
ddr_annotation.generalizable_rule: When growth-coupled production of an amino-acid-derived product (GABA) from glycerol stalls in minimal medium, switch to an amino-acid-rich complex medium and re-optimize feedstock concentration using growth rate as proxy, because biosynthetic precursor (L-glutamate) cost and carbon availability, not uptake capacity, limit product formation - demonstrated for E. coli W GABA production.
alternatives_considered: Continuing in minimal medium with higher glycerol alone (rejected: 0.2% glycerol itself limiting and growth inefficiency persists)

experiments.purpose: Quantify time-course GABA titer/productivity benefit of ALE strain.
experiments.intervention: 24 h time-course sampling of growth, GABA and glycerol in LB + 2% glycerol.
experiments.conditions: LB + 2% (v/v) glycerol, 37 C, 200 rpm.
experiments.readout: Max titer 0.15 +/- 0.01 (WT) vs 0.39 +/- 0.03 g/L (CY02); productivity 0.03 vs 0.08 g/L/hr (~2.6-fold); glycerol consumption totals similar.
experiments.analysis: Time-course comparison; HPLC.
experiments.outcome: ALE alone confers ~2.6-fold production gain attributed to improved metabolic efficiency/biomass yield rather than more glycerol consumed.

ddr_annotation.decision_type_rationale: Q1/Q3 fail for this record: it validates the already-evolved strain's production phenotype without any new modification.

experiments.purpose: Redirect acetate-overflow and bypass fluxes toward GABA production.
experiments.intervention: Lambda-Red deletion of ackA, mgsA, gabT singly, as three doubles, and as triple (CY02_TKO), in both CY02 and wild-type backgrounds.
experiments.conditions: LB + 2% (v/v) glycerol, 37 C, 200 rpm, 50 mL/250 mL flasks.
experiments.readout: Growth (lag phase prolonged in ΔackA strains, growth rate unaffected), glycerol consumption, final GABA titer: singles below WT; doubles ΔgabTΔackA 0.46 +/- 0.02, ΔgabTΔmgsA 0.45 +/- 0.01 g/L; ΔmgsAΔackA 0.37 +/- 0.04; CY02_TKO 0.59 +/- 0.04 g/L, productivity 0.13 +/- 0.02 g/L/hr (1.5/1.6-fold vs CY02; 3.9/4.3-fold vs WT).
experiments.analysis: Time-course HPLC; comparison across backgrounds.
experiments.outcome: Combined triple deletion synergistic in CY02 background only; benefit absent in wild-type background - epistasis with ALE-acquired mutations; gabT deletion most important single contributor.

ddr_annotation.decision_type_rationale: Q1 pass (targeted gene deletions); Q2 pass (constructed in this study); Q3 pass (outcomes - singles detrimental, doubles/triple beneficial, background-dependence - directly shaped the final strain choice CY02_TKO).
ddr_annotation.design_action_rationale: Blocking competing/bypass sinks (acetate overflow via ackA, methylglyoxal/lactate bypass via mgsA, GABA re-consumption shunt via gabT) to redirect carbon flux toward GABA; mgsA deletion additionally serves M8-type toxicity management.
ddr_annotation.trigger_observation: CY02 exhibited pronounced acetate overflow (EXP8) wiring excess substrate influx to acetate; known risk of methylglyoxal accumulation to cytotoxic levels in FBP-insensitive glpK backgrounds; GABA shunt recycles product into TCA.
ddr_annotation.evidence_grading_rationale: Acetate overflow measured in this study (Fig. 4B); knockout phenotypes measured directly (Fig. 6, Table 3).
ddr_annotation.reason_nature_rationale: ackA deletion was decided from the measured acetate overflow in CY02 (mechanistic, this study); mgsA and gabT choices additionally rest on cited literature mechanisms (methylglyoxal toxicity of glpK mutants; gabT deletion as common GABA-improvement practice), hence dual tagging.
ddr_annotation.generalizable_rule: When a glycerol-adapted E. coli strain with enhanced substrate influx channels excess carbon into acetate overflow during GABA production, delete ackA, mgsA and gabT in combination, because blocking the acetate sink, the methylglyoxal bypass and the GABA shunt redirects carbon toward GABA - validated only in the evolved E. coli W CY02 background; the same deletions did not improve production in the wild-type background, so the rule is background-dependent.
alternatives_considered: Other (unspecified) knockout targets were considered; ackA/mgsA/gabT chosen for the stated reasons

objective.value: Construct an Escherichia coli W derivative with improved gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) production from glycerol by combining adaptive laboratory evolution (1300 generations under glycerol limitation) with rational metabolic engineering (deletion of ackA, mgsA, gabT), and decipher the molecular basis of glycerol adaptation (mutation profiling, enzyme kinetics, transcriptomics).
objective.notes: Stated in abstract and section 2.7 opening.

hypothesis.value: ALE-improved glycerol uptake/utilization translates into superior growth-coupled GABA production, and redirecting acetate-overflow flux while blocking the methylglyoxal bypass and the GABA shunt in the evolved background further increases GABA titer and productivity.

inference.rationale: Section 2.7 states the objective to redirect acetate overflow flux to GABA and gives per-gene reasons; no single explicit hypothesis sentence exists in the text.

hypothesis.notes: Implicit working hypothesis; authors never state a formal null/alternative.

strain.value: Escherichia coli W (parental wild-type; reference genome NC_017635.1; ATCC 9637 per cited Archer et al. 2011); glycerol-evolved single clone CY02; reverse-engineered single mutants glpK^m and crp^m, double mutant glpK^m crp^m, and reverse-engineered mglC mutant; CY02 knockout derivatives CY02_ΔackA, CY02_ΔgabT, CY02_ΔmgsA, double KOs (ΔgabTΔackA, ΔgabTΔmgsA, ΔmgsAΔackA) and CY02_TKO; wild-type lacZ:mtGAD strain and its knockout derivatives; E. coli BL21(DE3) used only as GlpK overexpression host.
strain.notes: Exact strain list, plasmids and primers are in Supplementary Table S3, not available in the parsed document (requires_supplement).

genotype.value: CY02 carries 28 new mutations vs the lab parental stock, including glpK 707G>A (Thr235Met, glpK^m), crp SNV (Arg209His, crp^m), ptsP 522InsT (Pro174fs), rsfS 19G>C (Gln6*), mglC 15Adel (Asn4fs); engineered knockouts ΔackA, ΔmgsA, ΔgabT constructed singly, as doubles, and as triple (CY02_TKO); GABA production cassette = chromosomal insertion of mutant glutamate decarboxylase B (mtGAD) under promoter PLtetQ-1 at the lacZ locus (constitutive in E. coli W, which lacks the cognate repressor), marker-free.
genotype.notes: crp nucleotide change rendered as garbled '8516 > A' in Table 1 (OCR artifact; amino-acid change Arg209His reliable). rsfS codon position inconsistent between Table 1 (Gln6*) and text (7th codon) - see conflicts. Full 28-mutation list only in Fig. S1/Table 1 (shared 5 listed).

engineering_method.value: Serial-batch ALE in M9-glycerol with 12 h transfers and stepwise reduction of initial OD600 (0.0008 -> 0.0004 -> 0.00016) for 1300 generations; single-clone isolation on M9-glycerol agar; whole-genome resequencing (Illumina MiSeq 50-cycle SE); lambda-Red recombineering for point-mutation reverse engineering and KanR-mediated gene deletion (pKD13/pKD46/pCP20, marker cured at 42 C); chromosomal insertion of mtGAD cassette; GlpK overexpression/purification (pET28a, BL21(DE3), Ni-NTA) and coupled-enzyme kinetic assays; RNA-seq + DESeq2; RT-qPCR; intracellular cAMP ELISA; HPLC quantification of GABA/glycerol; Cedex Bio Analyzer glycerol/acetate assays.

experimental_groups.value: Per experiment: (ALE) single evolving lineage + parental reference; (fitness/GUR, Fig. 2A/B) parental WT, glpK^m, crp^m, glpK^m crp^m, CY02; (enzyme kinetics) purified WT GlpK vs GlpK T235M; (cAMP, Fig. 3B) WT, three reverse-engineered mutants, CY02; (RNA-seq) WT vs CY02; (acetate, Fig. 4B) same five strains; (minimal-medium GABA) WT vs CY02; (stationary-phase GABA screen) WT, glpK^m, crp^m, glpK^m crp^m, CY02; (time-course) WT vs CY02; (knockout, Fig. 6) CY02 + 3 singles + 3 doubles + TKO, and in parallel WT lacZ:mtGAD + its single/double/triple KO derivatives.
experimental_groups.notes: Fig. S2 (mglC reverse-engineered mutant) referenced but supplement unavailable.

controls.value: Parental E. coli W wild-type as baseline control in every phenotypic, enzymatic, transcriptomic and production comparison; wild-type GlpK (GlpK^w) as enzyme control; wild-type lacZ:mtGAD strain as background control to test whether knockout benefits are intrinsic or specific to the evolved CY02 background; no exogenous positive control reported.
controls.notes: 'wild-type' here = parental E. coli W stock (natural isolate lineage, lab-cultured), distinct from the mtGAD-bearing comparator strain.

culture_conditions.value: 37 C, 200 rpm, 50 mL culture in 250 mL Erlenmeyer flasks (growth, glycerol/acetate/GABA measurements); ALE: same flask format with transfer to fresh M9-glycerol every 12 h, initial OD600 stepped 0.0008 -> 0.0004 -> 0.00016; growth-rate screen (Fig. S7): 96-well EPOCH2 plate reader, 37 C, 807 rpm double-orbital, 110 uL working volume, OD600 every 10 min for 24 h; exponential-phase sampling for cAMP (OD not specified) and RNA-seq at OD600 0.4-0.5.
culture_conditions.notes: ALE total elapsed days not stated; only generations (1300) and 12 h transfer interval.

medium.value: M9 minimal medium (BD) + 0.2% (v/v) glycerol as sole carbon source (ALE, fitness, GUR, acetate); M9 + 0.2% (v/v) glycerol + 50 mg/L yeast extract for minimal-medium GABA production; LB + 2% (v/v) pure glycerol for optimized GABA production; M9 + 2 g/L glycerol for RNA-seq cultures; LB + kanamycin 50 ug/mL for mutant selection and BL21(DE3) expression.
medium.notes: Two distinct media were used for GABA production (minimal vs LB-based), each with its own HPLC quantification method.

dosage.value: Glycerol: 0.2% (v/v) in minimal medium; 2% (v/v) in LB production medium (optimum from growth-rate screen); 2 g/L for RNA-seq cultures; yeast extract 50 mg/L; kanamycin 50 ug/mL; IPTG 1 mM for GlpK induction; recombinogenic DNA 1 ug per electroporation; no chemical inducer needed for mtGAD (constitutive).

time.value: ALE: 1300 generations, serial transfer every 12 h; growth profiles sampled every 2 h; plate-reader screen 24 h; GABA time-course over 24 h; glycerol/acetate samples at 1 h intervals during exponential phase after 1.5 h initial incubation; RNA-seq harvest at OD600 0.4-0.5; stationary-phase GABA endpoint measurements.
time.notes: Calendar duration of ALE not reported.

replicates.value: Biological duplicates: specific growth rate, GUR (Fig. 2A/B) and acetate secretion (Fig. 4B). Biological triplicates: cAMP (each measured in technical duplicates), RNA-seq (high correlation among triplicates), GABA/glycerol time-courses in Fig. 5 and Fig. 6 (stated as three biological triplicates / biological triplicates). Enzyme specific activity: six replicates (WT GlpK) and five replicates (GlpK T235M), replicate type not defined. RT-qPCR: two biological replicates x three technical replicates. ALE: a single evolving lineage; single endpoint clone analyzed.
replicates.notes: Enzyme-assay replicate type (biological vs technical) unresolved; single ALE lineage limits evolutionary replication assessment.

assay.value: OD600 growth measurement; glycerol consumption and acetate secretion rates via Cedex Bio Analyzer (Glycerol Bio Test / Acetate V2 kits) with rate equations r=mu/Y; GABA by HPLC-UV - Primesep 100 column (20 mM phosphoric acid/ACN 80/20, 215 nm, 49 C) for minimal medium, dansyl-chloride derivatization + Zorbax Eclipse C18 (methanol gradient, 286 nm, 30 C) for LB medium; glycerol time-course by HPLC-RID (MetaCarb 87H, 6.57 mM H2SO4); GlpK kinetics via PK/LDH-coupled NADH decay at A340 (0-10 mM FBP for allostery); intracellular cAMP by commercial ELISA; RNA-seq (HiSeq 50-cycle SE); RT-qPCR of glpK (rrsA/ihfB normalization); WGS resequencing (MiSeq).

instruments.value: EPOCH2 plate reader/spectrophotometer (BioTek); Cedex Bio Analyzer (Roche); Nexera LC-40 HPLC with RID-20A RI detector and UV detectors (Shimadzu); MiSeq and HiSeq sequencers (Illumina); StepOnePlus Real-Time PCR System (Applied Biosystems); MicroPulser electroporator (Bio-Rad); Qubit 2.0 fluorometer; TapeStation 2200; Econo-Pac Ni-NTA chromatography setup.

analysis_methods.value: DESeq2 for DEG calling (fold change > 2 and adjusted P < 0.01); CLC Genomics Workbench read trimming (quality limit 0.05) and mapping to NC_017635.1 (mismatch cost 2, indel cost 3, length/similarity 0.9); independent t-tests (growth/GUR fold-changes with p-values); one-way ANOVA with Tukey's post hoc (cAMP, acetate); SigmaPlot 12 curve fitting of allosteric inhibition Eq. (4) (K0.5, Hill coefficient); generation number Eq. (1); rate equations Eqs. (2)-(3); CRP-regulon enrichment vs RegulonDB annotation; growth rate used as proxy for growth-coupled GABA optimization.

outcomes.value: CY02 specific growth rate in M9-glycerol improved ~40% (0.67 +/- 0.03 to 0.94 +/- 0.01 /hr) with significantly increased glycerol uptake; glpK^m explained most fitness gain (1.45-fold growth, 1.78-fold GUR; double 1.56-fold/1.70-fold; CY02 1.63-fold/1.60-fold), crp^m alone not significant; GlpK T235M lost FBP sensitivity (FBP K0.5 > 10,000 uM vs 386 uM WT; Vmax/Kcat essentially unchanged); glpK^m-harboring strains showed ~98% cAMP reduction, CY02 ~20% of WT, crp^m ~36%; 640 DEGs (149 up, 491 down) with CRP regulons over-represented > 2-fold; evolved strain showed acetate overflow (WT below detection); minimal-medium GABA identical (0.06 g/L both); LB + 2% glycerol: CY02 max titer 0.39 +/- 0.03 g/L and productivity 0.08 +/- 0.01 g/L/hr (~2.6-fold vs WT 0.15 g/L, 0.03 g/L/hr); single KOs lowered titer, doubles higher (0.45-0.46 g/L), CY02_TKO best 0.59 +/- 0.04 g/L and 0.13 +/- 0.02 g/L/hr (3.9- and 4.3-fold vs WT); knockout benefit absent in wild-type background (epistasis with evolved genotype).
outcomes.notes: Titer improvements are background-dependent: observed in CY02 background, not recapitulated in wild-type background.

experiments.purpose: Adapt E. coli W to glycerol limitation to improve glycerol utilization and growth as a chassis for growth-coupled GABA production.
experiments.intervention: Serial-batch adaptive laboratory evolution in M9 + 0.2% (v/v) glycerol; 50 mL / 250 mL flask, 37 C, agitation; transfer every 12 h; initial OD600 stepped down 0.0008 -> 0.0004 -> 0.00016; ~1300 generations; single clone CY02 isolated from fittest endpoint lineage on M9-glycerol agar.
experiments.conditions: M9 minimal, glycerol sole carbon, 37 C, 200 rpm.
experiments.control: Parental E. coli W grown in parallel assays (growth-rate and glycerol-consumption comparison, incl. M9-glucose reference).
experiments.replicates: single evolving lineage; endpoint characterized as single clone (replicate lineages not reported)
experiments.readout: Doubling time/growth rate trajectory (Fig. 1B/C), specific growth rate, glycerol consumption rate (Fig. 1D).
experiments.analysis: Generation number Eq. (1); fold-change comparison to parental strain.
experiments.outcome: Growth rate +~40% (0.67 -> 0.94 /hr); glycerol consumption rate significantly increased; negligible fitness change on glucose (glycerol-specialist adaptation).

ddr_annotation.decision_type_rationale: Q1 pass (ALE campaign initiated by authors); Q2 pass (performed in this study); Q3 pass (produced CY02 chassis that enabled all subsequent engineering choices).
ddr_annotation.design_action_rationale: ALE is an integrated selection/screening campaign enriching beneficial genotypes rather than a single targeted modification.
ddr_annotation.trigger_observation: Glycerol is a non-preferential, low-energy-density carbon source; prior work showed E. coli W among the best GABA producers from glycerol but without optimization (Hou and Kang, 2018).
ddr_annotation.evidence_grading_rationale: Outcome measured directly: growth rates, glycerol uptake rates, WGS mutation profiles.
ddr_annotation.reason_nature_rationale: ALE justified by established precedent of glycerol ALE in E. coli (Ibarra 2002; Fong 2005; Cheng 2014; Herring 2006; Kang 2019) and prior demonstration of E. coli W GABA production; no de novo mechanistic prediction drove the choice.
ddr_annotation.generalizable_rule: When improving an E. coli host for growth-coupled product formation from the low-energy-density feedstock glycerol, apply serial-batch ALE under glycerol limitation (order of 10^3 generations), because selection enriches substrate-uptake/utilization mutations (e.g., glpK, crp) that raise fitness and feedstock conversion, as validated for E. coli W glycerol utilization and GABA production in this study.

experiments.purpose: Identify causal mutations underlying fitness improvement.
experiments.host: Parental E. coli W, endpoint population, CY02
experiments.intervention: Whole-genome resequencing (MiSeq 50-cycle SE); background mutations of lab stock vs NC_017635.1 excluded; shared mutations between population and clone prioritized.
experiments.conditions: gDNA from cultures; TruSeq DNA LT library.
experiments.control: Parental strain sequence as reference baseline.
experiments.readout: Mutation calls: 30 (population) / 28 (CY02) new mutations; shared set incl. glpK T235M, crp R209H, ptsP fs, rsfS Q6*, mglC fs.
experiments.analysis: CLC Genomics Workbench mapping; recurrence-based prioritization against ALE literature.
experiments.outcome: glpK^m and crp^m nominated as key causal mutations; mglC judged hitchhiker (reverse-engineered mutant grew like WT, Fig. S2).

ddr_annotation.decision_type_rationale: Q1 fails: sequencing and mutation identification is measurement/characterization, not an engineering intervention.

experiments.purpose: Test whether glpK^m and crp^m recapitulate fitness benefits in the parental background.
experiments.intervention: Lambda-Red recombineering (Datsenko-Wanner) to construct glpK^m, crp^m singles and glpK^m crp^m double mutant.
experiments.conditions: M9 + 0.2% glycerol, 37 C, 200 rpm.
experiments.readout: Specific growth rate and specific glycerol uptake rate.
experiments.analysis: Independent t-tests; fold-change vs WT.
experiments.outcome: glpK^m +1.45-fold growth (p<0.022), +1.78-fold GUR (p=0.02); double +1.56/+1.70; CY02 +1.63/+1.60; crp^m alone not significant; glpK^m accounts for >90% of CY02 fitness increase (Discussion).

ddr_annotation.decision_type_rationale: Q1 pass (point mutations deliberately introduced); Q2 pass (constructed in this study); Q3 pass (results established glpK^m as the dominant contributor and informed downstream interpretation/engineering).
ddr_annotation.design_action_rationale: glpK encodes the rate-limiting enzyme (pacemaker) of glycerol dissimilation; introducing the T235M variant engineers the rate-limiting step (relief of FBP allosteric inhibition).
ddr_annotation.trigger_observation: WGS found glpK^m and crp^m shared between endpoint population and CY02 and recurrent across published glycerol/nutrient-limitation ALE experiments; mglC failed validation as hitchhiker.
ddr_annotation.evidence_grading_rationale: Fitness and GUR effects measured directly in reconstructed strains; enzyme phenotype confirmed by kinetics (EXP4).
ddr_annotation.reason_nature_rationale: The mutations were discovered by ALE selection and prioritized by recurrence, not rationally designed by the authors; mechanistic understanding (FBP site) was inferred after the fact.
alternatives_considered: ptsP, rsfS and mglC were candidate causal mutations but deprioritized (mglC shown phenotypically neutral; rsfS low recurrence; ptsP role left unresolved)

experiments.purpose: Determine whether T235M alters GlpK catalytic/allosteric properties.
experiments.host: In vitro: purified GlpK^w and GlpK T235M (overexpressed in BL21(DE3), pET28a, Ni-NTA).
experiments.intervention: Coupled PK/LDH kinetic assay; FBP titration 0-10 mM.
experiments.conditions: 50 mM PIPES pH 7.0, 5 mM MgCl2, 20 mM KCl, 2.5 mM ATP, 25 C, A340.
experiments.replicates: six replicates (WT), five (T235M); replicate type undefined
experiments.readout: Vmax, Km_gly, kcat, kcat/Km, FBP K0.5 (Table 2).
experiments.analysis: SigmaPlot 12 fit to Eq. (4) Hill-type inhibition model.
experiments.outcome: Catalytic parameters essentially unchanged; FBP K0.5 386 uM (WT) vs >10,000 uM (T235M): mutant insensitive to FBP inhibition; WT expected maximally inhibited at cytosolic FBP ~5.85 mM.

ddr_annotation.decision_type_rationale: Q1 fails: enzyme kinetics is characterization validating the glpK^m mechanism; no new engineering action.

experiments.purpose: Test whether glycerol adaptation rewires cAMP-CRP signaling.
experiments.host: WT, glpK^m, crp^m, glpK^m crp^m, CY02
experiments.intervention: Intracellular cAMP extraction (65% ethanol) and commercial ELISA (Invitrogen) at exponential phase.
experiments.conditions: M9-glycerol exponential cultures.
experiments.readout: cAMP relative to WT: glpK^m-harboring strains ~2% (98% decrease), CY02 ~20%, crp^m ~36%; all P<0.001.
experiments.analysis: One-way ANOVA + Tukey post hoc.
experiments.outcome: GlpK-driven cAMP depletion confirmed; crp^m unexpectedly lowers cAMP; CY02 intermediate level interpreted as adaptive vs maladaptive extremes of single mutants.

ddr_annotation.decision_type_rationale: Q1 fails: measurement of signaling state; no intervention beyond already-constructed strains.

experiments.purpose: Profile genome-wide expression changes after glycerol adaptation.
experiments.intervention: RNA-seq (RNASnap extraction, RiboZero depletion, TruSeq stranded, HiSeq 50-cycle SE) at OD600 0.4-0.5 in M9 + 2 g/L glycerol.
experiments.conditions: M9 + 2 g/L glycerol, exponential phase.
experiments.readout: 640 DEGs (149 up, 491 down); 181 DEGs are CRP regulons (>2-fold enrichment over genomic ~12%); 148/157 positively CRP-regulated genes downregulated; lower glycolysis up, TCA/respiration/ATP synthase down, pta-ackA up, acs down.
experiments.analysis: CLC mapping; DESeq2 (FC>2, adj P<0.01); CRP regulon annotation via RegulonDB.
experiments.outcome: Transcriptome consistent with cAMP depletion and aerobic acetate overflow phenotype.

ddr_annotation.decision_type_rationale: Q1 fails: transcriptomic measurement supporting mechanism, no engineering action.

experiments.purpose: Verify glpK mRNA downregulation across mutants.
experiments.intervention: RT-qPCR of glpK normalized to rrsA/ihfB.
experiments.conditions: M9-glycerol log-phase RNA.
experiments.readout: glpK expression 3-6% of WT in glpK^m-harboring strains incl. CY02; ~22% in crp^m; < half of glpK^m single in the double.
experiments.analysis: StepOne software v2.3; standard-curve efficiency from 10^1-10^4 gDNA dilutions.
experiments.outcome: Supports G3P-mediated auto-catabolite repression of the glpFKX operon.

ddr_annotation.decision_type_rationale: Q1 fails: targeted transcript measurement.

experiments.purpose: Test whether transcriptomic signs of overflow translate into acetate secretion.
experiments.host: WT, glpK^m, crp^m, glpK^m crp^m, CY02

experiments.purpose: Overcome negligible GABA production observed in minimal glycerol medium.
experiments.host: WT, glpK^m, crp^m, glpK^m crp^m, CY02 (lacZ:mtGAD)
experiments.intervention: Switch from M9 + 0.2% glycerol + 50 mg/L yeast extract to amino-acid-rich LB + glycerol; glycerol concentration screen (0-? %; optimum 2% v/v) using growth rate as proxy assuming growth-coupled production; stationary-phase GABA screen of all strains.
experiments.conditions: LB + 2% (v/v) glycerol, 37 C, 200 rpm, 50 mL/250 mL flask.
experiments.readout: Final GABA: minimal medium 0.06 vs 0.06 g/L (WT vs CY02, negligible); LB + 2% glycerol: WT 0.05, crp^m 0.06, glpK^m 0.07, glpK^m crp^m 0.07, CY02 0.17 g/L.
experiments.analysis: Growth-rate proxy screen (Fig. S7); HPLC GABA quantification (medium-specific methods).
experiments.outcome: Medium composition identified as integral; CY02 advantage manifests only in rich medium with sufficient carbon.

ddr_annotation.decision_type_rationale: Q1 pass (deliberate fermentation-condition change); Q2 pass (done in this study); Q3 pass (enabled all subsequent production gains and defined the assay medium for engineering).
ddr_annotation.design_action_rationale: Fermentation/process-level optimization of medium composition and substrate concentration.
ddr_annotation.trigger_observation: Final GABA titers in minimal glycerol medium were negligible and identical between WT and CY02 (0.06 g/L), despite improved glycerol uptake.
ddr_annotation.evidence_grading_rationale: Decisions followed measured titers and measured growth-rate optima (Fig. S7).
ddr_annotation.reason_nature_rationale: Amino-acid supplementation to restore growth efficiency and >=1% carbon feed are adopted from cited literature (Prensky 2021; Russell 1995; Waschina 2016; prior GABA studies); the growth-coupling assumption is an assumption, and the metabolic-cost argument is literature-sourced mechanism rather than mechanism demonstrated in this paper.
ddr_annotation.generalizable_rule: When growth-coupled production of an amino-acid-derived product (GABA) from glycerol stalls in minimal medium, switch to an amino-acid-rich complex medium and re-optimize feedstock concentration using growth rate as proxy, because biosynthetic precursor (L-glutamate) cost and carbon availability, not uptake capacity, limit product formation - demonstrated for E. coli W GABA production.
alternatives_considered: Continuing in minimal medium with higher glycerol alone (rejected: 0.2% glycerol itself limiting and growth inefficiency persists)

experiments.purpose: Quantify time-course GABA titer/productivity benefit of ALE strain.
experiments.intervention: 24 h time-course sampling of growth, GABA and glycerol in LB + 2% glycerol.
experiments.conditions: LB + 2% (v/v) glycerol, 37 C, 200 rpm.
experiments.readout: Max titer 0.15 +/- 0.01 (WT) vs 0.39 +/- 0.03 g/L (CY02); productivity 0.03 vs 0.08 g/L/hr (~2.6-fold); glycerol consumption totals similar.
experiments.analysis: Time-course comparison; HPLC.
experiments.outcome: ALE alone confers ~2.6-fold production gain attributed to improved metabolic efficiency/biomass yield rather than more glycerol consumed.

ddr_annotation.decision_type_rationale: Q1/Q3 fail for this record: it validates the already-evolved strain's production phenotype without any new modification.

experiments.purpose: Redirect acetate-overflow and bypass fluxes toward GABA production.
experiments.intervention: Lambda-Red deletion of ackA, mgsA, gabT singly, as three doubles, and as triple (CY02_TKO), in both CY02 and wild-type backgrounds.
experiments.conditions: LB + 2% (v/v) glycerol, 37 C, 200 rpm, 50 mL/250 mL flasks.
experiments.readout: Growth (lag phase prolonged in ΔackA strains, growth rate unaffected), glycerol consumption, final GABA titer: singles below WT; doubles ΔgabTΔackA 0.46 +/- 0.02, ΔgabTΔmgsA 0.45 +/- 0.01 g/L; ΔmgsAΔackA 0.37 +/- 0.04; CY02_TKO 0.59 +/- 0.04 g/L, productivity 0.13 +/- 0.02 g/L/hr (1.5/1.6-fold vs CY02; 3.9/4.3-fold vs WT).
experiments.analysis: Time-course HPLC; comparison across backgrounds.
experiments.outcome: Combined triple deletion synergistic in CY02 background only; benefit absent in wild-type background - epistasis with ALE-acquired mutations; gabT deletion most important single contributor.

ddr_annotation.decision_type_rationale: Q1 pass (targeted gene deletions); Q2 pass (constructed in this study); Q3 pass (outcomes - singles detrimental, doubles/triple beneficial, background-dependence - directly shaped the final strain choice CY02_TKO).
ddr_annotation.design_action_rationale: Blocking competing/bypass sinks (acetate overflow via ackA, methylglyoxal/lactate bypass via mgsA, GABA re-consumption shunt via gabT) to redirect carbon flux toward GABA; mgsA deletion additionally serves M8-type toxicity management.
ddr_annotation.trigger_observation: CY02 exhibited pronounced acetate overflow (EXP8) wiring excess substrate influx to acetate; known risk of methylglyoxal accumulation to cytotoxic levels in FBP-insensitive glpK backgrounds; GABA shunt recycles product into TCA.
ddr_annotation.evidence_grading_rationale: Acetate overflow measured in this study (Fig. 4B); knockout phenotypes measured directly (Fig. 6, Table 3).
ddr_annotation.reason_nature_rationale: ackA deletion was decided from the measured acetate overflow in CY02 (mechanistic, this study); mgsA and gabT choices additionally rest on cited literature mechanisms (methylglyoxal toxicity of glpK mutants; gabT deletion as common GABA-improvement practice), hence dual tagging.
ddr_annotation.generalizable_rule: When a glycerol-adapted E. coli strain with enhanced substrate influx channels excess carbon into acetate overflow during GABA production, delete ackA, mgsA and gabT in combination, because blocking the acetate sink, the methylglyoxal bypass and the GABA shunt redirects carbon toward GABA - validated only in the evolved E. coli W CY02 background; the same deletions did not improve production in the wild-type background, so the rule is background-dependent.
alternatives_considered: Other (unspecified) knockout targets were considered; ackA/mgsA/gabT chosen for the stated reasons

unsupported_values: Characterize E. coli transcript 3'-ends (T3PEs) genome-wide using Term-Seq plus machine learning to build a tunable collection of 3'-UTR/Rho-independent terminator bioparts, and apply them as synthetic 3'-UTR 'metabolic valves' to optimally balance flux between heterologous product pathways (2,3-butanediol from acetoin; myo-inositol production) and endogenous metabolism in E. coli.

3'-UTR terminator bioparts with graded transcription-termination strengths can modulate gene expression without trans-acting elements and with lower noise than inducible-promoter control, and inserting terminators of graded strength between pathway genes can tune the split of metabolic flux to maximize target-product titer; the optimal flux split differs between host strains.
Escherichia coli K-12 MG1655

Methods: 'E. coli MG1655 or eMS57 ΔpfkA Δzwf double knockout strains harboring the pMI plasmid'

Δzwf (coding sequence replaced by kanamycin cassette from pKD13 via pKD46 lambda recombination; cassette removed via pCP20 flippase) followed by ΔpfkA by the same method; pKD46/pCP20 cured at 42°C. Plasmids: pDRA1 (egfp-T3PE-mrfp1 in BBa_J04450-pSB1C3), pDRA2 (egfp-terminator-mrfp1 in pTrcHis2A, IPTG-inducible lac promoter), pGFP (pDRA2 minus mrfp1), pDRA2 DualP (araC-araBAD cassette added), pBDO (alsS[B. subtilis]-alsD[A. hydrophila]-terminator-bdh[T. brockii, codon-optimized] in pTrcHis2A), pMI (INO1[S. cerevisiae CEN.PK]-terminator-pfkA[E. coli MG1655] in pTrcHis2A).
Lambda-Red sequential gene knockout (pKD46/pKD13/pCP20, Datsenko-Wanner) to build ΔpfkA Δzwf hosts
Synthetic 3'-UTR terminator valve: 70-nt T3PE-upstream fragments inserted between genes (XhoI/SpeI for pathway plasmids; In-Fusion for reporter plasmids) to set transcriptional read-through ratio
Dual fluorescent reporter assay (pDRA1/pDRA2) to parameterize terminator read-through (RFP/GFP)
Term-Seq + KNN machine-learning classifier for genome-wide T3PE discovery
First-order mRNA decay mathematical model (Eqs 1-9) to correct fluorescence-based termination strength for differential mRNA decay
Heterologous pathway expression: alsSD + codon-optimized bdh (2,3-BDO); yeast INO1 + native pfkA (myo-inositol)
EXP-1 Term-Seq: MG1655 mid-log cultures, 3 biological replicates
EXP-2 pDRA1 screen: 150 plasmids (50 RITs + 100 motif-less T3PEs) + pDRA1 empty reference
EXP-3 pDRA2 IPTG titration: 49 RITs + 2 controls (empty, rrnBT) across IPTG concentrations

unsupported_values: Characterize E. coli transcript 3'-ends (T3PEs) genome-wide using Term-Seq plus machine learning to build a tunable collection of 3'-UTR/Rho-independent terminator bioparts, and apply them as synthetic 3'-UTR 'metabolic valves' to optimally balance flux between heterologous product pathways (2,3-butanediol from acetoin; myo-inositol production) and endogenous metabolism in E. coli.

3'-UTR terminator bioparts with graded transcription-termination strengths can modulate gene expression without trans-acting elements and with lower noise than inducible-promoter control, and inserting terminators of graded strength between pathway genes can tune the split of metabolic flux to maximize target-product titer; the optimal flux split differs between host strains.

ddr_annotation.decision_type_rationale: Q1 pass: authors designed and built the terminator-biopart single-promoter architecture (and the DualP reference) as a low-noise alternative to promoter/RBS-based control. Q2 pass: constructed in this paper. Q3 pass: the noise advantage is a stated design rule supporting use of terminator valves in downstream pathway constructs.
ddr_annotation.design_action_rationale: Choice of regulatory architecture (3'-UTR terminator instead of additional promoter/RBS) to balance expression of multiple genes from one transcript with low noise - an expression-balancing action.
ddr_annotation.trigger_observation: Promoter/5'-UTR control requires precious inducer molecules and introduces noise via trans-acting elements (Introduction); goal of reducing genetic-circuit complexity.
ddr_annotation.evidence_grading_rationale: Direct single-cell flow-cytometry noise measurements of both architectures in this study.
ddr_annotation.reason_nature_rationale: Paper gives an explicit mechanistic rationale: removing trans-acting elements and RNAP/TF initiation events reduces intrinsic noise sources (η_int), consistent with measured decomposition.
ddr_annotation.generalizable_rule: When balancing multi-gene expression in E. coli synthetic pathways where inducer cost and expression noise must be minimized, apply a single promoter with 3'-UTR terminator bioparts of graded strength instead of multiple inducible promoters, because terminator control removes trans-acting-element-dependent initiation noise (≈4-fold lower intrinsic noise) while retaining tunable relative expression.
alternatives_considered: conventional dual-promoter (lac + araBAD) system - higher intrinsic noise (η_int 18.4)

Q2 pass: pBDO valve series constructed in this paper. Q3 pass: results established the read-through-to-flux-split relationship used to select valves (and carried into the MI system).
ddr_annotation.design_action_rationale: Balancing relative expression of pathway genes (alsSD vs bdh) via intergenic terminator strength to redistribute flux between two products.
ddr_annotation.trigger_observation: RITs characterized by pDRA1/pDRA2 span a wide quantitative read-through range (0.004-91.4), providing a parts basis for graded downstream-gene control without extra promoters.
ddr_annotation.evidence_grading_rationale: Measured extracellular titers (HPLC) across the valve series plus prior measured read-through values; the Group B processing explanation (RBS exposure after cleavage) is supported by dRNA-Seq for 5/13 but remains partly inferential.
ddr_annotation.reason_nature_rationale: The valve mechanism (partial termination sets transcript ratio of upstream vs downstream cistrons) is mechanistically explicit in the paper; the Group B 'processing exposes RBS' sub-explanation is author interpretation supported by 5'-end mapping of a subset.
ddr_annotation.generalizable_rule: When tuning flux split between two consecutive products of a branched heterologous pathway in E. coli (validated for acetoin/2,3-BDO from pyruvate), apply an intercistronic Rho-independent terminator of chosen read-through strength to set downstream-enzyme expression, because the product ratio scales logarithmically with terminator read-through, allowing single-promoter, inducer-free pathway balancing.
alternatives_considered: changing gene order to obtain higher downstream expression - unnecessary because read-through >1 elements exist
Group C short-half-life terminators - reduced both product titers, rejected for production use

experiments.purpose: Apply terminator valve to balance glycolytic growth flux vs myo-inositol (MI) production in two host backgrounds
experiments.host: E. coli MG1655 ΔpfkA Δzwf and E. coli eMS57 ΔpfkA Δzwf (genome-reduced)
experiments.intervention: pMI plasmids: INO1(S. cerevisiae)-[RIT valve]-pfkA(E. coli); 5 valve plasmids tested in ΔpfkA Δzwf hosts; hosts built by sequential lambda-Red knockout (zwf then pfkA)
experiments.conditions: 60 mL M9 high-glucose (10 g/L) + 100 µg/mL amp + 0.1 mM IPTG, OD600 0.05, 300 mL flask, 30°C, up to 48 h, aerobic
experiments.control: conv. sys.: MG1655 wild-type (pfkA, zwf unperturbed) + pTrc-INO1 without valve
experiments.readout: MG1655 ΔpfkA Δzwf optimum at T3PE-383 (read-through 0.519): 0.682 g/L MI, 8.92× conventional system, +38% yield; eMS57 ΔpfkA Δzwf optimum at strong rrnBT: 0.864 g/L (1.27× MG1655 max); unvalved INO1 overexpression caused severe growth retardation and marginal MI
experiments.analysis: HPLC MI + glucose consumption; yield g/g; growth curves (OD-Monitor; Suppl. Fig S9/S10)
experiments.outcome: An intermediate pfkA read-through maximizes MI in MG1655 background; genome-reduced host optimum shifts to strong termination (lower carbon cost of growth); demonstrates host-dependent optimal flux balance findable by valve screening

ddr_annotation.decision_type_rationale: Q1 pass: knockout of pfkA/zwf plus INO1-valve-pfkA construct is an active engineering intervention coupling growth to production. Q2 pass: double-knockout strain and pMI series constructed in this study (eMS57 chassis itself from prior work - noted). Q3 pass: identified optimum valve per host and established valve-screening as the optimization method.
ddr_annotation.design_action_rationale: Blocking the competing glycolytic route at pfkA (with zwf removed to limit bypass) and reintroducing pfkA under a terminator valve to gate how much carbon re-enters glycolysis vs MI production - competition-node gating with controlled re-supply.
ddr_annotation.trigger_observation: Uncontrolled INO1 overexpression in the ΔpfkA Δzwf background caused severe growth retardation with marginal MI production, showing that hard blocking of glycolysis starves biomass/precursor supply and that a tunable intermediate pfkA level is needed.
ddr_annotation.evidence_grading_rationale: Measured MI titers, glucose consumption, yields and growth across 5 valve strengths in both hosts; pfkA is cited as the effective rate-limiting glycolytic enzyme (ref 54).
ddr_annotation.reason_nature_rationale: Explicit mechanism: production and biomass fluxes are interconnected and constrained by finite cellular resources; gating the rate-limiting glycolytic enzyme at intermediate expression balances resource allocation. Choice of pfkA as the node additionally rests on literature (ref 54).
ddr_annotation.generalizable_rule: When a heterologous production pathway in E. coli draws on glycolytic carbon and full knockout of the competing glycolytic step (pfkA) causes growth failure, apply a 3'-UTR terminator valve to reintroduce the blocked enzyme at graded expression levels in a ΔpfkA Δzwf background, because an intermediate glycolytic flux balances biomass generation against product flux; the optimal valve strength is host-dependent and must be screened per chassis (validated for myo-inositol production in MG1655 and genome-reduced eMS57 backgrounds).
alternatives_considered: constitutive INO1 overexpression without flux control (conventional pTrc-INO1 system) - severe growth retardation, marginal MI
complete glycolysis block with no pfkA re-expression - growth failure

objective.value: Characterize E. coli transcript 3'-ends (T3PEs) genome-wide using Term-Seq plus machine learning to build a tunable collection of 3'-UTR/Rho-independent terminator bioparts, and apply them as synthetic 3'-UTR 'metabolic valves' to optimally balance flux between heterologous product pathways (2,3-butanediol from acetoin; myo-inositol production) and endogenous metabolism in E. coli.

ddr_annotation.decision_type_rationale: Q1 pass: authors designed and built the terminator-biopart single-promoter architecture (and the DualP reference) as a low-noise alternative to promoter/RBS-based control. Q2 pass: constructed in this paper. Q3 pass: the noise advantage is a stated design rule supporting use of terminator valves in downstream pathway constructs.
ddr_annotation.design_action_rationale: Choice of regulatory architecture (3'-UTR terminator instead of additional promoter/RBS) to balance expression of multiple genes from one transcript with low noise - an expression-balancing action.
ddr_annotation.trigger_observation: Promoter/5'-UTR control requires precious inducer molecules and introduces noise via trans-acting elements (Introduction); goal of reducing genetic-circuit complexity.
ddr_annotation.evidence_grading_rationale: Direct single-cell flow-cytometry noise measurements of both architectures in this study.
ddr_annotation.reason_nature_rationale: Paper gives an explicit mechanistic rationale: removing trans-acting elements and RNAP/TF initiation events reduces intrinsic noise sources (η_int), consistent with measured decomposition.
ddr_annotation.generalizable_rule: When balancing multi-gene expression in E. coli synthetic pathways where inducer cost and expression noise must be minimized, apply a single promoter with 3'-UTR terminator bioparts of graded strength instead of multiple inducible promoters, because terminator control removes trans-acting-element-dependent initiation noise (≈4-fold lower intrinsic noise) while retaining tunable relative expression.
alternatives_considered: conventional dual-promoter (lac + araBAD) system - higher intrinsic noise (η_int 18.4)

experiments.intervention: pBDO plasmids: alsS(B. subtilis)-alsD(A. hydrophila)-[RIT valve]-bdh(T. brockii, codon-optimized); three RIT groups (A: read-through <1, 5 RITs; B: read-through >1, 4 RITs; C: 3 short-half-life RITs) + empty
experiments.conditions: 60 mL M9 high-glucose (10 g/L) + 100 µg/mL amp + 0.1 mM IPTG, OD600 0.05, 300 mL flask, 37°C, 24 h, aerobic
experiments.control: pBDO empty (fully induced, no termination) as negative control; pBDO rrnBT strong-termination reference
experiments.readout: HPLC titers of acetoin and 2,3-BDO at 24 h: rrnBT 0.126 g/L BDO; empty 0.382 g/L; Group B max 0.513 g/L; plateau at read-through 2.343 (T3PE-390); Group C lowest
experiments.analysis: BDO:acetoin ratio logarithmically proportional to T3PE read-through (Suppl. Fig S8)
experiments.outcome: Terminators quantitatively valve flux between acetoin and 2,3-BDO; read-through >1 Group B elements exceed no-terminator expression (attributed by authors to post-transcriptional processing exposing RBS; 5/13 Group B showed stable 5'-ends by dRNA-Seq)

ddr_annotation.decision_type_rationale: Q1 pass: deliberate insertion of selected RITs between alsSD and bdh to set bdh expression and flux split. Q2 pass: pBDO valve series constructed in this paper. Q3 pass: results established the read-through-to-flux-split relationship used to select valves (and carried into the MI system).
ddr_annotation.design_action_rationale: Balancing relative expression of pathway genes (alsSD vs bdh) via intergenic terminator strength to redistribute flux between two products.
ddr_annotation.trigger_observation: RITs characterized by pDRA1/pDRA2 span a wide quantitative read-through range (0.004-91.4), providing a parts basis for graded downstream-gene control without extra promoters.
ddr_annotation.evidence_grading_rationale: Measured extracellular titers (HPLC) across the valve series plus prior measured read-through values; the Group B processing explanation (RBS exposure after cleavage) is supported by dRNA-Seq for 5/13 but remains partly inferential.
ddr_annotation.reason_nature_rationale: The valve mechanism (partial termination sets transcript ratio of upstream vs downstream cistrons) is mechanistically explicit in the paper; the Group B 'processing exposes RBS' sub-explanation is author interpretation supported by 5'-end mapping of a subset.
ddr_annotation.generalizable_rule: When tuning flux split between two consecutive products of a branched heterologous pathway in E. coli (validated for acetoin/2,3-BDO from pyruvate), apply an intercistronic Rho-independent terminator of chosen read-through strength to set downstream-enzyme expression, because the product ratio scales logarithmically with terminator read-through, allowing single-promoter, inducer-free pathway balancing.
alternatives_considered: changing gene order to obtain higher downstream expression - unnecessary because read-through >1 elements exist
Group C short-half-life terminators - reduced both product titers, rejected for production use

experiments.purpose: Apply terminator valve to balance glycolytic growth flux vs myo-inositol (MI) production in two host backgrounds
experiments.host: E. coli MG1655 ΔpfkA Δzwf and E. coli eMS57 ΔpfkA Δzwf (genome-reduced)
experiments.intervention: pMI plasmids: INO1(S. cerevisiae)-[RIT valve]-pfkA(E. coli); 5 valve plasmids tested in ΔpfkA Δzwf hosts; hosts built by sequential lambda-Red knockout (zwf then pfkA)
experiments.conditions: 60 mL M9 high-glucose (10 g/L) + 100 µg/mL amp + 0.1 mM IPTG, OD600 0.05, 300 mL flask, 30°C, up to 48 h, aerobic
experiments.control: conv. sys.: MG1655 wild-type (pfkA, zwf unperturbed) + pTrc-INO1 without valve
experiments.readout: MG1655 ΔpfkA Δzwf optimum at T3PE-383 (read-through 0.519): 0.682 g/L MI, 8.92× conventional system, +38% yield; eMS57 ΔpfkA Δzwf optimum at strong rrnBT: 0.864 g/L (1.27× MG1655 max); unvalved INO1 overexpression caused severe growth retardation and marginal MI
experiments.analysis: HPLC MI + glucose consumption; yield g/g; growth curves (OD-Monitor; Suppl. Fig S9/S10)
experiments.outcome: An intermediate pfkA read-through maximizes MI in MG1655 background; genome-reduced host optimum shifts to strong termination (lower carbon cost of growth); demonstrates host-dependent optimal flux balance findable by valve screening

ddr_annotation.decision_type_rationale: Q1 pass: knockout of pfkA/zwf plus INO1-valve-pfkA construct is an active engineering intervention coupling growth to production. Q2 pass: double-knockout strain and pMI series constructed in this study (eMS57 chassis itself from prior work - noted). Q3 pass: identified optimum valve per host and established valve-screening as the optimization method.
ddr_annotation.design_action_rationale: Blocking the competing glycolytic route at pfkA (with zwf removed to limit bypass) and reintroducing pfkA under a terminator valve to gate how much carbon re-enters glycolysis vs MI production - competition-node gating with controlled re-supply.
ddr_annotation.trigger_observation: Uncontrolled INO1 overexpression in the ΔpfkA Δzwf background caused severe growth retardation with marginal MI production, showing that hard blocking of glycolysis starves biomass/precursor supply and that a tunable intermediate pfkA level is needed.
ddr_annotation.evidence_grading_rationale: Measured MI titers, glucose consumption, yields and growth across 5 valve strengths in both hosts; pfkA is cited as the effective rate-limiting glycolytic enzyme (ref 54).
ddr_annotation.reason_nature_rationale: Explicit mechanism: production and biomass fluxes are interconnected and constrained by finite cellular resources; gating the rate-limiting glycolytic enzyme at intermediate expression balances resource allocation. Choice of pfkA as the node additionally rests on literature (ref 54).
ddr_annotation.generalizable_rule: When a heterologous production pathway in E. coli draws on glycolytic carbon and full knockout of the competing glycolytic step (pfkA) causes growth failure, apply a 3'-UTR terminator valve to reintroduce the blocked enzyme at graded expression levels in a ΔpfkA Δzwf background, because an intermediate glycolytic flux balances biomass generation against product flux; the optimal valve strength is host-dependent and must be screened per chassis (validated for myo-inositol production in MG1655 and genome-reduced eMS57 backgrounds).
alternatives_considered: constitutive INO1 overexpression without flux control (conventional pTrc-INO1 system) - severe growth retardation, marginal MI
complete glycolysis block with no pfkA re-expression - growth failure

unsupported_values: Experimentally evaluate 40 computationally predicted candidate transcription factors in Escherichia coli K-12 MG1655 using multiplexed ChIP-exo to determine which are genuine DNA-binding TFs, map their genome-wide binding sites, compare their locations with RNAP/RpoD binding, classify them by target-gene count (global/local/single-target), and infer and validate the physiological functions of representative TFs via RNA-seq and deletion-mutant phenotyping.

A rank-ordered list of uncharacterized 'y-gene' proteins predicted by the TFpredict algorithm includes genuine transcription factors; multiplexed ChIP-exo combined with RNAP/sigma70 ChIP-exo and RNA-seq of knockout mutants can validate these TFs in vivo and reveal their regulatory and physiological roles, bringing the count of validated E. coli K-12 MG1655 TFs close to the estimated total of ~280.

Escherichia coli K-12 MG1655 (parental/wild type) and its derivatives: 40 C-terminally 8-myc-tagged strains (one per candidate TF) generated by lambda red-mediated site-specific recombination, and single-gene deletion strains used for functional validation (explicitly tested: ΔyfeC, ΔyciT, ΔybcM, ΔygbI; ΔyidZ used for RNA-seq). Full strain list in Dataset S1 (not available in parsed text).

Per-strain genotypes: MG1655 with chromosomal C-terminal 8-myc fusion at each of the 40 candidate TF loci; single-gene deletions ΔyidZ, ΔyfeC, ΔyciT, ΔybcM, ΔygbI (each separate; no combined genotypes shown). Deletion method and resistance markers not stated in the main text (Dataset S1).

Lambda red-mediated site-specific recombination to fuse an 8-myc epitope tag at the C-terminus of each candidate TF at its native chromosomal locus (method per Cho et al. 2006, ref 12); single-gene deletion mutants for phenotypic validation (construction method not described in main text). These are enabling modifications for a discovery/characterization study, not production-oriented engineering.

Group A: 40 myc-tagged strains, each subjected to multiplexed ChIP-exo (barcoded first adapters, pooled library) to map TF binding sites; most under standard glucose M9 conditions; YbcM additionally under paraquat-induced oxidative stress.
Group B: MG1655 wild type subjected to ChIP-exo with anti-RNAP beta' (NT63) and anti-sigma70 (2G10) antibodies to map RNAP and RpoD binding.
Group C: paired RNA-seq comparisons, wild type vs individual TF deletion strains (ΔyidZ, ΔyfeC, ΔyciT, ΔygbI explicitly; five additional TFs in supplement).
Group D: phenotype assays - ΔyciT vs WT growth on M9 with glucose/fructose/sorbitol and M9 sorbitol ± 0.5 M NaCl; ΔybcM vs WT survival after 60 mM H2O2; ΔygbI vs WT growth on 20 mM L-tartrate.
Group E: in silico analyses only - SUPERFAMILY/HMM family annotation, SWISS-MODEL homology models, MEME motif search, COG enrichment.
Wild type MG1655 as reference/comparator strain in all RNA-seq comparisons and phenotype assays.
Mock IP signal used as the noise denominator in ChIP-exo S/N peak-intensity calculation (IP/Mock).
Untreated cells at time zero as baseline for percent-survival calculation in the H2O2 assay.
RNAP and RpoD ChIP-exo maps used as reference layers to classify TF binding events (RNAP+RpoD / RNAP-only / others).
No explicit negative IP control strain (e.g., untagged MG1655 IP) is described in the main text beyond the Mock-based S/N filtering.

ΔyidZ: 74 genes differentially expressed (19 of 118 direct targets), including down-regulation of acid-stress/amino-acid genes (gadA, gadBC, hdeD, hdeAByhiD) and up-regulation of carbohydrate genes (rbsD, malM, malE, malX); no significantly enriched COG.

ΔyfeC: 124 up- and 81 down-regulated genes; 20/50 binding-site genes differentially expressed, 16/20 repressed; functions span transport/metabolism, translation, post-translational modification, cell envelope (lpp).

ΔyciT: target genes ybiV, ybiY, fsaA, cusF differentially expressed; no major growth defect on glucose/fructose/sorbitol (slightly lower stationary OD600); impaired growth under 0.5 M NaCl osmotic stress on sorbitol -> YciT involved in osmolarity control.

ΔybcM: 12 binding sites (11/12 upstream), autoregulation at ybcLM, targets include ucpA and ubiT-yhbS/ubiUV region; WT survival 8-fold higher than ΔybcM after 60 mM H2O2 15 min -> YbcM involved in ROS stress response.

ΔygbI: single divergent binding site overlapping ygbJ promoter; ygbJKLMN cluster upregulated upon deletion; ΔygbI (but not WT) grows on 20 mM L-tartrate -> YgbI is a repressor of the L-tartrate catabolic pathway.

reusable_design_patterns: Prediction-to-validation pipeline: homology-based TF candidate ranking (TFpredict) -> chromosomal epitope tagging (lambda red, C-terminal 8-myc) -> multiplexed barcoded ChIP-exo for parallel binding mapping of 40 proteins in pooled libraries.
Reference-layer integration: RNAP (beta') and sigma70 ChIP-exo maps used to classify TF binding events by promoter context (RNAP+RpoD / RNAP-only / others) for coarse functional assignment.

Triangulation for direct regulons: ChIP-exo binding + RNA-seq of TF deletion (|log2FC| >= 1, padj < 0.05) + motif enrichment (MEME) to separate direct from indirect targets (e.g., 20/50 for YfeC, 19/118 for YidZ).
Target-number-based TF classification (global >100, local <100, single-target) to prioritize representative TFs for deep phenotyping.

Condition-matched phenotyping: hypothesis-driven selection of stress/carbon conditions per TF (paraquat ChIP for YbcM; NaCl osmotic growth for YciT; L-tartrate growth for YgbI) rather than a uniform phenotype screen.
Growth-defect readout with Bioscreen C (OD600 every 30 min, 3 biological replicates x 2 repetitions) and CFU-based survival under lethal H2O2 with percent-survival normalization to t=0.

value: 34 of 40 candidate TFs confirmed as DNA-binding proteins in vivo; 588 total binding sites identified; six candidates (YgeR, YggD, YjjJ, YfjR, YeeY, YpdC) showed no binding under tested conditions.

experimental_design_object.paper_scope_note: This is a discovery/characterization study (TRN expansion), not a production-oriented engineering study. Per the Q1/Q2/Q3 filter in section 5.5, none of the experiments constitute engineering decisions aimed at a production or phenotype-engineering goal: the myc-tagging and gene deletions are enabling/perturbation tools for characterization, so they fail Q1 as defined (they are not metabolic/biosensor/evolutionary/protein/chassis engineering actions toward a product or performance objective) and fail Q3 (no future design choice is altered). Accordingly, ddr_annotation objects are not attached; per-experiment decision_type labels are provided instead, and no generalizable_rule fields are fabricated.

reusable_design_patterns: Prediction-to-validation pipeline: homology-based TF candidate ranking (TFpredict) -> chromosomal epitope tagging (lambda red, C-terminal 8-myc) -> multiplexed barcoded ChIP-exo for parallel binding mapping of 40 proteins in pooled libraries.
Reference-layer integration: RNAP (beta') and sigma70 ChIP-exo maps used to classify TF binding events by promoter context (RNAP+RpoD / RNAP-only / others) for coarse functional assignment.

Triangulation for direct regulons: ChIP-exo binding + RNA-seq of TF deletion (|log2FC| >= 1, padj < 0.05) + motif enrichment (MEME) to separate direct from indirect targets (e.g., 20/50 for YfeC, 19/118 for YidZ).
Target-number-based TF classification (global >100, local <100, single-target) to prioritize representative TFs for deep phenotyping.

Condition-matched phenotyping: hypothesis-driven selection of stress/carbon conditions per TF (paraquat ChIP for YbcM; NaCl osmotic growth for YciT; L-tartrate growth for YgbI) rather than a uniform phenotype screen.
Growth-defect readout with Bioscreen C (OD600 every 30 min, 3 biological replicates x 2 repetitions) and CFU-based survival under lethal H2O2 with percent-survival normalization to t=0.

ddr_annotation.decision_type_rationale: Q1 yes (active design and construction of a new high-resolution sgRNA library and its deployment); Q2 yes (library designed and constructed in this study per Results and Methods); Q3 yes (the dense 100-bp tiling design choice directly shapes how future fitness screens with this framework are designed).
ddr_annotation.design_action_rationale: Construction of an integrated pooled screening platform (library design, cloning, selection, NGS readout) - closest to M11 integrated screening; not a pathway flux intervention.
ddr_annotation.trigger_observation: Most CRISPRi library designs target a single or a few positions per gene, but CRISPRi efficiency varies with genomic structure and dCas9-DNA interactions, making consistent efficiency under all conditions hard to ensure (Results p001).
ddr_annotation.evidence_grading_rationale: Library coverage (39,574/39,591 = 99.96%) and colony counts were directly measured by amplicon sequencing and plating; the design rationale is a procedural observation, not a prediction.
ddr_annotation.reason_nature_rationale: Paper explicitly gives a mechanistic/technical rationale: position- and condition-dependent variation in CRISPRi efficiency motivates dense tiling at 100-bp intervals.
ddr_annotation.generalizable_rule: When designing genome-scale CRISPRi fitness screens in E. coli, apply dense sgRNA tiling across every ~100 bp of each CDS with off-target filtering and per-gene median enrichment aggregation, because position- and condition-dependent variation in dCas9 repression efficiency makes single-guide designs unreliable.
alternatives_considered: single- or few-position CRISPRi library designs (rejected: variable efficiency across genomic structures and conditions)

interventions.detail: Gentamicin 1 ug/mL sub-lethal (from dose-response Fig S1) and anaerobic culture as comparison conditions

ddr_annotation.decision_type_rationale: Q1 yes (deliberate selection of sub-lethal gentamicin dose and anaerobic condition as experimental interventions); Q2 yes (performed in this study); Q3 yes (dose choice from the dose-response curve determines screening stringency for all downstream ER calls).
ddr_annotation.design_action_rationale: Process/condition engineering - selection of cultivation stress conditions rather than a genetic change.
ddr_annotation.trigger_observation: Dose-response curve (Fig S1) identified 1 ug/mL as sub-lethal; literature reports this level induces resistance and stress responses including biofilm formation (ref 17); gentamicin known to be ineffective anaerobically (ref 16).
ddr_annotation.evidence_grading_rationale: Sub-lethal concentration derived from a measured dose-response curve (Fig S1); anaerobic resistance directly observed (Fig S2).
ddr_annotation.reason_nature_rationale: Paper justifies 1 ug/mL as 'reported to induce resistance and stress responses, including biofilm formation in E. coli (17)' and the anaerobic comparison on prior literature (ref 16); own Fig S1 data support the choice but the stated framing is literature-anchored.
ddr_annotation.generalizable_rule: When screening aminoglycoside fitness determinants in E. coli, apply a sub-lethal antibiotic dose chosen from a measured dose-response curve and include an anaerobic condition as a mechanistic comparator, because sub-lethal exposure elicits adaptive stress responses while anaerobiosis phenocopies uptake-blocked resistance.

interventions.detail: High-resolution sgRNA library targeting every 100 bp of CDS; dCas9-mediated repression; pooled competition growth in LB, LB+gentamicin 1 ug/mL, and anaerobic LB

ddr_annotation.decision_type_rationale: Q1 yes (active design and construction of a new high-resolution sgRNA library and its deployment); Q2 yes (library designed and constructed in this study per Results and Methods); Q3 yes (the dense 100-bp tiling design choice directly shapes how future fitness screens with this framework are designed).
ddr_annotation.design_action_rationale: Construction of an integrated pooled screening platform (library design, cloning, selection, NGS readout) - closest to M11 integrated screening; not a pathway flux intervention.
ddr_annotation.trigger_observation: Most CRISPRi library designs target a single or a few positions per gene, but CRISPRi efficiency varies with genomic structure and dCas9-DNA interactions, making consistent efficiency under all conditions hard to ensure (Results p001).
ddr_annotation.evidence_grading_rationale: Library coverage (39,574/39,591 = 99.96%) and colony counts were directly measured by amplicon sequencing and plating; the design rationale is a procedural observation, not a prediction.
ddr_annotation.reason_nature_rationale: Paper explicitly gives a mechanistic/technical rationale: position- and condition-dependent variation in CRISPRi efficiency motivates dense tiling at 100-bp intervals.
ddr_annotation.generalizable_rule: When designing genome-scale CRISPRi fitness screens in E. coli, apply dense sgRNA tiling across every ~100 bp of each CDS with off-target filtering and per-gene median enrichment aggregation, because position- and condition-dependent variation in dCas9 repression efficiency makes single-guide designs unreliable.
alternatives_considered: single- or few-position CRISPRi library designs (rejected: variable efficiency across genomic structures and conditions)

interventions.detail: Gentamicin 1 ug/mL sub-lethal (from dose-response Fig S1) and anaerobic culture as comparison conditions

ddr_annotation.decision_type_rationale: Q1 yes (deliberate selection of sub-lethal gentamicin dose and anaerobic condition as experimental interventions); Q2 yes (performed in this study); Q3 yes (dose choice from the dose-response curve determines screening stringency for all downstream ER calls).
ddr_annotation.design_action_rationale: Process/condition engineering - selection of cultivation stress conditions rather than a genetic change.
ddr_annotation.trigger_observation: Dose-response curve (Fig S1) identified 1 ug/mL as sub-lethal; literature reports this level induces resistance and stress responses including biofilm formation (ref 17); gentamicin known to be ineffective anaerobically (ref 16).
ddr_annotation.evidence_grading_rationale: Sub-lethal concentration derived from a measured dose-response curve (Fig S1); anaerobic resistance directly observed (Fig S2).
ddr_annotation.reason_nature_rationale: Paper justifies 1 ug/mL as 'reported to induce resistance and stress responses, including biofilm formation in E. coli (17)' and the anaerobic comparison on prior literature (ref 16); own Fig S1 data support the choice but the stated framing is literature-anchored.
ddr_annotation.generalizable_rule: When screening aminoglycoside fitness determinants in E. coli, apply a sub-lethal antibiotic dose chosen from a measured dose-response curve and include an anaerobic condition as a mechanistic comparator, because sub-lethal exposure elicits adaptive stress responses while anaerobiosis phenocopies uptake-blocked resistance.

unsupported_values: Establish modular synthetic microbial ecosystems in E. coli that realize different ecological interactions (competition and symbiosis) by reconfiguring the layout between a quorum-sensing communication module and a toxin-antitoxin effect module, and further build inducible synthetic ecosystems (Ara/aTc) to regulate subpopulation ratios over a wide range.

Reconfiguring cis- vs trans-acting QS activation of the ccd toxin-antitoxin effect module between two strains can convert interaction topology (competition <-> symbiosis), and replacing self-inducing QS promoters of HSL synthases with inducible promoters enables external, quantitative control of subpopulation ratios.

Experimental host: E. coli Top10 (TOP10) for all synthetic ecosystems; E. coli DH5a for plasmid construction only. Engineered strains: competitive CG01, CG02 (GFP) and CR01, CR02 (RFP); symbiotic SG01 (GFP), SR01 (RFP); inducible CGi, CRi, SGi, SRi; No QS Control strains NG and NR; unnamed control strains unable to produce signals (Supplementary Figure S7).

Circuit-level genotype (main text only): CG = intact tra* system self-inducing ccdA + partial las system controlling ccdB + genome-integrated GFP; CR = intact las system self-inducing ccdA + partial tra* system controlling ccdB + genome-integrated RFP; SG = intact las system self-inducing ccdB + partial tra* system controlling ccdA + GFP; SR = intact tra* system self-inducing ccdB + partial las system controlling ccdA + RFP; CGi = CG with EsaI synthase promoter replaced by Ara-inducible promoter; CRi = CR with LasI promoter replaced by aTc-inducible promoter; SGi = SG with aTc-inducible promoter regulating LasI; SRi = SR with EsaI promoter replaced by Ara-inducible promoter; NG/NR = toxin-antitoxin system without QS systems. GFP/RFP integrated via CRIM plasmid method with helper pAH69; multicopy clones selected.

Modular genetic-circuit design: two orthogonal HSL-based QS systems (tra*, las) as communication module; ccd operon toxin-antitoxin (CcdA/CcdB) as effect module; reconfiguration of cis/trans activation layout to switch ecological interaction; RBS engineering of HSL synthases, ccdA and ccdB to tune signal synthesis rate and effect-module expression; replacement of QS promoters of HSL synthases with L-arabinose- or aTc-inducible promoters to build inducible ecosystems; CRIM-based chromosomal integration of GFP/RFP reporters; selection of representative strains by growth/fluorescence characterization.
exp_comp_design: construction of CG and CR strain families (competitive ecosystem).
exp_comp_liquid: single-strain liquid characterization of CG01, CG02, CR01, CR02 with/without 3OC6HSL or 3OC12HSL.
exp_comp_coculture_liquid: pairwise CGxCR cocultures, four combinations (CG01/CR01, CG01/CR02, CG02/CR01, CG02/CR02).
exp_comp_plate: agar-plate coculture of the four CGxCR combinations under four spatial distributions (same position, adjacent, CR surrounded by CG, CG surrounded by CR).

exp_sym_liquid: single-strain characterization of SG01 and SR01 with/without HSLs; SG01+SR01 coculture at different inoculation ratios; dilution-stability test; coculture with signal-deficient control strains; 72 h time-course coexistence.
exp_sym_plate: agar-plate coculture of SG01 and SR01 without inducer (adjacent, in contact, SG01 surrounded by SR01).
exp_inducible: coculture of CGi+CRi and SGi+SRi in 24-well plates with inducer Combinations I-IV; flow-cytometric subpopulation ratio measurement.
exp_noqs_control: NG+NR coculture (toxin-antitoxin without QS) and dominant-strain switch attempt vs inducible competitive ecosystem.
No-inducer groups in single-strain HSL characterization (baseline growth).
Single-strain monocultures as reference for coculture comparisons (Figure 4c,d green/red lines).
Signal-deficient control strains cocultured with SG01 or SR01 (both unable to grow; Supplementary Figure S7) - negative control for cross-protection.
No QS Control system: NG and NR strains expressing toxin-antitoxin without QS; used as control for growth buffering and dominant-strain switch (Supplementary Figures S15-S17).
Single-strain growth on agar plates (Supplementary Figures S4, S9).

Seed culture: single colony into 5 mL LB with appropriate antibiotics and corresponding HSL, 220 rpm, 37 C, 12 h. Liquid characterization: 2% seeds washed 3x, inoculated into 24-well microassay plate with 1.5 mL LB, 37 C, vigorous shaking.
