experiments.purpose: Construct a synthetic competitive ecosystem by cross-wiring two orthogonal QS systems (tra*, las) to a ccd toxin-antitoxin effect module in two E. coli Top10 strains (CG: GFP; CR: RFP), each carrying a cis-acting positive feedback (self-rescue via antitoxin CcdA) and a trans-acting negative feedback (killing via CcdB induced by partner's HSL).
experiments.intervention: Genetic circuit construction: intact tra* system self-inducing ccdA + partial las system controlling ccdB in CG; intact las system self-inducing ccdA + partial tra* system controlling ccdB in CR; chromosomal GFP/RFP integration (CRIM method, helper pAH69, pHK-GFP/pHK-RFP, multicopy clones).
experiments.conditions: LB medium, antibiotics as appropriate, 37 C, 220 rpm seed cultures; characterization in 24-well plates (1.5 mL).
experiments.replicates: three experiments (Fig 2), replicate type unresolved; three independent biological replicates for plate cocultures (Fig 3).
experiments.readout: GFP/RFP fluorescence growth curves; agar-plate spatial fluorescence patterns.
experiments.analysis: Qualitative curve comparison; dominant-strain identification via subpopulation ratios.
experiments.outcome: Mutual growth inhibition achieved; competitive relationship confirmed in liquid and on plates; dominant strain switchable through HSL synthesis rate / effect-module expression tuning.

ddr_annotation.decision_type_rationale: Q1 yes (de novo circuit construction in this paper), Q2 yes (strains CG/CR built here, though orthogonal QS parts pre-existed), Q3 yes (demonstrates that module layout reconfiguration defines ecological relationship, motivating the symbiotic and inducible designs).
ddr_annotation.design_action_rationale: The design installs QS-linked positive/negative feedback regulation of a toxin-antitoxin module to couple interspecific communication to population-density-dependent growth control - a dynamic regulation architecture.
ddr_annotation.trigger_observation: Prior ecosystems lacked a general modular route to distinct ecological interactions; QS crosstalk causes circuit failure, so orthogonal QS systems plus a separable effect module were needed.
ddr_annotation.evidence_grading_rationale: Rests on previously measured orthogonality of the tra*/las systems (ref 30, measured) and the characterized CcdB-gyrase/CcdA-antidote mechanism; circuit function verified by growth assays.
ddr_annotation.reason_nature_rationale: Paper explicitly reasons that cis-acting HSL activation of antitoxin yields self-rescue while trans-acting activation of toxin limits population size, and that swapping aggressive behavior for suicidal behavior converts competition to symbiosis.
ddr_annotation.generalizable_rule: When constructing a two-strain E. coli consortium with a defined ecological interaction, reconfigure cis- vs trans-acting QS activation of a shared toxin-antitoxin effect module, because assigning self-HSL to antitoxin and partner-HSL to toxin yields competition whereas the inverse assignment yields symbiosis (validated in E. coli Top10 QS-ccd proof-of-concept consortia).
alternatives_considered: Cross-feeding/auxotrophy approaches (background, refs 10-14) noted to suffer metabolic burden and asymmetric strain ratios (Kerner et al.)
Toxin/lysis-based density-control ecosystems (refs 26,27) noted as unable to control subpopulation ratios

experiments.purpose: Construct a synthetic symbiotic ecosystem by inverting the cis/trans activation layout: each strain self-induces its own toxin (negative feedback) and is rescued by the partner's HSL activating its antitoxin (positive feedback).
experiments.host: Escherichia coli Top10 (SG: GFP; SR: RFP)
experiments.intervention: Circuit construction: intact las system self-inducing ccdB + partial tra* controlling ccdA in SG; intact tra* self-inducing ccdB + partial las controlling ccdA in SR; RBS tuning; selection of SG01 and SR01.
experiments.conditions: LB liquid and agar; different inoculation ratios; no-inducer plates.
experiments.control: Single strains; signal-deficient control strains cocultured with SG01 or SR01.
experiments.replicates: three experiments (Fig 4); three independent biological replicates (Fig 5).
experiments.readout: Fluorescence growth curves; plate images.
experiments.analysis: Coculture vs single-strain fluorescence; dilution stability; 72 h time-course proportion.
experiments.outcome: Mutual growth promotion: coculture fluorescence exceeded single strains; SG01 growth increased with SR01 inoculation ratio; symbiosis maintained after two dilutions and 72 h; neither strain grew with signal-deficient controls; SR01 grew toward SG01 on plates.

ddr_annotation.decision_type_rationale: Q1 yes (new circuit construction), Q2 yes (this paper), Q3 yes (demonstrates layout-reconfiguration generality and provides the symbiotic chassis later made inducible).
ddr_annotation.design_action_rationale: Installs QS-mediated negative self-limitation and trans-acting rescue feedbacks - dynamic regulation of population growth.
ddr_annotation.trigger_observation: The competitive design showed that cis/trans assignment of effect-module activation defines interaction type, predicting that inversion yields mutual protection.
ddr_annotation.evidence_grading_rationale: Symbiotic phenotypes measured in growth, dilution, coculture-with-control and 72 h coexistence assays.
ddr_annotation.reason_nature_rationale: Paper gives explicit mechanistic logic: self-induced toxin causes self-limitation while partner-HSL-induced antitoxin causes population rescue.
ddr_annotation.generalizable_rule: When engineering a two-strain E. coli mutualism from a QS-ccd toolkit, assign each strain's own HSL to toxin expression and the partner's HSL to antitoxin expression, because this converts aggression into suicidal behavior that is rescued only by the partner, yielding obligate-like mutual protection (validated for the SG01/SR01 E. coli Top10 pair in LB liquid and agar).

experiments.purpose: Enable external, quantitative regulation of subpopulation ratios by converting HSL synthase expression from self-induced to inducer-induced.
experiments.host: Escherichia coli Top10 (CGi, CRi, SGi, SRi)
experiments.intervention: Promoter replacement: in CGi, EsaI synthase promoter replaced with L-arabinose-inducible promoter; in CRi, LasI promoter replaced with aTc-inducible promoter; in SGi, aTc-inducible promoter regulating LasI; in SRi, EsaI promoter replaced with Ara-inducible promoter. Strains selected by same characterization method.
experiments.conditions: 24-well plates, 1.5 mL LB, 37 C, 12 h; inducer Combinations I-IV (Ara 0-1300 uM increasing; aTc 1000-0 ng/mL decreasing; exact values in Supplementary Table S5).
experiments.control: No QS Control system (NG/NR); same-inoculum cocultures across inducer combinations.
experiments.replicates: three independent biological replicates (representative shown; all replicates in Supplementary Figures S11/S12).
experiments.readout: Flow cytometry: 20000 events/sample, FITC (GFP) and PE-Texas Red (RFP) channels, FSC/SSC gating; quadrants Q1=RFP, Q3=GFP, Q4=impurities/dead cells.
experiments.analysis: Subpopulation ratio quantification across inducer gradients; time-course ratio variation (Supplementary Figures S13/S14).
experiments.outcome: Inducible competitive ecosystem: CGi 22.2% -> 92.8%, CRi 71.3% -> 3.14% from Combination I to IV. Inducible symbiotic ecosystem: SGi 12.2% -> 84.4%, SRi 81.1% -> 10.4%, with relatively stable dynamics. Dominant-strain switch achieved only in the QS-based inducible ecosystem, not in No QS Control.

ddr_annotation.decision_type_rationale: Q1 yes (promoter replacement), Q2 yes (this paper), Q3 yes (created the ratio-regulation capability that is the paper's main applied contribution).
ddr_annotation.design_action_rationale: Replacing QS self-induction of signal synthases with externally inducible promoters converts an autonomous feedback circuit into an externally tunable dynamic control system of population composition.
ddr_annotation.trigger_observation: Self-induced ecosystems couple signal production to population density and therefore do not allow external setting of subpopulation ratios; composition control is needed for community function.
ddr_annotation.evidence_grading_rationale: Ratio control measured directly by flow cytometry across four inducer combinations in two ecosystems, with independent replicates.
ddr_annotation.reason_nature_rationale: Paper states the causal chain explicitly: inducer-controlled synthase expression controls autoinducer production, which controls CcdA/CcdB expression and thereby subpopulation ratios.
ddr_annotation.generalizable_rule: When externally tunable subpopulation ratios are needed in a QS-based two-strain E. coli consortium, replace the self-inducing QS promoters of the HSL synthases with orthogonal inducible promoters (Ara/aTc), because inducer dosage then sets signal production, which propagates through the toxin-antitoxin feedbacks to set the steady-state strain ratio (validated in E. coli Top10 competitive and symbiotic ecosystems at 1.5 mL scale).
alternatives_considered: Microfluidic population regulation (refs 20,26,32-34) noted as requiring restricted culture conditions such as controlled flow rate; authors chose batch 1.5 mL inducible circuits instead

experiments.purpose: Enable distinguishing the two subpopulations in coculture, where OD600 cannot separate strains and dead cells distort density readings.
experiments.intervention: Chromosomal integration of GFP and RFP using the CRIM plasmid method: helper plasmid pAH69 into TOP10, integration induced at elevated temperature, electro-transformation of pHK-GFP / pHK-RFP, selection of multicopy clones for higher reporter expression.
experiments.conditions: Standard LB cloning conditions.
experiments.readout: GFP/RFP fluorescence.
experiments.analysis: Fluorescence-based indirect growth monitoring.
experiments.outcome: Unified indirect fluorescence readout for strain-specific growth in coculture; enabled plate, plate-reader and flow-cytometry discrimination.

ddr_annotation.decision_type_rationale: Q1 yes (chromosomal integration performed here), Q2 yes (strains made here; CRIM method itself is from ref 37), Q3 yes (readout choice enabled all subsequent coculture quantification).
ddr_annotation.design_action_rationale: Reporter integration is measurement/readout infrastructure supporting the screening and characterization pipeline.
ddr_annotation.trigger_observation: Dead cells affect OD600-based density detection and OD600 cannot distinguish the two strains in coculture.
ddr_annotation.evidence_grading_rationale: Reporter function demonstrated throughout measured experiments.
ddr_annotation.reason_nature_rationale: CRIM plasmid method adopted from Haldimann & Wanner (ref 37); paper gives a practical (readout limitation) rather than mechanistic justification.
ddr_annotation.generalizable_rule: When monitoring two E. coli subpopulations in coculture, integrate distinguishable fluorescent reporters into the chromosome (e.g., CRIM method) and use fluorescence rather than OD600 as the growth readout, because OD600 cannot resolve strains and is biased by dead cells (validated in LB liquid and agar cocultures of QS-ccd ecosystems).

experiments.purpose: Test whether the QS communication module is necessary for population regulation.
experiments.intervention: Construction of No QS Control strains expressing the toxin-antitoxin system without QS systems; coculture and dominant-strain switch attempt with inducers.
experiments.conditions: Same coculture conditions as inducible ecosystems (Supplementary Figures S15-S17).
experiments.control: Inducible competitive ecosystem as the QS-containing comparator.
experiments.readout: Growth and subpopulation dominance (supplementary).
experiments.analysis: Comparison of growth and switchability vs QS-containing ecosystem.
experiments.outcome: NG/NR coculture growth significantly inhibited (attributed by authors to lack of QS growth buffering); dominant-strain switchover not achieved, unlike the inducible competitive ecosystem.

ddr_annotation.decision_type_rationale: NG/NR construction serves as a negative control to validate QS necessity; although it is a new construct, it introduces no design strategy for future choices beyond confirming the existing design (classified as control/validation record; Q3 fails).

multi-detection microplate reader (Synergy HT, Biotek, USA)

objective.value: Establish modular synthetic microbial ecosystems in E. coli that realize different ecological interactions (competition and symbiosis) by reconfiguring the layout between a quorum-sensing communication module and a toxin-antitoxin effect module, and further build inducible synthetic ecosystems (Ara/aTc) to regulate subpopulation ratios over a wide range.
objective.notes: Author-stated aim; paper_claim level.

hypothesis.value: Reconfiguring cis- vs trans-acting QS activation of the ccd toxin-antitoxin effect module between two strains can convert interaction topology (competition <-> symbiosis), and replacing self-inducing QS promoters of HSL synthases with inducible promoters enables external, quantitative control of subpopulation ratios.

inference.rationale: Paper states aims and design logic but no explicit single hypothesis sentence; hypothesis reconstructed from 'we aimed to establish...' and the module-reconfiguration rationale.

hypothesis.notes: model_inference, not a verbatim paper statement.

Engineered strains: competitive CG01, CG02 (GFP) and CR01, CR02 (RFP); symbiotic SG01 (GFP), SR01 (RFP); inducible CGi, CRi, SGi, SRi; No QS Control strains NG and NR; unnamed control strains unable to produce signals (Supplementary Figure S7).

engineering_method.value: Modular genetic-circuit design: two orthogonal HSL-based QS systems (tra*, las) as communication module; ccd operon toxin-antitoxin (CcdA/CcdB) as effect module; reconfiguration of cis/trans activation layout to switch ecological interaction; RBS engineering of HSL synthases, ccdA and ccdB to tune signal synthesis rate and effect-module expression; replacement of QS promoters of HSL synthases with L-arabinose- or aTc-inducible promoters to build inducible ecosystems; CRIM-based chromosomal integration of GFP/RFP reporters; selection of representative strains by growth/fluorescence characterization.
engineering_method.notes: RBS variant libraries were screened; only selected representative strains are characterized in main text.

outcomes.value: Competitive ecosystem: CGs and CRs mutually inhibited growth; dominant strain tunable via HSL synthesis rate and effect-module expression (CR01 dominant in Combinations 1 and 3, CG01 dominant in Combination 2, both inhibited in Combination 4); distance-dependent interaction on solid medium. Symbiotic ecosystem: SG01 and SR01 mutually promoted growth, coculture fluorescence exceeded single strains, stable coexistence over 72 h and after two dilutions; no growth with signal-deficient control strains. Inducible competitive ecosystem: CGi proportion increased 22.2% -> 92.8% and CRi decreased 71.3% -> 3.14% across inducer Combinations I-IV. Inducible symbiotic ecosystem: SGi increased 12.2% -> 84.4%, SRi decreased 81.1% -> 10.4%; relatively stable dynamics. No QS Control: growth significantly inhibited and dominant-strain switch not achieved, indicating QS is key to population regulation. Regulation achieved in 1.5 mL culture volume with simplified culture conditions vs microfluidic systems.
outcomes.notes: Ratio values are direct_observation from Figure 6e,f; mechanistic explanations (e.g., HSL diffusion limitation on plates) are author_interpretation ('may be caused by').

experiments.purpose: Construct a synthetic competitive ecosystem by cross-wiring two orthogonal QS systems (tra*, las) to a ccd toxin-antitoxin effect module in two E. coli Top10 strains (CG: GFP; CR: RFP), each carrying a cis-acting positive feedback (self-rescue via antitoxin CcdA) and a trans-acting negative feedback (killing via CcdB induced by partner's HSL).
experiments.intervention: Genetic circuit construction: intact tra* system self-inducing ccdA + partial las system controlling ccdB in CG; intact las system self-inducing ccdA + partial tra* system controlling ccdB in CR; chromosomal GFP/RFP integration (CRIM method, helper pAH69, pHK-GFP/pHK-RFP, multicopy clones).
experiments.conditions: LB medium, antibiotics as appropriate, 37 C, 220 rpm seed cultures; characterization in 24-well plates (1.5 mL).
experiments.replicates: three experiments (Fig 2), replicate type unresolved; three independent biological replicates for plate cocultures (Fig 3).
experiments.readout: GFP/RFP fluorescence growth curves; agar-plate spatial fluorescence patterns.
experiments.analysis: Qualitative curve comparison; dominant-strain identification via subpopulation ratios.
experiments.outcome: Mutual growth inhibition achieved; competitive relationship confirmed in liquid and on plates; dominant strain switchable through HSL synthesis rate / effect-module expression tuning.

ddr_annotation.decision_type_rationale: Q1 yes (de novo circuit construction in this paper), Q2 yes (strains CG/CR built here, though orthogonal QS parts pre-existed), Q3 yes (demonstrates that module layout reconfiguration defines ecological relationship, motivating the symbiotic and inducible designs).
ddr_annotation.design_action_rationale: The design installs QS-linked positive/negative feedback regulation of a toxin-antitoxin module to couple interspecific communication to population-density-dependent growth control - a dynamic regulation architecture.
ddr_annotation.trigger_observation: Prior ecosystems lacked a general modular route to distinct ecological interactions; QS crosstalk causes circuit failure, so orthogonal QS systems plus a separable effect module were needed.
ddr_annotation.evidence_grading_rationale: Rests on previously measured orthogonality of the tra*/las systems (ref 30, measured) and the characterized CcdB-gyrase/CcdA-antidote mechanism; circuit function verified by growth assays.
ddr_annotation.reason_nature_rationale: Paper explicitly reasons that cis-acting HSL activation of antitoxin yields self-rescue while trans-acting activation of toxin limits population size, and that swapping aggressive behavior for suicidal behavior converts competition to symbiosis.
ddr_annotation.generalizable_rule: When constructing a two-strain E. coli consortium with a defined ecological interaction, reconfigure cis- vs trans-acting QS activation of a shared toxin-antitoxin effect module, because assigning self-HSL to antitoxin and partner-HSL to toxin yields competition whereas the inverse assignment yields symbiosis (validated in E. coli Top10 QS-ccd proof-of-concept consortia).
alternatives_considered: Cross-feeding/auxotrophy approaches (background, refs 10-14) noted to suffer metabolic burden and asymmetric strain ratios (Kerner et al.)
Toxin/lysis-based density-control ecosystems (refs 26,27) noted as unable to control subpopulation ratios

experiments.purpose: Construct a synthetic symbiotic ecosystem by inverting the cis/trans activation layout: each strain self-induces its own toxin (negative feedback) and is rescued by the partner's HSL activating its antitoxin (positive feedback).
experiments.host: Escherichia coli Top10 (SG: GFP; SR: RFP)
experiments.intervention: Circuit construction: intact las system self-inducing ccdB + partial tra* controlling ccdA in SG; intact tra* self-inducing ccdB + partial las controlling ccdA in SR; RBS tuning; selection of SG01 and SR01.
experiments.conditions: LB liquid and agar; different inoculation ratios; no-inducer plates.
experiments.control: Single strains; signal-deficient control strains cocultured with SG01 or SR01.
experiments.replicates: three experiments (Fig 4); three independent biological replicates (Fig 5).
experiments.readout: Fluorescence growth curves; plate images.
experiments.analysis: Coculture vs single-strain fluorescence; dilution stability; 72 h time-course proportion.
experiments.outcome: Mutual growth promotion: coculture fluorescence exceeded single strains; SG01 growth increased with SR01 inoculation ratio; symbiosis maintained after two dilutions and 72 h; neither strain grew with signal-deficient controls; SR01 grew toward SG01 on plates.

ddr_annotation.decision_type_rationale: Q1 yes (new circuit construction), Q2 yes (this paper), Q3 yes (demonstrates layout-reconfiguration generality and provides the symbiotic chassis later made inducible).
ddr_annotation.design_action_rationale: Installs QS-mediated negative self-limitation and trans-acting rescue feedbacks - dynamic regulation of population growth.
ddr_annotation.trigger_observation: The competitive design showed that cis/trans assignment of effect-module activation defines interaction type, predicting that inversion yields mutual protection.
ddr_annotation.evidence_grading_rationale: Symbiotic phenotypes measured in growth, dilution, coculture-with-control and 72 h coexistence assays.
ddr_annotation.reason_nature_rationale: Paper gives explicit mechanistic logic: self-induced toxin causes self-limitation while partner-HSL-induced antitoxin causes population rescue.
ddr_annotation.generalizable_rule: When engineering a two-strain E. coli mutualism from a QS-ccd toolkit, assign each strain's own HSL to toxin expression and the partner's HSL to antitoxin expression, because this converts aggression into suicidal behavior that is rescued only by the partner, yielding obligate-like mutual protection (validated for the SG01/SR01 E. coli Top10 pair in LB liquid and agar).

experiments.purpose: Enable external, quantitative regulation of subpopulation ratios by converting HSL synthase expression from self-induced to inducer-induced.
experiments.host: Escherichia coli Top10 (CGi, CRi, SGi, SRi)
experiments.intervention: Promoter replacement: in CGi, EsaI synthase promoter replaced with L-arabinose-inducible promoter; in CRi, LasI promoter replaced with aTc-inducible promoter; in SGi, aTc-inducible promoter regulating LasI; in SRi, EsaI promoter replaced with Ara-inducible promoter. Strains selected by same characterization method.
experiments.conditions: 24-well plates, 1.5 mL LB, 37 C, 12 h; inducer Combinations I-IV (Ara 0-1300 uM increasing; aTc 1000-0 ng/mL decreasing; exact values in Supplementary Table S5).
experiments.control: No QS Control system (NG/NR); same-inoculum cocultures across inducer combinations.
experiments.replicates: three independent biological replicates (representative shown; all replicates in Supplementary Figures S11/S12).
experiments.readout: Flow cytometry: 20000 events/sample, FITC (GFP) and PE-Texas Red (RFP) channels, FSC/SSC gating; quadrants Q1=RFP, Q3=GFP, Q4=impurities/dead cells.
experiments.analysis: Subpopulation ratio quantification across inducer gradients; time-course ratio variation (Supplementary Figures S13/S14).
experiments.outcome: Inducible competitive ecosystem: CGi 22.2% -> 92.8%, CRi 71.3% -> 3.14% from Combination I to IV. Inducible symbiotic ecosystem: SGi 12.2% -> 84.4%, SRi 81.1% -> 10.4%, with relatively stable dynamics. Dominant-strain switch achieved only in the QS-based inducible ecosystem, not in No QS Control.

ddr_annotation.decision_type_rationale: Q1 yes (promoter replacement), Q2 yes (this paper), Q3 yes (created the ratio-regulation capability that is the paper's main applied contribution).
ddr_annotation.design_action_rationale: Replacing QS self-induction of signal synthases with externally inducible promoters converts an autonomous feedback circuit into an externally tunable dynamic control system of population composition.
ddr_annotation.trigger_observation: Self-induced ecosystems couple signal production to population density and therefore do not allow external setting of subpopulation ratios; composition control is needed for community function.
ddr_annotation.evidence_grading_rationale: Ratio control measured directly by flow cytometry across four inducer combinations in two ecosystems, with independent replicates.
ddr_annotation.reason_nature_rationale: Paper states the causal chain explicitly: inducer-controlled synthase expression controls autoinducer production, which controls CcdA/CcdB expression and thereby subpopulation ratios.
ddr_annotation.generalizable_rule: When externally tunable subpopulation ratios are needed in a QS-based two-strain E. coli consortium, replace the self-inducing QS promoters of the HSL synthases with orthogonal inducible promoters (Ara/aTc), because inducer dosage then sets signal production, which propagates through the toxin-antitoxin feedbacks to set the steady-state strain ratio (validated in E. coli Top10 competitive and symbiotic ecosystems at 1.5 mL scale).
alternatives_considered: Microfluidic population regulation (refs 20,26,32-34) noted as requiring restricted culture conditions such as controlled flow rate; authors chose batch 1.5 mL inducible circuits instead

experiments.purpose: Enable distinguishing the two subpopulations in coculture, where OD600 cannot separate strains and dead cells distort density readings.
experiments.intervention: Chromosomal integration of GFP and RFP using the CRIM plasmid method: helper plasmid pAH69 into TOP10, integration induced at elevated temperature, electro-transformation of pHK-GFP / pHK-RFP, selection of multicopy clones for higher reporter expression.
experiments.conditions: Standard LB cloning conditions.
experiments.readout: GFP/RFP fluorescence.
experiments.analysis: Fluorescence-based indirect growth monitoring.
experiments.outcome: Unified indirect fluorescence readout for strain-specific growth in coculture; enabled plate, plate-reader and flow-cytometry discrimination.

ddr_annotation.decision_type_rationale: Q1 yes (chromosomal integration performed here), Q2 yes (strains made here; CRIM method itself is from ref 37), Q3 yes (readout choice enabled all subsequent coculture quantification).
ddr_annotation.design_action_rationale: Reporter integration is measurement/readout infrastructure supporting the screening and characterization pipeline.
ddr_annotation.trigger_observation: Dead cells affect OD600-based density detection and OD600 cannot distinguish the two strains in coculture.
ddr_annotation.evidence_grading_rationale: Reporter function demonstrated throughout measured experiments.
ddr_annotation.reason_nature_rationale: CRIM plasmid method adopted from Haldimann & Wanner (ref 37); paper gives a practical (readout limitation) rather than mechanistic justification.
ddr_annotation.generalizable_rule: When monitoring two E. coli subpopulations in coculture, integrate distinguishable fluorescent reporters into the chromosome (e.g., CRIM method) and use fluorescence rather than OD600 as the growth readout, because OD600 cannot resolve strains and is biased by dead cells (validated in LB liquid and agar cocultures of QS-ccd ecosystems).

experiments.purpose: Test whether the QS communication module is necessary for population regulation.
experiments.intervention: Construction of No QS Control strains expressing the toxin-antitoxin system without QS systems; coculture and dominant-strain switch attempt with inducers.
experiments.conditions: Same coculture conditions as inducible ecosystems (Supplementary Figures S15-S17).
experiments.control: Inducible competitive ecosystem as the QS-containing comparator.
experiments.readout: Growth and subpopulation dominance (supplementary).
experiments.analysis: Comparison of growth and switchability vs QS-containing ecosystem.
experiments.outcome: NG/NR coculture growth significantly inhibited (attributed by authors to lack of QS growth buffering); dominant-strain switchover not achieved, unlike the inducible competitive ecosystem.

ddr_annotation.decision_type_rationale: NG/NR construction serves as a negative control to validate QS necessity; although it is a new construct, it introduces no design strategy for future choices beyond confirming the existing design (classified as control/validation record; Q3 fails).

source_locations.excerpt: In this study, we aimed to establish synthetic ecosystems that can realize diferent ecological interactions through module reconfiguration.
By using modular design, we constructed synthetic competitive and symbiotic ecosystems with Escherichia coli.
By reconfiguring the layout between the communication and efect modules, we simulated competitive and symbiotic ecological relationships
by changing signal expression from self-induced to inducer-induced, the production of autoinducers could be controlled
E. coli DH5a was used for plasmid construction. E. coli Top10 was used to construct synthetic ecosystems.
Two strains, NG and NR, were engineered in this control system.
In CG, the intact tra* system self-induced the expression of CcdA, and the partial las system controlled the expression of CcdB.
the promoter of EsaI was replaced with the promoter induced by L-arabinose (Ara) in CG; this engineered strain was termed CGi
GFP and RFP were integrated into the chromosome using the CRIM plasmid method.
Two completely orthogonal QS systems we established in previous work, the tra* and the las systems, were utilized as the communication module
diferent ribosome binding sites (RBSs) were used to control HSL synthases, CcdA, and CcdB
(a) Combination 1: coculture of CG01 and CR01...
Subpopulation ratios in each inducible synthetic ecosystem were regulated by adding four combinations of inducers
We also cocultured SG01 or SR01 with the control strains, which cannot produce signals
As a control, we constructed a No QS Control system
Following culturing at 220 rpm and 37 C for 12 h, 2% seeds were washed three times and inoculated in a 24-well microassay plate containing 1.5 mL of LB medium.
Luria-Bertani (LB) broth (5 g/L yeast extract, 10 g/L tryptone, 10 g/L NaCl)... chloramphenicol, 34 ug/mL; kanamycin, 25 ug/mL; and ampicillin, 100 ug/mL
When 10 uM 3OC6HSL was added... A concentration of 100 nM 3OC6HSL had no inhibitory efect
the concentration of Ara increased from 0 to 1300 uM, and the concentration of aTc decreased from 1000 ng/mL to 0 ng/mL
CR02 was completely inhibited within 12 h
a timecourse population proportion was analyzed for 72 h
cultured at 37 C under vigorous shaking for 12 h
Data show the means +/- SD of three experiments.
one representative sample of three independent biological replicates
A total of 20 000 events were collected for each sample. Green fluorescence and red fluorescence were detected in the FITC channel and PE-Texas Red channel
we unified an indirect method to monitor strain growth by detecting fluorescence expression
multi-detection microplate reader (Synergy HT, Biotek, USA)
photographed with a multifunctional gel imager
Events in quadrant Q1 represent strains expressing RFP. Events in quadrant Q3 represent strains expressing GFP.
We further identified the dominant strain in each combination by analyzing the subpopulation ratios
the proportion of CGi increased from 22.2% to 92.8% and the proportion of CRi decreased from 71.3% to 3.14%
the inducible competitive ecosystem realized the switchover of the dominant strain, whereas the No QS Control system did not

Many RBS variants were screened but are evidence details, not independent engineering decisions.

unsupported_values: Improve N-acetyl-D-neuraminic acid (NeuAc) production in Escherichia coli from glucose as sole carbon source by (1) optimizing amino sugar metabolism pathway kinetics via screening AGE and NeuB enzymes from different sources and their combinations, (2) optimizing expression intensity of the two key enzymes via RBS engineering, and (3) reserving the phosphoenolpyruvate (PEP) pool by engineering the PEP catabolic pathway (knockout of ptsG, pykA, pykF, ppc, pck, gltA candidates).

NeuAc synthesis is bottlenecked by amino sugar metabolism (the GlcNAc-to-NeuAc steps catalyzed by AGE and NeuB are rate-limiting) and by unbalanced precursor PEP supply due to inherent glycolytic regulation; systematically optimizing enzyme kinetics/expression and metabolic flux distribution at the PEP node should holistically improve NeuAc production.
Escherichia coli DH5α
DN5 (E. coli DH5α derivative with nan operon (nanATEK), nag operon (nagEBAC), ldhA, poxB and ackA deleted)
DN5/pB, DN5/pBa, DN5/pBc, DN5/pBm, DN5/pBac, DN5/pBam (enzyme-combination screening)
DN5/pBac2 (AGE RBS = ARBS2)
DN5/pBacR (ARBS2 + NRBS3)
DN5 single-knockout series with pBacR: ΔptsG, ΔpykA, ΔpykF, Δppc, Δpck, ΔgltA
DN11 = DN5ΔpykA/pBacR
DN12 = DN11ΔptsG (i.e., DN5ΔpykAΔptsG)/pBacR
DN11ΔgltA/pBacR (decreased production)
Anabaena sp. CH1 (AGE_a)
Synechocystis sp. PCC 6803 (AGE_s)
Campylobacter jejuni NCTC 11168 (NeuB_c)
Moritella viscosa (NeuB_m)
Escherichia coli K1 (NeuB_k)
Escherichia coli K12 (GlmS*)
Saccharomyces cerevisiae (GNA1)
E. coli DH5α ΔnanATEK ΔnagEBAC ΔldhA ΔpoxB ΔackA
DN5 ΔpykA
DN5 ΔpykA ΔptsG
pTrc99a-based plasmid carrying GlmS* (E. coli K12), GNA1 (S. cerevisiae), AGE_a (Anabaena sp. CH1) with ARBS2 RBS, NeuB_c (C. jejuni NCTC 11168) with NRBS3 RBS, under Ptrc promoter
ppc
pck
Heterologous expression and combinatorial screening of AGE (2 sources) × NeuB (3 sources) enzymes on pTrc99a-based plasmids under Ptrc
RBS engineering of AGE_a and NeuB_c using RBS Calculator 2.0 (four strengthened RBS variants each; selected ARBS2 and NRBS3)
Copy-number and strong-promoter (PT7) expression attempts (p15a/pCDF/pUC/pET constructs) — abandoned due to severe growth inhibition
Gene knockout using pTKRed helper plasmid (lambda Red recombineering) with PKD3/PKD4 templates and IPTG (2 mM) induction; electroporation
Gibson assembly and restriction-ligation (NotI/SpeI, T4 ligase) cloning; codon optimization and gene synthesis for heterologous enzymes
Experiment 1 (enzyme combination): 6 plasmid groups (pB, pBa, pBc, pBm, pBac, pBam) in DN5, batch fermentation at 25, 30, 37 °C (Figure 2A); fed fermentation of DN5/pBac (Figure 2B)

Experiment 2 (expression intensity): copy-number/PT7 promoter constructs (p15a-cagg, pCDF-cagg, pUC-cagg, pET-cagg, pET-acgg, p15a-T7p-cam) — growth-inhibited groups; AGE RBS variants ARBS1–4 vs original ARBS0 in DN5/pBac (Figure 3C); NeuB RBS variants NRBS1–4 vs NRBS0 in DN5/pBac2 (Figure 3D); fed fermentation of DN5/pBacR (Figure 4)

Experiment 3 (PEP supply): six single-knockout strains (ΔptsG, ΔpykA, ΔpykF, Δppc, Δpck, ΔgltA in DN5) with pBacR, fed fermentation in shake flasks (Figure 5A–D); then DN11-based second-round knockouts (DN11ΔgltA, DN11ΔptsG=DN12); fed fermentation of DN12 (Figure 6)
DN5/pB (original AGE_s + NeuB_k plasmid) as baseline combination for enzyme-screening comparison
Original RBS strains (ARBS0 for AGE; NRBS0 for NeuB) as baselines for RBS engineering
Non-knockout DN5/pBacR as reference for knockout-strain comparisons
Single colony into 5 mL LB with appropriate antibiotics, 12 h, 37 °C

Same as batch; glucose added when below 10 g/L
Shake flasks (fed fermentations stated to be in shake flasks)
pTKRed-harboring strains induced with 2 mM IPTG
Luria-Bertani (LB) medium, 37 °C, aeration
Modified terrific broth (MTB): 12 g/L tryptone, 24 g/L yeast extract, 5 g/L NaCl; plus 20 g/L glucose and 200 μM IPTG at fermentation start
ampicillin 100 μg/mL; kanamycin 25 μg/mL; chloramphenicol 17 μg/mL; spectinomycin 100 μg/mL (added when necessary)
20 g/L (batch); feeding when glucose < 10 g/L (fed-batch)
200 μM (fermentation); 2 mM (pTKRed knockout induction)
4% (v/v, inferred unit)

36 h (20 g/L glucose nearly consumed)

Three independent experiments conducted simultaneously to obtain error bars (stated for Figures 2, 3, 4 and 6); Figure 5D shows a representative curve from three independent experiments with RSD < 10%.
OD600 measurement for cell growth
HPLC quantification of glucose, NeuAc, acetate, ethanol, formate, pyruvate, GlcNAc, ManNAc (extracellular, supernatant after 10,000 rcf 5 min)
Resorcinol-based colorimetric assay for NeuAc
Colony PCR and sequencing for plasmid/knockout verification
Spectrophotometer (Shimazu [Shimadzu], Japan) for OD600
HPLC (Shimadzu, Japan) with refractive index detector RID-10A (Shimadzu) and Aminex HPX-87H ion exclusion column (Bio-Rad, USA)

Electroporation apparatus for transformation (method stated; instrument model not reported)
RBS Calculator 2.0 (denovodna.com) used to design/select RBS variants by predicted translation initiation intensity
Comparative fermentation analysis across temperatures (25/30/37 °C) and knockout backgrounds; error bars from three independent experiments; RSD < 10% criterion for representative curves
Km values from cited literature used to rationalize AGE substrate-affinity differences (author interpretation)

pBac (AGE_a Anabaena sp. CH1 + NeuB_c C. jejuni NCTC 11168) gave 1.9 g/L NeuAc at 30 °C, 1.5× the DN5/pB titer at 37 °C; NeuB_c better suited lower temperatures; DN5/pBac fed fermentation reached 4.7 g/L at 72 h

Copy-number/PT7 strong-expression constructs severely inhibited growth and decreased NeuAc (data not shown). AGE RBS ARBS2 → 3.2 g/L (pBac2); NeuB RBS NRBS3 → 3.7 g/L (pBacR); DN5/pBacR fed fermentation reached 7.1 g/L at 96 h with 12.6 g/L GlcNAc and 2.5 g/L ManNAc accumulation

Single knockouts in DN5/pBacR: ΔpykA highest at 9.9 g/L (strain DN11); Δppc severely reduced growth; Δpck reduced NeuAc; ΔpykF and ΔgltA poor growth in LB but good growth in TB. Second round: DN11ΔgltA dropped to 5.6 g/L; DN11ΔptsG (DN12) reached 16.7 g/L NeuAc — reported as the highest NeuAc production from glucose as sole carbon source
Combination screening +0.5-fold, expression optimization +1.04-fold, PEP pathway engineering +1.35-fold relative increases (author summary); final 16.7 g/L

objective.value: Improve N-acetyl-D-neuraminic acid (NeuAc) production in Escherichia coli from glucose as sole carbon source by (1) optimizing amino sugar metabolism pathway kinetics via screening AGE and NeuB enzymes from different sources and their combinations, (2) optimizing expression intensity of the two key enzymes via RBS engineering, and (3) reserving the phosphoenolpyruvate (PEP) pool by engineering the PEP catabolic pathway (knockout of ptsG, pykA, pykF, ppc, pck, gltA candidates).

hypothesis.value: NeuAc synthesis is bottlenecked by amino sugar metabolism (the GlcNAc-to-NeuAc steps catalyzed by AGE and NeuB are rate-limiting) and by unbalanced precursor PEP supply due to inherent glycolytic regulation; systematically optimizing enzyme kinetics/expression and metabolic flux distribution at the PEP node should holistically improve NeuAc production.
hypothesis.notes: Rate-limiting-step attribution for GlcNAc→NeuAc steps is cited by the authors to prior studies (refs 36, 37); PEP bottleneck inference in this study is triggered by observed GlcNAc/ManNAc accumulation.

ddr_annotation.decision_type_rationale: Q1 pass (heterologous enzyme combination constructed in this study), Q2 pass (constructed here, though pB plasmid template derives from prior study ref 36 — the six combination plasmids were built in this work), Q3 pass (combination choice drove subsequent RBS and knockout decisions).
ddr_annotation.design_action_rationale: Replacing rate-limiting enzymes with natural high-activity orthologs and screening their combinations = rate-limiting enzyme identification and engineering.
ddr_annotation.trigger_observation: Prior directed evolution could only improve enzymes within inherent characteristics; GlcNAc→NeuAc steps reported as rate-limiting (refs 36,37); existing titers far from cost-effective.
ddr_annotation.evidence_grading_rationale: Choice of orthologs based on reported high enzymatic activities (literature-reported measured kinetics); outcomes measured by fermentation titers in this study.
ddr_annotation.reason_nature_rationale: Enzymes explicitly 'chosen because they have reported high enzymatic activities' (refs 28, 41–43) — selection justified by literature-reported properties rather than new mechanistic analysis in this paper.
ddr_annotation.generalizable_rule: When the two terminal steps of an amino-sugar-to-NeuAc pathway are rate-limiting in an E. coli production system, apply screening of natural high-activity AGE and NeuB orthologs and their source combinations, because orthologs differ in substrate affinity and temperature adaptation which jointly determine pathway flux.
alternatives_considered: Directed evolution of AGE via high-threshold riboswitch (used previously, ref 37) — set aside because it can only improve inherent enzyme characteristics

ddr_annotation.decision_type_rationale: Q1 pass (RBS engineering performed), Q2 pass (this study), Q3 pass (established pBacR chassis for subsequent PEP engineering; revealed next bottleneck).
ddr_annotation.design_action_rationale: Modulating translation initiation strength of the two key enzymes to balance pathway expression = expression balancing.
ddr_annotation.trigger_observation: GlcNAc accumulation remained very high during fermentation, indicating downstream conversion capacity insufficient; strong PT7 expression caused metabolic discoordination, so moderate tunable tuning was needed.
ddr_annotation.evidence_grading_rationale: RBS selection based on RBS Calculator 2.0 predicted translation initiation intensities — predictive tool output; predictions were then confirmed by fermentation, but the design rationale itself rests on prediction (需实测确认, which the authors did perform).
ddr_annotation.reason_nature_rationale: Paper gives an explicit mechanistic rationale: high GlcNAc accumulation means AGE/NeuB throughput limits flux, so raising their translation intensity should drain GlcNAc toward NeuAc; non-monotonic response at highest RBS is mechanistically attributed (with hedging 'may') to low NeuB_c solubility.
ddr_annotation.generalizable_rule: When an intermediate (GlcNAc) accumulates in an E. coli NeuAc production system, apply moderate RBS-strength tuning of the downstream enzymes (AGE/NeuB) rather than maximal-strength promoters, because balanced translation increase raises pathway throughput while avoiding metabolic burden or solubility limits of heterologous enzymes.
alternatives_considered: Strong PT7 promoter / high-copy vectors — abandoned due to severe growth inhibition

experiments.intervention: Knockout of six PEP-node genes (ptsG, pykA, pykF, ppc, pck, gltA) individually from DN5 via pTKRed recombineering; second round: gltA or ptsG knocked out from DN11; pykF double-knockout deliberately not attempted
experiments.conditions: Fed fermentation in shake flasks, 30 °C, 220 rpm, pH ~7.0 (30% NH4OH), sampling 6/12 h, stopped at 120 h

ddr_annotation.decision_type_rationale: Q1 pass (genome knockouts performed), Q2 pass (this study), Q3 pass (results selected DN11 and DN12 and defined which PEP routes are safely blockable).
ddr_annotation.design_action_rationale: Blocking competing PEP consumption routes to increase precursor PEP availability for NeuB reaction = precursor and reducing-power supply (precursor supply).
ddr_annotation.trigger_observation: DN5/pBacR fed fermentation accumulated 12.6 g/L GlcNAc and 2.5 g/L ManNAc, indicating amino sugar supply sufficient and the bottleneck had shifted to PEP supply.
ddr_annotation.evidence_grading_rationale: Target selection based on literature-reported stoichiometric distribution of PEP consumption (ref 44: PTS ~50%, ppc 16.2%, pyruvate kinase 14.5%, aromatics 3.3%) — chemical-stoichiometric knowledge; outcomes experimentally measured.
ddr_annotation.reason_nature_rationale: Paper gives explicit mechanism: ptsG knockout reroutes glucose transport from PEP-consuming PTS to ATP-consuming transport, sparing PEP; pykA knockout reduces flux toward pyruvate kinase; gltA double-knockout harms energy supply; pck catalyzes oxaloacetate→PEP direction so its removal lowers PEP supply. These are mechanistic (though partly hedged with 'may') explanations tied to pathway topology.
ddr_annotation.generalizable_rule: When PEP-dependent product synthesis is bottlenecked by PEP supply in an E. coli glucose-fermentation system, apply stepwise deletion of major PEP-consuming nodes (pyruvate kinase pykA, then PTS component ptsG) while preserving anaplerosis and at least one pyruvate-kinase route, because PTS and pyruvate kinase consume the largest PEP shares, but complete glycolytic or TCA blockage (pykA+pykF, gltA on ΔpykA) collapses precursor/energy supply.
alternatives_considered: pykF knockout on DN11 background — not tried because pykA+pykF would fully block glycolysis and deprive acetyl-CoA supply for GNA1

objective.value: Improve N-acetyl-D-neuraminic acid (NeuAc) production in Escherichia coli from glucose as sole carbon source by (1) optimizing amino sugar metabolism pathway kinetics via screening AGE and NeuB enzymes from different sources and their combinations, (2) optimizing expression intensity of the two key enzymes via RBS engineering, and (3) reserving the phosphoenolpyruvate (PEP) pool by engineering the PEP catabolic pathway (knockout of ptsG, pykA, pykF, ppc, pck, gltA candidates).

hypothesis.value: NeuAc synthesis is bottlenecked by amino sugar metabolism (the GlcNAc-to-NeuAc steps catalyzed by AGE and NeuB are rate-limiting) and by unbalanced precursor PEP supply due to inherent glycolytic regulation; systematically optimizing enzyme kinetics/expression and metabolic flux distribution at the PEP node should holistically improve NeuAc production.
hypothesis.notes: Rate-limiting-step attribution for GlcNAc→NeuAc steps is cited by the authors to prior studies (refs 36, 37); PEP bottleneck inference in this study is triggered by observed GlcNAc/ManNAc accumulation.

ddr_annotation.decision_type_rationale: Q1 pass (heterologous enzyme combination constructed in this study), Q2 pass (constructed here, though pB plasmid template derives from prior study ref 36 — the six combination plasmids were built in this work), Q3 pass (combination choice drove subsequent RBS and knockout decisions).
ddr_annotation.design_action_rationale: Replacing rate-limiting enzymes with natural high-activity orthologs and screening their combinations = rate-limiting enzyme identification and engineering.
ddr_annotation.trigger_observation: Prior directed evolution could only improve enzymes within inherent characteristics; GlcNAc→NeuAc steps reported as rate-limiting (refs 36,37); existing titers far from cost-effective.
ddr_annotation.evidence_grading_rationale: Choice of orthologs based on reported high enzymatic activities (literature-reported measured kinetics); outcomes measured by fermentation titers in this study.
ddr_annotation.reason_nature_rationale: Enzymes explicitly 'chosen because they have reported high enzymatic activities' (refs 28, 41–43) — selection justified by literature-reported properties rather than new mechanistic analysis in this paper.
ddr_annotation.generalizable_rule: When the two terminal steps of an amino-sugar-to-NeuAc pathway are rate-limiting in an E. coli production system, apply screening of natural high-activity AGE and NeuB orthologs and their source combinations, because orthologs differ in substrate affinity and temperature adaptation which jointly determine pathway flux.
alternatives_considered: Directed evolution of AGE via high-threshold riboswitch (used previously, ref 37) — set aside because it can only improve inherent enzyme characteristics

ddr_annotation.decision_type_rationale: Q1 pass (promoter/copy-number engineering action), Q2 pass (constructed in this study), Q3 pass (negative result redirected strategy toward RBS fine-tuning).

ddr_annotation.trigger_observation: AGE and NeuB shown critical to NeuAc production; authors hypothesized enhancing expression intensity could further increase production.
ddr_annotation.evidence_grading_rationale: Outcome (growth inhibition, decreased production) was experimentally observed, though data not shown.

experiments.purpose: Fine-tune expression intensity of AGE_a and NeuB_c to efficiently metabolize accumulated GlcNAc
experiments.intervention: RBS substitution upstream of AGE_a in pBac (ARBS1–4, predicted initiation strengths 32,837–146,797 vs ARBS0 10,146) then NeuB_c in pBac2 (NRBS1–4, 12,109–109,625 vs NRBS0 6,993), designed with RBS Calculator 2.0; reverse PCR with RBS-containing primers
experiments.conditions: Batch fermentation, 20 g/L glucose, 30 °C, 36 h; fed fermentation of DN5/pBacR
experiments.control: Original RBS strains (ARBS0 / NRBS0) (baseline, inferred role)
experiments.readout: NeuAc titer, glucose consumption, GlcNAc/ManNAc accumulation
experiments.analysis: Titer vs predicted RBS intensity; selected ARBS2 (3.2 g/L) and NRBS3 (3.7 g/L)
experiments.outcome: pBacR (ARBS2+NRBS3); fed fermentation 7.1 g/L NeuAc at 96 h; 12.6 g/L GlcNAc + 2.5 g/L ManNAc accumulated, indicating amino sugar supply sufficient and bottleneck shifting to PEP supply

ddr_annotation.decision_type_rationale: Q1 pass (RBS engineering performed), Q2 pass (this study), Q3 pass (established pBacR chassis for subsequent PEP engineering; revealed next bottleneck).
ddr_annotation.design_action_rationale: Modulating translation initiation strength of the two key enzymes to balance pathway expression = expression balancing.
ddr_annotation.trigger_observation: GlcNAc accumulation remained very high during fermentation, indicating downstream conversion capacity insufficient; strong PT7 expression caused metabolic discoordination, so moderate tunable tuning was needed.
ddr_annotation.evidence_grading_rationale: RBS selection based on RBS Calculator 2.0 predicted translation initiation intensities — predictive tool output; predictions were then confirmed by fermentation, but the design rationale itself rests on prediction (需实测确认, which the authors did perform).
ddr_annotation.reason_nature_rationale: Paper gives an explicit mechanistic rationale: high GlcNAc accumulation means AGE/NeuB throughput limits flux, so raising their translation intensity should drain GlcNAc toward NeuAc; non-monotonic response at highest RBS is mechanistically attributed (with hedging 'may') to low NeuB_c solubility.
ddr_annotation.generalizable_rule: When an intermediate (GlcNAc) accumulates in an E. coli NeuAc production system, apply moderate RBS-strength tuning of the downstream enzymes (AGE/NeuB) rather than maximal-strength promoters, because balanced translation increase raises pathway throughput while avoiding metabolic burden or solubility limits of heterologous enzymes.
alternatives_considered: Strong PT7 promoter / high-copy vectors — abandoned due to severe growth inhibition

experiments.purpose: Reserve PEP pool for NeuAc synthesis by blocking PEP consumption pathways
experiments.intervention: Knockout of six PEP-node genes (ptsG, pykA, pykF, ppc, pck, gltA) individually from DN5 via pTKRed recombineering; second round: gltA or ptsG knocked out from DN11; pykF double-knockout deliberately not attempted
experiments.conditions: Fed fermentation in shake flasks, 30 °C, 220 rpm, pH ~7.0 (30% NH4OH), sampling 6/12 h, stopped at 120 h
experiments.replicates: Three independent experiments; Figure 5D representative curve RSD < 10%
experiments.readout: NeuAc, GlcNAc, ManNAc titers; OD600; growth phenotype in LB vs TB
experiments.analysis: Titer comparison across knockout strains; growth defect interpretation
experiments.outcome: ΔpykA best single knockout (9.9 g/L, strain DN11); Δppc severe growth defect; Δpck reduced NeuAc; DN11ΔgltA fell to 5.6 g/L; DN11ΔptsG = DN12 reached 16.7 g/L — highest reported NeuAc production from glucose as sole carbon source

ddr_annotation.decision_type_rationale: Q1 pass (genome knockouts performed), Q2 pass (this study), Q3 pass (results selected DN11 and DN12 and defined which PEP routes are safely blockable).
ddr_annotation.design_action_rationale: Blocking competing PEP consumption routes to increase precursor PEP availability for NeuB reaction = precursor and reducing-power supply (precursor supply).
ddr_annotation.trigger_observation: DN5/pBacR fed fermentation accumulated 12.6 g/L GlcNAc and 2.5 g/L ManNAc, indicating amino sugar supply sufficient and the bottleneck had shifted to PEP supply.
ddr_annotation.evidence_grading_rationale: Target selection based on literature-reported stoichiometric distribution of PEP consumption (ref 44: PTS ~50%, ppc 16.2%, pyruvate kinase 14.5%, aromatics 3.3%) — chemical-stoichiometric knowledge; outcomes experimentally measured.
ddr_annotation.reason_nature_rationale: Paper gives explicit mechanism: ptsG knockout reroutes glucose transport from PEP-consuming PTS to ATP-consuming transport, sparing PEP; pykA knockout reduces flux toward pyruvate kinase; gltA double-knockout harms energy supply; pck catalyzes oxaloacetate→PEP direction so its removal lowers PEP supply. These are mechanistic (though partly hedged with 'may') explanations tied to pathway topology.
ddr_annotation.generalizable_rule: When PEP-dependent product synthesis is bottlenecked by PEP supply in an E. coli glucose-fermentation system, apply stepwise deletion of major PEP-consuming nodes (pyruvate kinase pykA, then PTS component ptsG) while preserving anaplerosis and at least one pyruvate-kinase route, because PTS and pyruvate kinase consume the largest PEP shares, but complete glycolytic or TCA blockage (pykA+pykF, gltA on ΔpykA) collapses precursor/energy supply.
alternatives_considered: pykF knockout on DN11 background — not tried because pykA+pykF would fully block glycolysis and deprive acetyl-CoA supply for GNA1
ppc knockout — severe growth reduction (oxaloacetate replenishment blocked)
pck knockout — reduced PEP supply
gltA knockout on DN11 — NeuAc fell to 5.6 g/L (energy shortage)
'some other PEP consumption routes were adopted for engineering but all ended in failure' (unspecified)

unsupported_values: Design, evaluate (in silico) and implement novel non-natural biosynthetic routes for isopentyldiol (IPDO) production in Escherichia coli; compare a RetroPath RL-computationally designed route (route B) with the previously published route A and two intuitively designed routes (C from alpha,beta-DHIV; D from mevalonate) regarding theoretical yield, thermodynamics (MDF), energy cost, number of non-native steps and enzyme/intermediate penalties, and test their in vivo IPDO production.

A priori in silico evaluation (FBA theoretical yield + MDF thermodynamic driving force + energy cost + enzyme/intermediate penalties) can predict the relative feasibility of alternative non-natural IPDO pathways; the route with the most favorable profile (route B) is more likely to function in vivo than intuitively designed routes C and D.
Escherichia coli BL21(DE3) (routes B, C, D implementation; protein expression; whole-cell catalysis)
Escherichia coli W3110 with chromosomally integrated sfp under artificial promoter J23105 (strains IPB05, IPB06, IPB07, IPB08)

Theoretical yields (mol/mol glucose): A 0.628, B 0.667, C 0.827, D 0.667. MDF (kJ/mol): A 31.54, B 31.54, C 6.96, D 38.37; after removing the shared PDDH-catalyzed bottleneck: A 84.67, B 74.93. Route B judged best overall (fewest non-native steps, no condition-dependent/uncharacterized enzymes).

experiments.purpose: Design candidate IPDO pathways (RetroPath RL) and rank routes A-D by FBA theoretical yield, MDF thermodynamics, ATP/NADPH cost, non-native steps and enzyme/intermediate penalties
experiments.host: in silico (E. coli K-12 W3110 model iY75_1357)
experiments.intervention: computational pathway design and evaluation
experiments.conditions: glucose uptake 15 mmol/g/DCW; MDF concentration boundaries per Methods 5.5
experiments.control: route A (previously published) as reference route
experiments.readout: theoretical yield, MDF, bottleneck reactions, energy cost
experiments.analysis: FBA; MDF (equilibrator); component contribution method
experiments.outcome: Route B ranked highest overall priority; route C highest yield but lowest MDF; route D highest MDF but all upstream reactions rate-limiting
experiments.decision_type_rationale: Q1: deliberate design action (selection of route B for implementation). Q2: performed in this paper. Q3: determined which pathway was implemented and shaped all subsequent experiments.

ddr_annotation.design_action_rationale: Pathway-level design choice: select and implement the RetroPath RL-predicted route B (HPD -> CAR -> ADH from alpha-KIC) over intuitive routes C and D.
ddr_annotation.trigger_observation: Previously reported route A reached only 310 mg/L IPDO, far from practical requirement; in silico comparison showed route B has fewest non-native steps, high thermodynamic driving force (after removing the shared PDDH bottleneck, MDF 74.93 kJ/mol), low energy cost, and no condition-dependent or poorly characterized enzymes.
ddr_annotation.evidence_grading_rationale: The decision was driven by predictive tool outputs (RetroPath RL, FBA, MDF); these are computational predictions requiring experimental confirmation, which the authors then performed. Route A's 310 mg/L titer is hard prior data but from a previous study.
ddr_annotation.reason_nature_rationale: The paper explicitly articulates mechanistic grounds: thermodynamic driving force topology (oxidative + reductive hydroxyl formation), carbon loss via decarboxylation, ATP/NADPH burden, and enzyme substrate-affinity penalties.
ddr_annotation.generalizable_rule: When designing a non-natural pathway for IPDO (short-chain diol) production in E. coli, prioritize candidate routes that combine oxidative and reductive hydroxyl-group formation, maximize MDF while inspecting thermodynamic topology (not only the single MDF number), and minimize non-native steps and cofactor/ATP cost, because thermodynamic driving force and energy burden determine in vivo feasibility; validated only for IPDO routes in E. coli.
alternatives_considered: Route C (from alpha,beta-DHIV): highest theoretical yield but lowest MDF (6.96 kJ/mol), GDHt requires vitamin B12; implemented but produced no IPDO
Route D (from mevalonate): highest MDF but driven by one highly exergonic ADO step with all upstream reactions rate-limiting; ADO mechanism controversial; implemented but produced no IPDO
Second RetroPath RL route via ethyl 3-hydroxyisovalerate hydrolysis: rejected because the precursor is not a natural E. coli metabolite

ddr_annotation.design_action_rationale: Coexpression of the phosphopantetheinyl transferase Sfp with CAR to obtain fully functional enzyme (expression/activation balancing).
ddr_annotation.trigger_observation: CAR apoenzyme requires post-translational phosphopantetheinylation of a conserved serine to be active; authors cite prior report that Sfp from B. subtilis performs this modification (ref 22) and observed that coexpression is crucial for CAR activity (Table S3).
ddr_annotation.evidence_grading_rationale: Text states measured activity comparison (Table S3) showing coexpression enhances CAR activity; however the underlying table is in the unavailable supplement, so direct numbers could not be verified.
ddr_annotation.reason_nature_rationale: The paper explicitly states the Sfp requirement 'has been reported' (Finnigan et al., ref 22) and adopted it based on that literature.
ddr_annotation.generalizable_rule: When expressing a carboxylic acid reductase (CAR) in E. coli for pathway implementation, coexpress a 4'-phosphopantetheinyl transferase such as Sfp, because CAR requires post-translational phosphopantetheinylation of its conserved serine to be catalytically functional.

experiments.decision_type_rationale: Q1: deliberate choice between two candidate enzymes. Q2: performed here. Q3: AaHPD was carried into the final route-B strain (pTrc-cgh).

ddr_annotation.design_action_rationale: Rate-limiting enzyme identification/engineering via homolog comparison: select the more active HPD for the alpha-KIC to 3-OH-IV step.

experiments.host: E. coli W3110 with chromosomal J23105-sfp + pTrc-car (strain IPB05)
experiments.intervention: chromosomal integration of sfp under artificial constitutive promoter J23105; car overexpressed from pTrc99a

ddr_annotation.design_action_rationale: Expression balancing of CAR and its activating enzyme Sfp across chromosome (J23105-driven sfp) and plasmid (pTrc-car) to maximize functional CAR.
ddr_annotation.trigger_observation: CAR activity depended on the CAR:Sfp expression ratio; the initial pCDFDuet coexpression (IPB01) was suboptimal for the production host context.
ddr_annotation.evidence_grading_rationale: Based on measured CAR activities across configurations (Table S3); however Table S3 is in the unavailable supplement, so the comparison cannot be independently verified from the main text.

ddr_annotation.generalizable_rule: When a CAR-dependent pathway is moved to a production host, tune the expression ratio of CAR to its phosphopantetheinyl transferase (e.g., chromosomal constitutive sfp plus plasmid-borne car), because CAR activity is limited by the balance of apo-CAR and its activating enzyme; validated only for CAR/Sfp in E. coli W3110/BL21(DE3).

experiments.purpose: Achieve de novo IPDO production from glucose via route B
experiments.host: E. coli W3110 chr::J23105-sfp; IPB06 (pTrc-cgh), IPB07 (IPB06 + p15-leu-acd), IPB08 (IPB06 + empty p15AS, negative control)
experiments.intervention: pTrc-cgh (car+GRE2+AaHPD) pathway plasmid; then overexpression of leuAfbrBCD (E. coli), alsS (B. subtilis) and ilvCD (E. coli) on p15AS to enhance alpha-KIC supply
experiments.conditions: FM-II medium, 0.1 mM IPTG at OD600 0.4-0.6, 30 C, 200 rpm, 48 h, shake flask
experiments.readout: IPDO titer (GC and GC-MS confirmation with standard and 1,3-PDO internal standard)
experiments.analysis: GC-FID; GC-MS identity confirmation
experiments.outcome: IPB06: no IPDO detected. IPB07: 2.2 mg/L IPDO from glucose. IPB08: no IPDO.
experiments.decision_type_rationale: Q1: deliberate precursor-supply engineering (leuAfbrBCD/alsS/ilvCD overexpression). Q2: constructed in this paper. Q3: converted a non-producing strain into a producing one, establishing route B in vivo.

ddr_annotation.design_action_rationale: Precursor and flux supply enhancement: overexpress the feedback-resistant leucine operon and upstream BCAA-pathway genes to raise the alpha-KIC pool feeding route B.
ddr_annotation.trigger_observation: IPB06 carrying the complete route B produced no detectable IPDO from glucose; authors hypothesized that the supply of the precursor alpha-KIC is insufficient (consistent with efficient competing conversion of alpha-KIC to leucine by endogenous IlvE).
ddr_annotation.evidence_grading_rationale: Measured outcome: IPB07 produced 2.2 mg/L IPDO while the empty-vector control IPB08 produced none (GC + GC-MS verified).
ddr_annotation.reason_nature_rationale: The intervention directly follows a stated mechanistic hypothesis (precursor alpha-KIC limitation), later reinforced in the Discussion by kinetic comparison of IlvE (Km 0.08 mM, kcat 24.7 s-1) versus HPD (Km 0.32 mM, kcat 6.5 min-1) competing for alpha-KIC.
ddr_annotation.generalizable_rule: When an alpha-KIC-diverting heterologous pathway in E. coli yields no detectable product despite functional pathway enzymes, enhance precursor supply by overexpressing the feedback-resistant leucine biosynthesis operon (leuAfbrBCD) together with alsS and ilvCD, because the endogenous high-efficiency transaminase IlvE drains the alpha-KIC pool toward leucine; validated only at proof-of-concept level (2.2 mg/L IPDO) in E. coli W3110.

experiments.purpose: Implement route C (alpha,beta-DHIV -> IPDO via CAR, PDDH/YqhD, GDHt) in vitro and in vivo
experiments.host: E. coli BL21(DE3), strains IPC01 (pCDF-car-sfp + pCOLA-yqhD-dhaB) and IPC02 (system-engineered IPC01)
experiments.intervention: heterologous expression of car, sfp, yqhD, dhaB (GDHt from Klebsiella); then system metabolic engineering to increase alpha,beta-DHIV flux and block BCAA pathways (Figure S3, supplement unavailable)
experiments.conditions: in vivo: FM-II, 48 h cultivation; in vitro: 25 mM alpha,beta-DHIV, CAR 1 h then YqhD+DhaB 3 h
experiments.control: BA positive control for CAR activity
experiments.readout: IPDO (GC); CAR activity on alpha,beta-DHIV (0.093 umol/min/mg)
experiments.analysis: GC; enzyme assay
experiments.outcome: CAR active on alpha,beta-DHIV in vitro but <half of BA activity; no IPDO from IPC01, IPC02, or the in vitro cascade
experiments.decision_type_rationale: Q1: deliberate engineering (pathway construction; precursor enhancement + competing-pathway blocking in IPC02). Q2: performed here. Q3: represents a strategy choice (precursor supply + competition removal), even though it failed.

ddr_annotation.design_action_rationale: Precursor supply enhancement combined with competitive-pathway removal: increase flux through the alpha,beta-DHIV biosynthesis pathway and block branched-chain amino acid pathways draining it.
ddr_annotation.trigger_observation: IPC01 carrying route C produced no detectable IPDO after 48 h; alpha,beta-DHIV is efficiently consumed by endogenous IlvD, and CAR shows low affinity/activity toward alpha,beta-DHIV.
ddr_annotation.evidence_grading_rationale: Negative GC results are direct measurements; however the specific genetic modifications of IPC02 are only in Figure S3 (supplement unavailable), so the intervention content cannot be fully verified.
ddr_annotation.reason_nature_rationale: The stated logic (raise precursor flux, block competing BCAA consumption) is mechanistic, but the intervention failed to yield IPDO, so the mechanism-to-outcome link is not validated.

experiments.purpose: Implement route D (MVA -> IPDO via CAR and ADO) in E. coli
experiments.host: E. coli BL21(DE3), strain IPD01 (pCDF-car-sfp + pCOLA-af: ado from Prochlorococcus marinus, fdx from Synechocystis sp. 6803, fnr from E. coli)

ddr_annotation.design_action_rationale: Pathway implementation with cofactor supply design: assemble route D including a ferredoxin/ferredoxin-NADP+ reductase module to feed NADPH to ADO.
ddr_annotation.trigger_observation: Route D was the in silico-designed alternative using pyruvate/MVA as precursor; ADO requires reducing equivalents, motivating fdx/fnr coexpression.
ddr_annotation.evidence_grading_rationale: Negative in vivo GC result is a direct measurement; the design rationale for fdx/fnr is stated in text.
ddr_annotation.reason_nature_rationale: The fdx/fnr module follows an explicit mechanistic requirement (NADPH supply for the ADO-catalyzed reaction); the overall route choice, however, relied partly on predictive MDF analysis.

experiments.purpose: Improve CAR activity on alpha,beta-DHIV and MVA (and GDHt/ADO activities) to rescue routes C and D
experiments.host: in vitro (purified CAR mutants) and E. coli route-D strains
experiments.intervention: computational saturation mutagenesis/virtual screening and structure-guided rational design of CAR (binding pocket and adjacent loop residues); rational protein design of GDHt and ADO (Figures S4, S5)
experiments.conditions: in vitro CAR activity assay on MVA; mutants introduced into route D in place of wild-type CAR
experiments.readout: relative CAR activity on MVA; in vivo IPDO
experiments.analysis: enzyme assay; GC
experiments.outcome: Most CAR mutants showed increased activity on MVA; best mutant N227A reached 2.28-fold of wild type in vitro; no CAR, GDHt or ADO mutant enabled IPDO production in vivo
experiments.decision_type_rationale: Q1: deliberate enzyme engineering. Q2: performed here. Q3: mutants were deployed into route D strains, a new design iteration (which nonetheless failed in vivo).

ddr_annotation.design_action_rationale: Rate-limiting enzyme engineering: structure-guided mutation of CAR binding-pocket and loop residues to improve activity on non-native substrates MVA and alpha,beta-DHIV.
ddr_annotation.trigger_observation: CAR showed poor catalytic activity on alpha,beta-DHIV (0.093 umol/min/mg) and MVA relative to its native substrate BA, identified as a key reason for routes C/D failure; CAR's known substrate-preference rule (second functional group at least three carbons from carboxylate) explains the poor fit.
ddr_annotation.evidence_grading_rationale: In vitro mutant activities were measured (Figure 4b; N227A 2.28-fold); the preceding virtual screening is predictive (soft) but was confirmed by in vitro assays. In vivo rescue failed.
ddr_annotation.reason_nature_rationale: Mutagenesis targeted the binding pocket and adjacent loop based on the CAR crystal structure, an explicit structure-mechanism-guided rationale.
ddr_annotation.generalizable_rule: When CAR shows poor activity on a non-native carboxylic acid substrate, apply structure-guided saturation mutagenesis of binding-pocket and adjacent loop residues, because these positions shape substrate accommodation; validated only in vitro for MVA (N227A, 2.28-fold) and did not rescue in vivo IPDO production, so transfer to in vivo pathway contexts is unproven.

objective.value: Design, evaluate (in silico) and implement novel non-natural biosynthetic routes for isopentyldiol (IPDO) production in Escherichia coli; compare a RetroPath RL-computationally designed route (route B) with the previously published route A and two intuitively designed routes (C from alpha,beta-DHIV; D from mevalonate) regarding theoretical yield, thermodynamics (MDF), energy cost, number of non-native steps and enzyme/intermediate penalties, and test their in vivo IPDO production.

hypothesis.value: A priori in silico evaluation (FBA theoretical yield + MDF thermodynamic driving force + energy cost + enzyme/intermediate penalties) can predict the relative feasibility of alternative non-natural IPDO pathways; the route with the most favorable profile (route B) is more likely to function in vivo than intuitively designed routes C and D.
hypothesis.notes: The paper does not state an explicit hypothesis sentence; this is reconstructed from the stated purpose of comparing in silico predictions with implementation results.

inference.rationale: Abstract, Introduction final paragraph and Results 2.1/4 jointly state that the study tests whether in silico criteria (FBA, MDF) predict pathway implementability; no single sentence declares a formal hypothesis.
